PARABLES. Earth sings her parables of loss and gain In boldest speech, Yet heights sublime which spirits shall attain She cannot reach. Aerial whispers float o'er land and sea, "It cloth not yet appear what we shall be." f: Her royal purples and her crowns of gold, . Her white attire, The sceptred lilies which her summers hold, With flames afire,— 'All fail to show the glory we shall see,— "It cloth not yet appear what we shall be." Who from unsightly bulb or slender root Could guess aright The glory of the flower, the fern, the fruit. In summer's heights? Through tremulous shadows voices call tame, "It cloth not yet appear what we shall be." Triumphant guesses from the seer and.sage Through shadows dart, And tender meanings on the poet's page Console the heart. - 0 songs prophetic! though so sweet are ye, "It doth not yet appear what we shall be." «—eara Thwaites in Sunday Magazine for June.

I'm just as unhappy, unhappy, As ever a kitten can be; If you'll let me, I'll tell you about it, Then perhaps you will pity me. For it's a great mistake in your thinking That kits have no feeling at all. Nor a thought beyond having a frolic, Or the chasing aftera sow, how could I know (please tell me If you could help me to see) That the cold roast fowl in the pantry Was not put there for me? ▪ They left the door temptingly open, So I helped myself to that, r: But they drove me out with the broomstick, And called me "that mean thieving cat !" ;"--7 Then those pans of milk in the dairy, • With cream like the yellow-est gold, I thought I should like to taste it, For it's very delicious, Pin told; 1▪ 4- So I climbed to one of the nicest, And was just getting ready to taste, • When they found me—and such a commotion, • I ran to the barn in hotshaste. [24 Don't they think cats ever get hungry Between meals, I'd like to know? - And that rats and mice cannot always be found? I have sat for an hour or so P: Beside some nice-looking rat-hole, • And not even a mouse came to view; And I found, after waitinc, and waiting, ▪ They had moved off to lodgings anew. ..7.; I heard the folks talking this morning About kit, and a bag, and the pond, I didn't quite understand it, fit For of water I'm not very fond. Ef,. -I don't dare to go near the kitchen, For fear they meant harm by that; Oh dear! all in all, I've concluded, r- It's a very hard world—for a cat. --Leols Mercury Supplement.l

"Ali," yawned a All bachelor, "this world is but a gloomy prison." "To those in solitary confinement," added a witty young lady. "If all the world were blind," said an Irishmaniwhe had just been insNcting a school for the blind," what a melancholy sight it would be !" THE TUNIC AND THE SMOCKFROCE.—Among the gar- ments worn by the Anglo-Saxons was the tunic, bearing a good deal of resemblance to the ancient Roman tunic. The aperture at the top was sometimes only large enough to admit the head, but was in other instances enlarged so as to be open in front. It was also, in 'many cases, open from the hips downward on either side, so as to give full liberty to the limbs. It rarely descended below the knee. On persons of superior quality the tunic was bordered at the edges with embroidery and coloured weaving. This short tunic was a garment worn by all classes, from the slave to the monarch; and Strutt Offers a suggestion that the garments so commonly worn by the rustics in all parts of England in latter times, under the denomination of a " smockfrock," tho collars and I,vristbands of which are often fancifully worked, is a descendant of the Anglo-Saxon tunic, with no greater change than might naturally be looked for in the differ- ence of period. How PETER POPPED THE Qm3sTioN.—Me and Sal got along middlin' well for same time, but things was gettin' on no furrer ler' so I made up my mind to fetch 'em to a ned, for I luvd her harder and harder every day. But how to do the thing! I got some luv books, red how fel- lers got down on their marrow-bones, and talked like parsons, and how the girls would gently fall into the fel- ler's arms. But somehow that way didn't suit my no- tion. I asked marm how dad courted her, but she said it had been so long since that she's forgot all about it. (Unkle Joe allers says marm done all the courtin'.) At last I made up my mind to try it anyhow, for I couldn't stand it no longer. So I goes over to her daddy's house, and when I got there I sot like a fool thinkin' how I should begin. Sal she saw somethin' was troublin' me, and sed she " aint you sick, Peter?" "Yes—well, no," sea I; that is, I aint exactly well. I thought I'd come over to-night," sea I, and there I stuck. " Sal, ' sea I startin' at it again. "Yes," sea she. "Sal," sea I again and stuck once more, the perspiration comin' out all over me. "Peter," says she, "there's somethin' a troublin' you, I know, and it's mighty wrong for you to keep it from a body, for an innerd grief, Peter, is a consumin' fire." Then I !ooks at her. "Sal," says I, getting des- perate, " does you luv anybody?" 'Well," sea she, "1 luvs dad and marm, and—let me see." see she; "yes, there's old Pyde,',--that was a cow of hern. "I can't think just right off," sea she, of anybody else just now." This was orful for a feller dead in love, so after a while I tries another shute. "Sal," sea I, wipin' my brow with my pocket handkerchief, "I'm powerful lonesome to hum, and I sometimes think if I'd only a pretty wife," sea I, "I'd be a tremenjous feller." Well, with that what does she do but begins and names over all the gals with- in five miles of thar, and never wunst 'come a-nigh namin' of herself, and sed I ort to get one of them. That sorter got my dander up, and so I hitched my cheer close to hem, and shet my eves, and stedies myself, and sez I desperate, "Sal." sea I, "you're' the very gal I've been hankerin' after for a long time, and, if you say so, we'll be joined in the happy bonds of matrimony, e plu- ribus unum, world without end!" sea LP -And I felt like I'd throw'd up an allygatur, I felt so relieved. Sal she fetched a sorter scream, and, after a while, she sea,' sea she. "Peter?" "Well, Sal," sea I, "which is it to be?'" "Well, ves," sea she. "Glory, glory!" sea I, with a shout; and with that I kissed her—and such a kiss 1 0 Jehosifat! Talk about yer sugarcandy !--talk about yer molasses! yer blackberry jam! They couldn't come ten miles nigh to it.—From "Popping the Question"' by the Rev; David Macrae. _ _ .

OLD FLEET MARRTAGES.—It is stated that the Fleet- street marriages .1 London originated with the incum- bents of Trinity, Minories, and St. James's, Duke-place. The incumbents claimed to be exempt from the jurisdic- tion of the Bishop of London, and performed the mar- riages without banns or license. It is not exactly known in what year these gentlemen started their lucrative profession; but one named Elliot, who was rector of St. James's, was suspended by the Bishop of London in 1616' for performing these ceremonies. The trade was then taken up by clerical prisoners living within the Rules of the Fleet; and Mr. Burn tells us that, as a rule, these were just the men—having neither money, character, nor liberty to lose—to adopt the profession; and he further says that they were in the main" lusty, jolly fel- lows, but thorough rogues and vagabonds, guilty of various offences." That they were not ashamed of the business is evident from the Tact that they advertised in the Daily Advertiser of that year to the following- effect : "G. R.—At the true chapel, at the Old Red Hand and Mitre, three doors up Fleet-lane, and next door to the White swan, marriages are performed by authority by the Rev. Mr. Sympson, educated at the University of Cambridge, and late chaplain to the Earl of Rothes.-N.B. Without imposition." "J. Lilley, at the Hand and Pen, next door to the China Shop, Fleet Bridge, London, will be performed the solemnisation of marriages by a gentle- man regularly bred at one of our universities and law- fully ordained according to the institutions of the Church of England, and is ready to wait on any person in town or country." There must have been great competition in the business, for we are told that there might be seen in corners of windows tickets stating, "Weddings per- formed cheap here," "The Old and True Register," Sce. The parson, and landlord—the latter usually acting as clerk—divided the fees between them, after paying a shilling to the tout who brought in the customers. The Grub-street Journal of January, 1735, has the following : "There are a set of drunken, swearing parsons, with their myrmidons, who wear black coats and pretend to be clerks alid registers of the Fleet, and who ply about Lud- gate Hill, pulling and forcing people to some peddling alehouse or brandy shop to be married; even on a Sun- day stopping them as they are going to church and almost terrine, their clothes off their backs." This is confirmed by Pennant, who says :—" In walking along the streets in my youth, on the side next *the prison, I have often been tempted by the question, 'Sir, will you be pleased to walk in and be married?' The parson was seen to be walking before his shop, a squalid, profligate figure, clad in a tattered plaid nightgown, with a fiery face, and ready to couple you for a dram of gin or roll of tobacco." That the parsons did not always get the best of it may be supposed from the following extract from the register of the Fleet Marriages :—" 170. Geo. Grant and Ann Gordon, bachelor and spinster, stole my clothes brush." "Married at a barber's shop next Wil- son's—namely, one Karrifs, for half a guinea; after which it was extorted out of my pocket, and for fear of my life delivered." We are told that all sorts and:condi- tions of men flocked to the Fleet to be married in haste —from the barber to the officer in the Guards, from the parson to the peer. The Bishop of London attempted little ptleidt to put a stop to these marriages in 1702, but with very effect; and it was not until 1754 that anActotfhPaatrltihea- ment was passed to prevent them. It is stated day before the Act was to come into force (March 24), there were no fewer than 217 marriages recorded in one register book, and these were the last of the Fleet wed- dings. A collection of the registers of Fleet Marriages was made in 1821, and was purchased by the Govern- ment; they weighed over a ton.—Chambers s Journal. Te a fond mother, whose children were at the time I making themselves disagreeable, a gentleman observed : "I have a decided preference for bad children, madam." "How strange—and, pray, for what reason ? " said she. "Because they are always sent out of the room." "Ma, haven't I been a real good boy since I've been going to Sunday school ?" "Yes, my lamb," answered the maternal parent fondly. "And you trust me now, don't you, ma ?" "Yes, darling, yes." "Then." spoke up the little innocent, "what makes you keep the pre- serves locked up in the pantry the same as ever ?" A widow married a young man and her daughter married his father. By the widow's marriage with the son he became her husband's grandmother, consequently great-grandmother to a son, the issue of this marriage. Now, as the son of a great-grandmother must be a great- grandfather or great grand-uncle, this boy must be his own grandfather. It is the specialist, the man who can do some one thing, however small, though it may be only to make bread or button-hooks, better than anyone else, who now a-days is secure of his living. And it is the man who sticks to his own trade, who imitates and courts nobody, who lives simply and sincerely according to his own conscience, convictions, and taste, who is secure of his Social position. Dr. Jasper Main, who lived in the reign of James I. of England, was celebrated as a scholar and a wit. He dis- played through life a strong propensity for innocent raillery and practical jokes. Just before he expired, he told his servant, who was sadly addicted to intemper- ance, that he had left him something that would make him drink. The servant, as soon as his master was dead, impatiently opened the legacy, expeatinee of course, to find a heap of treasure; but, alas! his disappointment was great in finding nothing but a red herring-. The atraostphere of a household has everything to do -with the developement of its inmates, and one can hardly expect to find soft-mannered, delicately, sensitive young people brought up under the influence of irascible or bickening or choleric parents. For their sakes, disputa- tions and irritable people should master themselves, lest the evil crop of seed sown in moments of unreason ' should rise, like the fabled dragon's teeth, in the harvest . of armed men whom no restraints may be strong 'enough to repress. There was an amateur theatrical performance a few nights ago, in a fashionable mansion avenue. Gus de Smith was engaged to play the ghost in "Hamlet." "Now, Gus," said the manager, "-all in the world you have to do is to come in and say, I am thy father's ghost,' and you must do it in a deep, sonorous voice." Gus said he wanted some hard part where he might have a chance of spreading himself, but finally agreed to do as he was told. When the ghost's turn came, he somewhat spoiled the tragic effect of the whole performance by saying, " I am thy father's ghost, and you must do it in a deep, sonororas voice." A story of 'Miss Mary Anderson comes feom America While she as rehearsing the part of Juliet an eminent physician, ,an intimate friend, was present. The perfor- mance .lighted him till towards the conclusion of the wi)laj• W nen his countenance wore a troubled expression. it was over he went up to the actress. "My dear L4,"117. ig lady," he said, "you are wrong in one of your cts.you Don't know that a corpse doesn't stiffen for at least six hours after death ?" "My dear doctor," re- f j sponded Mary, slowly, speaking in deep rich tones, and adopting a strong American twang, "do you think I'm goin to keep my audience waiting for six hours while I stiffen ?" One day when Colman and his son were walking from Soho-square to the Haymarket, two whitlings, Miles Peter Andrews and William Augustus Miles, were coming the contrary way, on the opposite side of the street. They had each sent a dramatic manuscript for the Sum- mer Theatre, and being anxious to get the start of each other in the production of their several works, they both called out "Remember, Colman, I am first oar." "Humph," muttered the manager, as they passed on, "they may talk about first oars, but they have not a scull between them." This reminds one of the witticism of Douglas Jerrold. Two conceited young authors were boasting that they rowed in the same boat with a celebrated wit of the day. " Ah," replied Jerrold, "but not with the same sculls. The contemplation of beauty and sublimity in nature and in heart, or of high and noble character in history, the influence of fine poetry upon the imagination, the wonders of telescope and microscope—everything, in fact, that tends to enlarge the soul and expand the faculties, and lead to thoughts of the infinite beyond, has a direct bearing upon the spirit of morality. It has been said that "an undevote astronomer is mad," and it is equally true that an enthusiastic lover of truth, or beauty, or purity, or sublimity in any of the phases, who is a vicious- or immortal man, must also be mad. It is to snch possitive inspiration and such actual de- velopement of impulses, now too often slumbering within men's breasts' that we must chiefly look for an enlarged and purified morality. "We have often been amused, and no doubt our readers have also, with a mighty fuss about nothing; or, as some one expresses it, an ocean into a tempest test to waft a feather or to drown a fly. But the best story of this kind is one that has been sent to us of a lady, while engaged in the pursuit of her domestic duties, who encountered a mouse in the flour barrel. Now, most ladies, under similar circumstances, would have uttered a few feminine shrieks and then sought refuge in the garret. But this one possessed more than the ordinary degree of feminine courage. She summoned the hire-cl man, and told him to get the shot-gun, call the bull-dog, and station himself at a convenient distance. Then she climbed half-way upstairs, and began to punch the flour- barrel vigorously with a pole. Presently the mouse made its appearance, and started across the floor. The man fired, and the dog dropped dead; the lady fainted, and fell downstairs; and the hired man, thinking that she was killed, and fearing that he would be arrested for murder, disappeared, and has not been seen since. The mouse escaped. EPPS'S COCOA. GRATEVITI. THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY. NOVEMBER 139 1886 NOTES ON AGRICULTURE ORTI- THE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY. Zit ITLTUR.I3. SOME AMERICAN BREEDS OF POULTRY. JAVAS. To America we owe several of the best of our varieties of domestic poultry, and there has recently come from the United States yet one more than we have already possessed, namely, the Javas, some of which have been exhibited at one or two of our shows. As it is quite possible that the Javas may become popular, we may be permitted to give a description of them. First, however, it may be well to say what is their origin, and on this point there is considerable difference of opinion. There are those who state that the Java is a perfectly pure breed, imported from Asia, but this contention does not appear to be supported by the evidence, and it is pro- bable that this variety is the result of some intentional or unintentional cross, which has been perpetuated. The black Java is by no means a new breed in America, for it has been bred there for upwards of twenty years, but strange to say it has only been brought over here during the last few months. It is supposed to have been one of the breeds used in tho formation of the Plymouth Rock, and thus it seems as if the child had taken the place of the parent. If it had been the means of pro- ducing the Plymouth Rock, and then have died, it would have done a work deserving of recognition. The following notes on the Black Java, which appeared in the Poultry Monthly some time ago, are from the pen of Mr. J. Y. Bicknell, of New York, tell all that is known about the origin of the variety. Mr. Bicknell says : The chain of facts relating to their origin, although traceable for the space of over thirty years is not com- plete, one end is lost. After utilising every available resource, we fail to exhume the missing links, yet cir- cumstances lead us to believe that they are of American origin. The first known record of their existence comes from Missouri, where, more than a quarter of a century ago, a noted physician bred them, but even his name, and whether he still survives are unknown to us. Here our history begins. Beyond this searching is vain. The doctor was unwilling to share his stock with his neigh- bours, refusing to part with it. But a way was pro- vided. Javas did not belong to the class of flowers that were "born to blush unseen." They were destined to make a record. The gateway was opened and they went forth to "multiply and replenish the earth." The doc- tor's coachman disposed of enough eggs to plant the seed. From this very source all modern Javas have descended. From a pair or trio to build upon, they in- creased in numbers, some of which found their way into New York State about twenty years since, after which all trace of them in Missouri is lost. All true Javas of the present day, all standard Javas, wherever they may be found, descended from that win, of the original stock that was brought into New York. The progeny was divided among neighbours, some of whom retained it in purity, while others crossed it with other fowls, and soon lost sight of it. There is not a breeder of Javas now living, unless in obscurity, who has any right to the claim of their origin, Not one of the known Java breeders had anything to do, directly or indirectly, with their origin. The above-named facts are all that we possess throwing light on their genealogy, and here the case must rest. In shape the Black Javas are something like the Ply- mouth Rock, but have less of the Cochin type. They are said to be better layers, but of this we are unable to speak from personal werience. They do not look quite so big, but this is more from the closer feathering of the Java. They are good on the table, and in America are said to be well liked as market fowls. In plumage the Black Javas is of a brilliant metallic black, with black beaks, and almost black legs. The eyes are brown and mild, the comb red, single, and evenly serrated, while the wattles and lobes are red. The tail of the cock is ornamented with long and graceful sickle feathers; the breast is deep and full, the body broad, long, and deep, giving the bird a compact appearance. The thighs are strong and covered with soft fluff, and the bottoms of the feet are yellow, the shanks being clean, without feathering, and, although black, approach willow as age comes on. The weight of the cock is about ten pounds, and the hen eight pounds ; cockerele weigh eight pounds, and pullets about six and a half pounds. There is an evident relationship between the Cochin, the Langshan. and the Black Java, and it may be well, therefore, to indicate the differences between the three. We do not mean that we think they are all the same, but that there is some relationship between them. The Cochins and Langshans have feathers on their legs, the former profuse, the latter scanty, while the legs of the Javas are clean. The Lan,shan has pink between the toes, the bottoms of the feet being whitish flesh colour, while the bottoms of the feet of the Javas are Yellow. Both the Langshans and the Javas have beautifu/ flowing sickle feathers, while the tail of the Cochin is full but not flowing. The colour of these three birds is very similar, and they make capital crosses with each other. i There s another variety of the Java fowl known as the Mottled Javas. These only differ from the blacks in that their plumage is black and white intermixed. In all other respects they are identically the same. DOMINIQUES. There is an old American breed called the Dominique, of which a few have been imported into this country, but they have never become popular. They are said to have been taken over to America by the early Puritans. but what evidence there is in support of this statement we have not been able to learn. A recent American writer says that they are the oldest of the distinctive American breeds, being mentioned in the earliest poultry books as ' an indigenous and valued variety. They weigh front six to eight pounde when fully matured. They are excellent layers, very hardy, unexceptional as mothers, and are good for the table. They grow both fat and feathers quickly, while their plain " home-spun " suits make them very suitable for countless localities where larger and more valuable looking fowls would be liable to be stolen. The merits of this breed will recommend it to persons residinc, in the coant7y as well worthy of promotion in the poultry yard,. whether as producers of eggs or meat, as sitters or nurses. The colour of the plumage may be described as a light or steel grey ground, with each feather distinctlystriped or barred across with a darker or bluish grey, the bars; &lading off gradually from dark into light. The cock is a very showy bird; with full saddle and hackle, and abun- dant, well-curved feathers. The comb should be a neat rose, with face, wattles, and ear lobes red; wattles- neat., well rounded, and of medium size ; legs bright yellow. There are some other breeds of American fowls, two of which are called Danvers Whites and Jersey Blues, but, as these have not attained any degree of popularity;it is not necessary that they should be described. SEM‘ONABLE HINTS. In, many places the trees are entirely denuded' of leaves, which are thiekry scattered on the ground. These leaves- may be put to a good use by poultry keepers. They should be gathered and stored in some barn or store-- house; where they can be thoroughly dried. Kept in this way for a few weeks they will be very useful when the severe weather comes, in the way of providing the fowls with-employment. Their use is by covering the.flbor of the poultry-house or shed with them, as this gives the birds- plenty of employment in scratching to find corn buriedbelow. After-being used in this way they should. agairebe stored, when they will be found splendid for manurial purposes.

MILCII Cows ON PASTURES.—" Anxious Farmer" says: —" We have been grazing our Home Park with dairy cows for two years. All the milk has been sold to go to London. The cows have had no artificial ff)od of any description; the grass is of good quality, and much of it in a favourable season. Would some of your scientific subscribers be good enough to inform me whether the grass will deteriorate and be of poor feeding qualities if we continue to graze year by year without artificial food? A detailed account of this would be gladly accepted by an ANXIOUS FARMER." Generally the answer must be that you are making constant draughts upon your fertility in the soil, which, not being an unlimited quantity, must ultimately be exhausted unless artificially replenished. You will probably find bone-dust in some form to be the most efficient dressing. Phosphates in some form will ultimately under such treatment be the body in minima, whose quantity therefore determines the productiveness of the land; and additions of this will tell most imme- diately on the growth of your grass and clover. THE ACTION OF RENT ON FARMING.—III the course of an address recently, at Lancaster, Mr. Rigby said: All men are ready to say it never was more difficult to make farming pay than it is just now. Both landlords and tenants are agreed in this—the former by making allow- ances or reductions of rent in many cases, and the latter by urging its necessity as one of the things essential to success, and it is an undoubted fact that rent and success have relative terms. When the seasons are adverse, when epidemics prevail, or when importations of farm produce come in quantity and low price, it is clear that as much success cannot be realised as when the seasons are fairer or the attending circumstances are more favourable. The claim for reduction of rents and against payment of tithe is an expression of this feeling. It may be that it lays too much of the charge of non- i success on excessive rent. Still, lam bound to say that I one of the things on which successful farming depends ! . ! is rent proportion to value and to the use the farm may be made of. My proposition that one of the conditions lof successful farming is a fair rent will be gener- ally allowed. Perhaps it is as unnecessary to add that a low rent, as opposite to a high rent,*or to a fair rent, is not a guarantee of success. A low rent which a tenant thinks he can easily make is a snare. Easy-going habits have brought their usual attendants. No striving, no effort has had to be made; drifting has ensued, and ended where drifting always does. Ido not plead for low rents, but for rents that can be made by industry and fair effort ; nor for uniform rents,'7or uniform reduction all round. Situation, aspect of lands, soil,"buildings, capability, in fact, should be the rule— not capability of the tenant, but of the holding. I am , afraid many tenants measure their farm's capacity by their own skill and management. It would be impos- sible to some men to make any farm pay; it is difficult just now for any man to do it. It is not an unfriendly suggestion, however, which says to every tenant, "Be frequently asking, it lor the farm that is at fault ?' " It will at least stimulate inquiry, and that in turn will lead to knowledge, and knowledge to conviction of 'what is best to be done. AGRICULTURAL NOTES.—A correspondent writes to A contemporary :—" Since I last wrote, fair weather with some little sunshine during the day has been generally followed by more or less rain at night, leaving the land much in the same condition as it was in at the beginning of the week. In most parts of our district the plough- man is hard at work, and everywhere farmers are busy lifting their potatoes. The results are very various. IThough the quantity of tubers seems to be large every- where, in many places disease is showing itself, and it is feared we shall have some bad keepers this winter. Owing to the absence of severe frost the trees still pre- sent a wonderful show of leaves, which, turning as they are to every shade of brown, orange, red, and green, give to the landscape a richness and beauty seldom seen so late as November in this part of England. There have bean this year an unusual number of croakers forecasting a severe winter. Do they remember the year Inkermann was fought? The driving snow came down that Sunday the sth of November, in a way few who saw it will for- get; and since then we have had one autumn three days' skating in October on the Dunham Park ponds. As we have got so far with mild weather, we may hope our winter is not to be such a very long and bad one after all. Sheep, both fat and lean, still continue to improve in price; and, with wool firm at the advance sheep farmers are having a better time than for many years past. One of the most characteristic birds of this district is the common starling, and I have been very much struck by their increase of late years. One seems to see them everywhere, either flying about in small par- ties or in large flocks, more often than not associating themselves with rooks. When these birds and rooks are feeding in company the starlings always keep together. No satisfactory reason for this, so far as I am aware, has ever been given. In autumn, when the young are reared, the habits of the starling are most interesting, and the size of the flocks is sometimes almost beyond belief. In the daytime they may be seenofeeding on the fields, and keeping up an almost incessant babel of sounds. Their evolutions in the air are most wonderful at nightfall before they settle to rest. It is astonishing with what regularity they wheel and gyrate in the air, as though moved by one common impulse. There is a certain regularity of movement peculiar to gregarious birds. Every evening at sunset the starlings may be seen at their accustomed roosting places, perched on the topmost branches, and blackening the trees with their numbers. When alarmed, the starlings, as if obeying orders, fly off in a compact mass, and if the danger soon passes they will wheel and return again in the greatest order. LANCASEHRH Crfrassa.—A writer in the Agricultural Gazette says :—" An Old Yeoman" writes—lf I remem- ber rightly, good ofd' Ben Franklyn said, "A word to the wise is sufficient." Mr. Rigby asks, "Is all our butter and cheese as good as it can b. made?" Of course the answer is "No," or else why this wide difference in the prices? He then goer on to say," A good judge observed to him recently, There is no better quality of cheese anywhere than the beat Lancashire—it is rich, pure flavoured, and will continue to improve to the last.'" This, of course, only applies to a portion of them, where properly made and well managed. I may say that I have had quite a little experience in most kinds of cheese, and will say that I have never tasted, or tried, any cheese to come up to a first-class. Lancashire. My humble opinion is that it arises mainly on account of the peculiarities of the land on which the cattle feed. I could adduce some peculiar observations if time and space allowed, and assure my readers that I am not "talking off the stick end." I say there is a vein of land extending from the Ribble into Westmoreland, bounded by the Yorkshire hills on the' east, and west by the am, that is calculated to make cheese' to compete with the world, if conducted upon proper scientific prin- ciples. The example is being set at Chester ;we want a like sort of Technical School here. After a little while they might be coming from Chester to look at our manipulation of the curd. I: would here observe that what the public demand is mild cheese, not developed ripe old cheese, as our forefathers used; we have to cater to modern tastes and not to that of our forefathers, although individually I prefer for my own eating a developed one; but my individual taste is not that of the multitude of consumers. There is one pecu- liarity about a Lancashire cheese, if properly made at the beginning. Whatever stage of development, it always suits someone—it is always a pleasant cheese for some palates; whereas, I have often tried real fine Cheshire cheese when over-devetopecrthey have assumed a tallowy flavour which is most objectionable, although the cheese may be good in every respect only for the development of this most obnoxious flavour; it then becomes real prime good meat wasted—none of its good qualities will redeem, a tallowy flavour. And American cheese, when it does get over-ripe or strong, it is strong, and no mistake; they smell and taste as "ram as an old fox," and can be "scented afar off," whereas, when a Lancashire cheese gets strong it always suits some, hence the advantage. If the Lancashire business: was pro- perly taken in hand on system, the demand for these goods would grow enormously; then, instead of having three fairs in a year, there would be more cheese pitched every month than there ever has been since October cheese fair was inaugurated at time-honoured Lancaster. We should then have the buyers from Lancaster town ex- tending their journeys more South, like the Scotchmen, where there is ample profit and good ground to work on. We want some energy and life. I quite think that fifty times the quantity would be made if we were once fairly launched on the royal road of system and method; and don't forget that the cheese would be used ere long in the Royal household. Your cheese are not known in the great Markets of London, Birmingham, Manchester, or Liverpool, except possibly in an individual sort of way. Lancashire cheese wants a little free trade applying to its tail (at any rate south of the Wyre). Once fairly on the highway of system, we should soon have other markets to send the cheese to. If we apply system and method in the manufacture we shall most certainly suit those :who "want a bit of rale good cheese" at a good price. We must get out of the rut of how it was, and study how it is, and cater to it. You see the first lessons at Chester have improved the prices round that district ss. to 10s., when the improvement is only in its infancy.

One of the best stories connected with the Bulgarian business is told of a mechanic's wife, who had brought her husband's dinner to a house adjoining his workshop, and while waiting for her lord and master to appear, solaced herself with the evening paper. Presently the hungry man entered the compartment, and proceeded to demolish his repast. "I say, Jack," observed the-wife, still perusing the newspaper," I see that the poor young kidnapped Prince- is goin' back to Sophia." "Yes (mouth full); T wish you'd put more seasoning-with the pork." (Pause.) "Ah, its hard, Jack, for a man to be tore away from his wife by a lot of scamps." " Wife ! Sophia's not his wife "Not his wife! Then the Czar done quite right!" Several years ago, in'a well-known wholesale house in New York, an old bachelor bookkeeper, who had been years- with the firm, suddenly announced that he,was to be married. The partners gave him a week's holiday, and his fellow-clerks raised a little purse and presented it to pay the expenses of his wedding trip. A couple of days after the wedding one of the members of the firm went down to Newport, and there lounging about the Ocean House, and apparently enjoying himself immensely, he saw his recently Married old bookkeeper, but alone. "Where's your wife?" "She's at home." "But I thought you had money given you for a wedding trip?" "Sol had, but I did'nt understand that it was intended to include her."

Fruit trees may be improved by cutting a trench round each tree a few feet distant, from the stem accord- ing to the size of the tree, and the depth must be regu- lated by that of the subsoil, which in this ea* is best left undisturbed. Assuming that there is the 'filotlerate depth of 18 inches of fairly good soil, six or eight inches of the best of it may be put back in the trench, and the remaining space should be filled with fresh soil, with a little manure added to it. But if the first is not avail- able, mix manure with the best soil in the garden, and tread in firmly; but first of all cut all the roots, even fibres, close to the ball of earth, or the consequence will be that in pressing the soil the points of the roots will be directed downwards, and would most likely continue that course until they come to the subsoil. ic few years ago several very large apple trees, chiefly Livesey's, were served in this way by cutting out celery trenches on each side of the row of trees, but just clear of .the branches, lest drip should interfere with the growth and success of the celery. By the time the earthing up of the celery was completed, there was a trench 3ft. nearer the trees pght down to the subsoil, and numbers of roots of various thickness had to be cut. In that way celery was planted three successive years, but the trenches were made a foot or so further from the trees each time, and now the roots revel in the sweet, rich soil that usually results from Celery culture. The space between the trenches and underneath the trees was covered over with the content 4 of an old hot-bed, and neither spade nor fork has desecrated that sacred spot for the roots. The covering had very- little fertilising virtue in it, and was really applied to smother the weeds and facilitate the operation of hoeing those that might come hereafter. It is only waste of time and money to plant crops of vegetables that will be overhung by the branches of trees and the irreparable injury that is in- flicted on the roots of the latter in the process of prepar- ing the ground is something serious. Under the trees in question Lily of the Valley was planted for trial, but only- a single row, in a line with the stems of the trees, and it has succeeded beyond expectation. Now there is always demand for this chaste and sweet flower, and the space under the branches of our fruit trees might be far more profitably utilised than it is at present, and it is not unlikely that in certain seasons the Lily flowers would realise more than the crop on some of the trees. THE FRONT GArinEN.—The Rose is often seen under such conditions in front gardens as to give ample evi- dence of want of care and attention, and that the owner has no anxiety for its requirements. Some no doubt fear to meddle with the roots of their Roses. and yet it is at the root we must comritence if we make any sub- stantial improvement, but so long as the plants continue a lingering existence no attempt is made to improve them. Our experience is that the Rose is not ono of those plants that readily succumb when its roots are dis- turbed, providing the proper season is selected for the operation. Few will deny that November is not the best month in the whole year for the work and plants moved early in this month will have formed nice roots before the end of the year. Old plants, if they are to he moped, might have some previous preparation if there is any extent of top, and the old soil should be cleared down to the roots, and replaced by a mixture of good soil and manure, and pack some of it round the stem up to the ground level. This will be the means of roots emitting from the stem as well as the old roots throwing out fibres. A trench might be dug round the tree at two or three feet from the stem, with the view of cutting the big roots, and cause them to form fibres near home. The above expedients are equally applicable to all plants that it may be desirable to improve without moving. Moderate sized plants should be decidedly taken up and planted in deeply-dug, well-marn!red ground, introducing as much fresh loam as possible into the immediate vicinity of the roots. Few people have recognised the value of the latter pabulum for Roses. as the Rev. C. Wood, of Preston, and it is stated that during the past few years he has ha l carted hundreds of loads for them and his fruit trees into his garden near Bamber Bridg Bridge. The cottager will be amply repaid if he can only provide each Rose tree with two or three inches under its roots as well as over them. Strong lengthy roots without fibres on them must be cut to within afoot or so of the stem to induce them to branch out and form more feeders. Intending planters of the Rose should select plants on their own roots, and plant them obliquely in order to minimise the effects of the wind on them and facilitate pegging down, and some of the larger shoots if pegged at once would be the means of steadying the plants until they got root hold. Standards ana haif standards will need staking immediately they are planted. Some contend that Roses on the brier are the best for cold, smoky districts; but there are few localities where the following sorts refuse to thrive on theirown roots. or budded on the brier :—Princess Beatrice, Pierre Notting, Duchess of Bedford, Chas. Darwin, Horace Vernet, Dupay Jamain, Chas. Lefevre, Mons. E. Y. Teas, Marie Bauman, Sir G. Wolseley, Louis Van Houtte, Harrison Weir, Fisher Holmes, and La France,with a few others that might be named.

div.head: HOGHTON TOWER AND ITS SCENERY. DESCRIBED ltt A STRAWEIBR.
div.p: HOGHTON TOWER AND ITS SCENERY. DESCRIBED ltt A STRAWEIBR.

We extract the subjoined passages from an article on " Hoghton Tower," in " Cassel's Magazine of Art" for November, written by the Thy. Professor Mandel Creighton, to accompany a series of illustrations of the Tower build- ings, after very beautiful drawings by Mr. Herbert Railton. The article commences as follows :

"The neighbourhood of the busy town of Preston, in Lancashire, does not, to those who know- the district only from the railway, suggest the search for pic- turesqueness, or for records,of the former life of England. Yet in the region between the-great commercial centres of Preston and Blackburn Hee a tract of country- which possesses all the charms of cur English landscape; and on its 'most favoured site is built an house of exceptional interest in the history of English architecture, and one which recalls, more vividly perhaps than any other in England, the characteristics of English life and society in the great turning point of our civilisation, the age of Elizabeth and James I. The- house of Hoghton Tower and its surroundings have a harmony and suggestivness of their own. The impression which they give is complete and simple. They require little effort of the imagination to fill in the picture; no modern disfigure- ments need be removed by our fancy; the additions which we are called upon to make are slight andubvious. We may sit on the garden turf and people the quiet house with the men andy women of the Seventeenth Century; there is nothing save the occasional sound of a railway whistle to disturb our reverie by reminding us of another age.

" Moreoveic Hoghton Tower makes no excessive demand upon our historical knowledge of the conditions of life in the past. It does not require us to.call up the uncomfortable grandeur of the vast establishment of a great baron. It does not call for a knowledge of the warfare of former times, for it has only slight reminis- cences of the days when an Englishman's castle was his house, rather than his house his castle. It was built to be lived in, and was fashioned to the needs of family life. It was not meant to harbour a crowd of retainers, but to be the home of an opulent country gentleman, where he dispensed comfortable hospitality to his friends and neighbours. It tells us of the quiet times- when English life was above all things a country life, when English society was pre-eminently provincial, and when Enghsh civilisation centred round the houses of its gentry, who lived among their tenants, were useful according to their capacities, and were respected according, to their deserts "It is not without reason that this district of the Tla. ley of the Darwen should thus tell thetale of England's development in the Sixteenth Century. Its folk were, on the whole, favourably situated, and their lines had fallen in comparatively pleasant places. They were far enough from the border-land of England to be free, as a rule, from the devastations of the Scots. The troubles, of the Welsh Monarchs did not greatl3r afiect them. The great estates of the Duke of Lancaster had passed to the I Crown on the accession of Henry IT., and tho smaller I , lords were not so ,overshadowed by great feudatories as those who dwelt in the more settled and bustling dis- tricts of the south. The whole neighbouchood bears signs of the early existence of comfort, which are notably absent a little farther north. The northern part of Lan- cashire has all the characteristics of the Scottish Border. It seems to have been a land where men in old days en- camped ratherthan lived, and have consequently left few traces of their presence. But as we draw nearer to the Ribble we find many farm houses, and even cot- tages, which were built in Tudor times, solid and sub- stantial. It would seem that the district was flourishing in a quiet way, and only needed a little encouragement to show clear signs of the civilization of peace. "In this favoured district of Central Lancashire, on a spur of the rendle Hills—the last high ground before the plains are reached which fringe the sea—standsHoghton Tower. Its site is such an one as the castle-builders of former times would have chosen; for the river Darwen and a tributary brook have eaten channels on two sides of the hill, while the third side slopes gently down- wards, so that the house stands on a triangular piece of ground, of which two sides are strong with natural de- fences. But, unlike the castles of older times, Hoghton Tower stands boldly on the highest ground in the neigh- bourhood. It seeks no shelter, and makes no attempt at concealment. If its natural defences were a reminis- cence of the traditions of the past, its conspicuous and inviting position was an earnest of the future. The lords of Hoghton were foremost to perceive the advent of a time of internal peace, and to express their confi- dence by the new dwelling which they chose for them- selves."

After noticing the builder of Hoghton Tower, the visit of James the First in 1617, and the events at the Tower in the Civil War, the writer refers as follows to its later condition and its recent restoration : .. . _ _ _ _

"After this [the extensions by Sir Charles de Hoghton, in the reign of' William lII.] the palmy days of Floghton Tower were ended for s9ilne time, and it was neglected by its owners. The political aspirations of the Hoghtori baronets connected them with the neighbouring town of Preston, which generally counted one of them amongst its Parliamentary representatives in the Eighteenth Century. But during this time the conditions of English life were greatly changed. The smaller gentry lived upon their estates, whde those who wished to make a

figure in society hastened to London and deserted the homes of their ancestors. In old days a landowner recognised that land-owning was an occupation, requiring care and management as much as any other pursuit. The landowners of England, from the great nobles to the smaller gentry, were thorough men of business, and might be seen in their office by any one who had a request to prefer. The buildings of Hoghton Tower shows clearly enough that the idea in the mind of those who erected them was that of providing a com- fortable abode for one who had abundant occupation at his doors. The house was intended for one engaged in the management of his estate, who was himself a practical farmer, but whose position involved the duty of hospitality "The expenses of contested elections and of a London life soon began to tell upon Hoghton Tower. [Really, however, it was the circumstance that the Hoghtons , had a comfortable mansion in a more convenient and , sheltered situation at Walton Hall, on the south bank of the Ribble, near Preston, which caused Hoghton Tower to cease to be their country residence in the last century, and to be suffered to go to decay.—EmTou.] Its spacious park, which in former times was so full of timber that a man passing through it could scarce see the sun shine at mid-day,' disappeared, and its trees were sold. The 'red deer in great plenty' no longer attracted a Royal hunter. The house itself was allowed to fall into decay, and was even let out in tenements to families of weavers, who tore down the wainscots for fire-wood. Until late years it remained an interesting ruin. The walls, it is true, remained uninjured by man's ravages, but the roofs fell in and the rooms were left desolate. Within the last twenty years Hoghton Tower again became the residence of the family which has such a long record of continuous possession. Its repair was gradually undertaken, and has been carried on with scrupulous care. There was no need of restoration, for the main fabric remained unaltered, even in the dis- position of the rooms. All that was necessary was the repair of the woodwork and the adaptation of the house to the requirements of our own day. The process is still going gradually on. Enough of the old tenantless rooms remain to show us into what neglect the house had fallen, and to enable us to appreciate the scrupulous care shown in all that has been done to restore it to its ancient dignity. In its main characteristics, Hoghton Tower remains unaltered. Inside as outside the house, there is nothing which jars with the memories of the days when James I. held high festival within its walls."
ACTION FOR FALSE IMPRISONMENT

BY A WARRINGTON CABMAN. TIGHE V. THE CHESHIRE LINES COMMITTEE AND OTHERS.—The plaintiff in this action, which was tried at Liverpool Assizes, on Tuesday, was Patrick Tighe, a cabdriN er, living at Latchford, Warrington, and he sought to recover from the Cheshire Lines Committee, and Benjamin llickson and Charles Lambert, their servants, damages for false imprison- ment and for being falsely charged with assault. The defence alleged that the plaintiff committed a breach of the peace, and was therefore arrested by the defendants to prevent its continuance, and without admitting any liability they paid £5 into court in satisfaction of the plaintiff's claim. Mr. Little (instructed by Mr. S. Yearsley) appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Hamilton (instructed by Mr. Lingard) was for the three defendants. From plaintiff's evidence it appeared that Tighe drove two gentlemen to the Central Station at Warrington last Christmas Day in order that they might catch the 10-33 p.m. train. The train was in the station on arrival there, and the gentlemen got into one of the carriages. He followed them in order to obtain his fare, and stood upon the footboard. The defendant Hickson then came up from behind, and pushed the plaintiff into the railway carriage and slammed the door upon him. He got his fare from the gentle- man, and as the train was moving out of the station he opened the door and jumped out. Hickson again came up to him and charged him with leaving the train whilst it was in motion. Plain- tiff explained .to Hickson and Lambert that he had been getting his fare, and that it was the former who shoved him into the train. He was then pushed into a room by the officials, and in re- sisting was thrown down. A police constable was brought, and he told the officials it was a case for a summons. He (plaintiff) was then taken to, the police office, where the sergeant in charge, and also Inspector Berry (who had since been drowned at Warrington), told the railway officials that it was not a case for the lockup, but for a summons. The officials, however, insisted on the plaintiff being locked up, and the police having informed them that it was upon their responsibility, they then locked plaintiff up. On the following morning he was taken before the magistrates, who dismissed the charge made against him of leaving the train while in motion. Several polico constables were called to prove) that the plaintiff was sober, and that the defendants were told when they brought him to the police office that it was a case for a summons and not the lockup. For the defence Hickson was called, and stated that he saw Tighe in the train, and on plaintiff trying to jump out of the train while in motion he caused witness to be thrown from the train on to the platform, and from there to the permanent way, just behind the train. The plaintiff also fell, and had to be picked up by Lambert, and on his being asked to go to the inspector's office he resisted and kicked them. They took him to the inspector's office; where he refused to give his name and address, and when told he would have to be locked up he answered, "All right, I will be locked up." Up to that time the plaintiff had not said a word as to why he was on the company's premises. Plain- tiff was afterwards taken to the police station, where witness asked that Tighe should be locked up, but on learning that the plaintiff had entered the train for a cab fare he and Lambert agreed to the plaintiff appearing to a summons, but the policeman on duty there then said, "I will keep him till the inspector comes, and see what he says about it" They waited about forty-minutes to see the inspector, but he did not come. Witness then alleged that the man in charge of the police station said! that he would lock the plaintiff up, as_he was the worse for drink. Two other railway officials were called to prove that through the unwarrant- able conduct of the plaintiff the defendant Hickson was thrown down and might have been killed; and, further, that Tighe became violent in the rail- way-station, and refused to give his name and ad- dress when asked to do so. After counsel on both sides had addressed the jury, his lordship, in sum- ming up, said the question the jury would have to consider was, were the defendants responsible for the plaintiff being locked up, and, if so, was £5 a suffiCient compensation ?—The jury found for the plaintiff—damages £2O, including the amount paid into) court.

LONDON: AND 'MR LORD MAYOR'S Snow..—The Lqrd Mayor's show, which took place on Tuesday, and gave rise to considerable anxiety in the Metropolis' passed off with. out any serious incident occurring. The Lord Mayor met with a warm reception in his ewn ward of Eastcbeap, but at some points he was groaned at, and at Ludgate Circus the crowd was especially rough. At the Law Charts there was a dense mass, but the people were orderly and well be- haved,. After the presentation to the Judges and the usual ceremony of swearing in, the procession was resumed west_ wards. Upon reaching Charing Cross the City magnates were received with groans and hisses from the assembled Socialists, intermingled with feeble cheering. After the Lord Mayor's procession had passed, a number of Socialists mounted the steps of the Nelson Column in Trafalgar. square, though none of the leaders put in an appearance. Some brisf speeches were made, and a resolution, proposed by Citizen Mann, of the Amalgamated Society of Engineers, was adopted calling upon the Government to provide work for the unemployed by erecting dwellings for artisans upon the sites of disused prisons, and demanding that the Gov- ernment should reduce the working day to eight hours. The police then commenced to clear the square, and several scuffles occurred; but a clearance was effected in a few minutes, and the crowd made for Hyde Park. On their way they came into collision with the Police, who used their truncheons to disperse the mob. Upon reaching the park the Socialists gathered at the Achilles Statue, where they were immediately surrounded by the police and a large force of cavalry, who did not, however, interfere with the speech-making that followed, which was ultimately pat a stop to by a heavy shower of rain. On Tuesday night it was stated that several persons received injuries during the day, and that a number of cases were treated at the hospitals..

The ladies of England are celebrated the world over for their rosy complexions and robust health. This reputation has been justly earned, for our ladies have in personal perfection certainly equalled, if not surpaesed, the women of other lands. But it has been manifest to every careful observer, and is confirmed by the report of the commissioner of vital statistics that a great increase of deaths among ladies has taken place recently. Many homes containing bloom- ing daughters, happy wives and hopeful inothers, have beeek suddenly invaded, and one or more of the number mysteriously removed. To ascertain the cause of this increase of mortality among women seems almost impossible. The habits of life, the demands of fashion, and many other similar acts undoubtedly contribute to this being an established fact. The great and valuable question must be how to avoid them, or being contracted, how can they be cured? It is doubtless true that many women have to-day the elements of the most alarming diseases without being fully aware of it. They are not as well as formerly, their strength is uncertain, and appetite variable. They have frequent depression of spirits, which they attribute to the weather, or their surroundings, when the cause is really within their own system. Possibly they may feel dull or shooting pains in various parts of the body for which:they cannot account, or a sense of weariness for which there is no reason. All these are the premonitions of disease which should be checked without delay. As an illustration of the alarming condition some ladies will permit themselves to get in, we beg to give the experiences of Mrs. Louisa Norman, of Fairview Villa, Clifton Road, Rugby, as recently related to the writer. The inter- esting lady said: "I consider the health of women one of the great- est problems of our modern life. I have been brought to this belief after a most unusual experience. Let me particularise. For years I have not known what it was to have a day's peace. I.suffered constantly from backache, headache, sleeplessness, tired-out feelings, and a soreness and pain that extended around my waist, as though a cord was drawn about it. These troubles were followed by displacements and enlarge- ment of the uterus, together with severe leucorrheea. I lost flesh until I became a mere shadow of my for- mer self, my appetite was entirely gone, and I was quite given over to despair. Medical aid was tried at various times, but no permanent good obtained. Dur- ing all these long years I simply existed. At times I was so bad that I could walk but a short distance without being out of breath. Black specks were al- most constantly before my eyes, and large dark clouds occasionally passed before them which invol- untarily caused me to put my hand to my head to brush them away. I was so weak that once while at- tending Divine serviee I fainted in church. "I had been to America some years previous to my sickness, and heard of Warner's Sams Cure so I de- termined to give it a trial. After taking a few bot- tles all my pain left me as if by magic. I took War- ner's SAFE Care during the day, and Warner's SATE ITERVINE on going to bed, as directed, to obtain sleep. The pains between my shoulders and in the small of my back left me, all the unpleasant discharges ceased, I have regained my lost -flesh, my appetite is good, and in fact, after so many years of discomfort, I am at last resstored to health, all owing to Warner's Sipe Cure, which I earnestly adviseevery woman suffering from troubles peculiar to our sex to take, as it will certainly mire them. - I shall be pleased to hear from any lady wishing to know further details respecting my case, and indeed I should esteem it a pleasure, and a duty, to write them of the benefits I have received. I have recommended the medicine to numerous friends, and all have derived great benefit." In view of statements like the above, the truth of which can be easily verified, we see no reason why the women of England should -submit to the ban of ill-health when, by proper precaution and the use of the right remedy, they can so readily reach that con- dition of health which secures hap pillage. Warner's SAFE Cure can be had of all chemists, or direct of the manufacturers. 11. H. WARNER & CO., 47, Farringdon Street, BC. London, price 4s. 6d. per bottle.

Cannes. where the Prince is staying at the present time. M. Karaveloff has resigned his post of Regent. THE REPLY OF PRINCE WALDEMAR. CANNES, THUILSDAY.—Prince Waldemar, replying to the notification made to him by t.l?e Bulgarian Regents of his election as Prince of Bulgaria, expressse his grateful sense of the honour conferred upon him by the Sobranje, and states that the decision in the matter must rest with his father, the King of Denmark. The Prince adds, however, that he may be prevented from accepting by other duties. His Royal Highness's reply is regarded as presaging his re- fusal of the Bulgarian throne. . Sy. PETERSBURG, TIILIRSDAY.—The rit:ssian Govern- ment contemplates bringing forward as its candidate for the Throne of Bulgaria, when the fitting moment arrives, the Prince of Mingrelia, a descendant of the distinguished Cau- casian race, now a subject of Russia. MR. GLADSTONE AND THE BULGARIANS. The " Daily News" says Mr. Gladstone has received a telegram from Tirnova, signed on behalf of the Bulgar- ian deputies, to which he has sent the following reply : " Hawardan Castle. Cnester, November 7, 386. "Gentlemen —I have had the honour to receive your ap- peal for a public declaration on my part in relation to Bul- garian affairs, in which you are good eneugh to notice my efforts now removed from us by the lapse of ten years. My opinions and desires concerning emancipated or autonomous provinces of the Ottoman Empire have at all times been the same. Liberties obtained for them from the Sultan I look upon as intended for their own use and benefit, and as not proper to be handed over in whole or in part to any- body else. It was, I think, a noble act on the part of the last emperor of Russia to obtain freedom, subject to certain just obligations, for Bulgaria, but if she is to fall into ser- vitude in that quarter the nobleness of the act disappears. I cling ta the hope that the present Sovereign of Russia will be faithful to traditions which earned just honour and gra- titude for his lamented predecessor. "I have never thought it my duty to raise my voice on the present occasion because I have bad, and still have, the belief that in this country there is happily no difference of opinion on the subject, and I have no good reason to doubt that the sentiment of the United Kingdom is faithfully represented in the councils of Europe by the Foreign Minister of to-day.—l have the honour to be gentlemen, your most faithful servant, W. E GLApsTolng."

TNDIA.—THE CAMPAIGN IN BURMAH. RANGOON, SATURDAY.—At a council of war held to-day. it was resolved to give Commissioners and officers in Bur- mah more power to despatch troops to points where their services may be needed. It was also decided to organise four mounted columns to scour the country between the Eyendwen and Moo rivers for the purpose et hunting down the rebel leaders and destroying their heunts. CALCUTTA, SUNDAY.—General Sir Frederick Roberts left Calcutta on Thursday morning for Rangoon. The Viceroy. replying to an address of the Lahore municipality, said that he accepted their congratulations on the annexation of Bur- mah. The difficulties now being met with there were the inevitable results of their endeavours to restore order among a people who for centuries had been a prey to anarchy. He had no doubt that within a reasonable time tranquilitY would be restored. AMERICA.—ARREST OF THE TICHBORNE CLAIM- ANT.—MURDER OF AN ENGLISH ARTIST. NEW YORK, SUNDAY NlGHT.—Arthur Orton, the Tich- borne Claimant, has once more fallen foul of the law. He has been arrested in Brooklyn on a aharge of impersonating a certain man with the object of drawing a pension. NEW Yonir, SUNDAY NIGHT. The United States re- venue steamship Manhattan has foundered in a gale off Newhaven. All on board, numbering, it is believed,2s per- sons, beiag lost. NEW Yonx, MONDAY.—Intelligence from San Jose, Cali- ferule, announces the murder of Mr. Owen Leggett, de- scribed as an English artist, from jealoußv. FRANCE.—THE NAVY.—THE OCCUPATION OF EGYPT. PARIS, SATURDAY.—The Budget Committee has expressed itself in favour of granting to -the Minister of Marine the sum of 33 million francs for 1887, in order to commence the construction of one iron clad, six large and swift armed cruisers, six light cruisers attached to the squadron, and 24 torpedo boats. Paaras, MONDAY.—The Republique Fraueaise publishes a London telegram, stating that M. Waddington had commu- nicated to Lord Salisbury the view of the French Govern- ment that England should herself fl x the date of her evacua- tion of Egypt. ALLEGED EMBEZZLEMENT OF '3,000,000 FRANCE. An Exchange Company's telegram, dated Paris, Thurs- day, says :—M. Franck, director of several flnencial papers, who was arrested on a charge of embeteeling 3.000.000 francs insecurities and money, managed to effect his escape from the officers while on his way to prison. SERIOUS INUNDATIONS IN FRANCE AND ITALY. PARIS, THURSDAY, 3 P.m.—Several bridges over tbe Durance have been swept away. At Digne that river has reached a height of six metre'. Heavy rains continue, and serious destruction of property is apprehended at several points. Railway communication between Nice and Genoa is interrupted. M. Millaud, Minister of Public Works, has left Paris to visit the flooded districts. ROME, THURSDAY.—A telegram from Genoa announces that a railway bridge near Albenaa having 'been suddenly swept away by the floods, a goods train was precipitated into the river, and five persons were killed. At Alessandria the river Bormida has overflowed its banks and .11)oded the country between that place and Marengo. The town of Como 'has been partially submerged by the waters of the lake.

The Speach from the Throne -stated that the relations between 'Belgium and all Powers were excellent. It announced, in reference to the regret- table occurrence at Charleroi and Liege, that some indi- Tiduals, convicted of rioting, would be pardoned, and im- portant reforms introduced

THE BULGARIAN CRISIS. AUSTRIA'S ATTITUDE.—THE REVOLUTIONARY PARTY THANKED.—THE BOURGAS PLOT. BUCHAREST, MONDAY.—The Czar has telegraphed to General Kau'bar& ins,ructing him to thank in bis MaiesrY'B name those of the Bulgarian people who, by their action or public speeches, have expressed full confidence towards Russia and a desire for the carrying out of the Imperial *counsels. TIRNOVA, SUNDAY NlGHT.—General ,Kaulbars, eeplYing to a note from the Bulgarian Government, asking the owers to nominate a candidate for the Bulgarian throne, says he will not communicate it to his Government, as Rus- sia had declared she would consider the decisions of the Sobranje null and void. PESTE., SUNDA.Y.—The Austrian and Hungarian Delege" tions were formally received by the Emperor of Austria to- day in the Throne Hall of the Royal Castle. His Majest'irt in his speech from the throne on the occasion, referred to the Bulgarian question as follows :—" The excellent vase tions in wtich we stand with all the great Powers, and the assurances of peaceful intentions which we receive from all the Governments, justify the hope that, notwithstanding the difficult situ ition in the East, it will be •found possible, while safe-guarding the interests of Austria-Hungary, to preserve the blessings of peace to Europe." The President of the Hungarian Delegation, in his address to the Emperor, assured his Majesty that, if the inseverable interests of the throne and the monarchy recuired it, the Hungarian nation would shrink from no sacrifice to aid the army in its heroic task. Great dissatisfaction prevails among the members of the Hungarian Delegation at the policy pursued by Count Kal- noky, which, it is believed, will be the object of violent at- tacks. In confirmation of this view it is stated that at a recent court soiree, the Emperor remarked to a member of the Delegation that that body would incur a great re- sponsibility in the decisions wnich it might adopt at its present meetirne. PHILLIPPOPOLIS, SUNDAY.—On.cial advices from Bourgas state that the revolt in that city has been quelled, and that the Prefect and Government authorities have been rein- stated in office, perfect order now prevailing. PHILLIPPOPOLIS, Sunnave—Thanks to the vigilance of the Prefect, M. Dimitroff, a plot like that at Bourgao has been discovered and defeated here. The ringleader is a Russian named Nivateki, who was abetted by the dragoman of the Russian Consulate, one Kovandjeff. In the tatter's house papers have been found which show that all was ready for an insurrection, which was to have broken out yesterday. Novitzki has fled. Kovandieff pleads his immu- nity from arrest as a consular official. BERLIN, SUNDAY NIGHT.—A collective Note, signed by all the signatory Powers of the Berlin Treaty, will shortly eye presented to Russia demanding a definite explanation of Ler policy in Bulgaria. TIRNOVA, MONDAY.—The Ziebraka, ems of the Russian warships, has arrived at Boargas from Varna with a crew 0./150 men. She carries on board 1,200 infantry and 12 cannon. VIENNA, MONDAY NlGHT—Perhaps the matter of most sigae,e'cance to-day is the fact that Count Kainoky travelled here from Pesth yeeterday expressly to confer with Sir A Paget, who started for London this afteruoon on two months' leave of absence. After his interview with the British Ambassador Count Kalnoky returned to Pest.h. ELECTION OF NEW PRINCE OF BULGARIA. TimgovA, WEDNESf;AY.—The Sebranje met at ten o'clock this moreing, when M. Radoslavoff, the Premier, proposed Prince Waldemar of Denmark as the new Prince of Bulgaria. Cheers were thereupon given by the House, which, rising in a body, elected his Royal Highness by ac- clamation as pre-arranofl• No enthusiasm was, however, manifested ley the public in the galleries, who preserved a cold. indifferent demeanour. The sitting continued after the Prince's election. Another sitting of the Sobranje will take place to-morrow in order to diecuae the resignation of M. Keraveloff. who, it is believed, will be replaced by another Regent. In order to enable the Heim to more easily accept M. Keravelofre resignation, M. Ste-nbnloff and Colonel Motkeroff will also tender theirs, but it is generally understood that they will be re-elected. The Government has telegraphed to Prince Waldemar an- noencing his election as Prince of Bulgaria, at the same time conveying their congretulatiens to his Highnese and expressing their conviction that he will accept the decision of the SAranje. TIRNOYA, Nov. 10, 11-30 aser,—M. Shifkoff, President of the Sobranie, MM. MicheiloiT, B,aikosshofl, and Greceff, and Kesim Zaade. a Turk, are the members selected to con- vey to Prince Waldemar the announcement of his election to the throne of Bulgaria. They will proceed direct to

div.head: LORD SALISBURY AT THE MANSION
div.p: LORD SALISBURY AT THE MANSION

- HOUSE. The principal members of the Cabinet were present at the Lord Mayor's banquet on Tuesday night. Lord George Hamilton, in responding for the navy, assured the company that efforts were being made to remove all defects, and promised that in addition to a powerful fleet on active service we should shortly have a very strong reserve.—The Marquia of Salisbury responded to the toast of her Majesty's Ministers, and referred to the state of public affairs end the work whiCh lies before the Ministers of the Crown He said that if he confined himself to the work immediately before them he would not be able to state any novelty, because all that could be undertaken would be that which the Ministry had pledged themselves previous- ly to undertake. As far as domestic affairs were concerned, the whole interest of home polities was ab- sorbed in the one—the Irish question—which now dis- tracted the councils of the realm. The business of the Government was to legislate on the lines of the man- date in favour of the unity of the Empire which they received from the constituencies last summer. to en- force the law, which had been too long neglected, and to enforce rights which had been trodden under foot. The state of things was better than it was before. Rights were more fully recognised; and although he would not found too sanguine hopes, he might say the relation between landlord and tenant had been solidly improved. He denied that a "dispensing power" had been exercised. It might still be neces- sary to legislate for Ireland, brit what was done should be done with as little haste as possible. The salvation of Ireland was to be found more in good government and administration of the law than in legis- lation. Turning to Egypt, he said that it had been for a long time a subject of interest wherever foreign policy had been discussed. He hoped that it might be a subject of interest for some time longer. Our stay in Egypt has been upheld by politicians of all colours, to be limited in duration, but that limit was not a limit of time, hut a limit of the work we had to de. We had bound ourselves by Pledges so distinct and so repeated that we could not retract from them not to leave that country until we left it in such a position that it would be secure from foreign oppression and that confusion would be ban- I ished from its domestic affairs. The Government had. been encouraged in that task by the assurance that the country was making a distinct advance. One of the great evils with which they had to contend was the invasion from the desert. but that apprehension was nov7 almost at an end. The finances of Egypt were more promising than ever they had been before, but the Government bad not reached a point at which they Gould say for certain that the moment had come for their task to be at an end. With regard to the Eastern Question, at the present day there was something novel in the diffieulty with which they had to deal. The Ralkan Penin- sula had occupied their attention, but it was not the Turkish Empire that was in question. The territory in question was a Christian State, inhabited by a free Population, whose troubles had engaged the feelings and sympathy of the people of this country. The speetacle of the struggle in Bulgaria had ex- cited the feelings of the people of this country in favour of the people of Bulgaria, whose Prince had been the victim of a "midnight conspiracy ;" and the languacCe of diplomatic menace which had been held towarde Bulgaria by a European State had been heard with the deepest regret and the most ear- nest reprobation. If the powers of Earope, or any considerable portion of those Powers, recognised the duty that lay upon them of vindicating the Treaty of Berlin in this contingency, he was sure the people of England would not be backward in aeknowledging their duty in the naetter. But England would not act alone unless her own honour end intoreste re- quired it. The noble Premier intimeted that his policy was bound up in that of the Austrian Empire, and that Austria was looking on without apprehen- sion. He trusted that the tranquility of Europe would not be disturbed, and that by the influence of the public opinion of Europe the infant liberties of Bulgaria would not be impaired. He further expres- sed the hope that the future moult]. be one of recover- ' lug trade and industry, and not of destructive war;
