div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 13, 1886.
and said that the only reward the Government would crave would be that of attaining the victories of peace.

WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL. ELrOTION OF MAYOR AND ALDERMEN. At noon on Tuesday the first quarterly meeting of the Warrington TOWII Council for the year ISB6- was held in the Town Hall for the purpose of elect- ing the Mayor for the ensuing year, four aldermen, and transacting other business. There were present the retiring Mayor (Alderman Harrison). Alaermen Crosfield, Webster, Holmes, Davies, Burgess, Chand- ley, Pickmere ; Councillors W. Pierpoint, Francomb, Tinsley, Barker, Brown, Wright, Jolley, Ttiylor, Greening, Sutton, Roberts, Greenall, Mackie, Broad- bent, Dakin, Bolton, Ashton, Hutchinson, J. Pier- point ; W. H. Brook (town clerk), J. L. Whittle, (deputy town clerk), C. Chorlay (borough treasurer), T. Longdin (borough surveyor), and J. H. Gornall (medical officer.) There was also a considerable nutn- ber of persons present in the space set apart for the public.

The 11i AToa, in returning thanks for his election, said he hail looked over the list of his 213 predeceasore, all of whona I he had known personally, and he rejoiced that in every ease he was able to veleenue the coming end speed the part- frig Mayer. (Heat.. hear.) He felt that the well deserved eulogies he passed upon them laid upon him the heaviest obligations. He could not as Mayor be base without being degenerate, and he therefore determined to aim as high as he could, and he claimed from them—especially they who had passed the chair—all that general and generous aid they were so able to give. (Cheers.) He felt he could far more easily be that day a successor of Richard Whittington, thrice Lord Mayor of London, and of Sir William Wal- worth, the red-handed Mayor of that ancient city, than of William Beamont, the first Mayor of Warrington. The two Lord Mayors of London be had named were dead and gone —they were but memories or myths. But their own William Beamont, who would have been there that day persanally if he could, was there in all the reality which a first-class painter would create; in all the felt though unseen spirit which a remembrance of his more than sixty years' public service almost turned into a vital force, heartily rejoicing that the municipal machine he set in motion forty years ago, still ran well, kept time and time, aud had a good reputation; nay, better, a good character in his native town. (Cheers.) He recognised further that it was no easy matter to follow Mr. Joseph Harrison, who had just vacated this chair, after filling it for three year with an ability unexcelled by any of his already long line of able predecessors. (Hear, hear.) He rejoiced to say that he knew the Town Council to be in a state of harmony, activity, and determination to go for- ward in every good work. (Hear, hear.) They had work on hand. They had rates to reduce as far as practicable, that traders might be tempted to join with them in utilising the bounties which nature and river and railway enterprise had bestowed upon them fat beyond most towns. In 1722 Warrington, Manchester, and Liverpool had 8,000, 12,000, and 15,000 inhabitants respectively. Had they the 81 MO proportion to-day they should have at least a quarter of a million ineteed of 4,5,000 inhabitants. They, he believed, had achieved greatness in sanitary and salutary matters by a slow but persevering process, with which the name of Alderman Burgess would ever be associated. (Hear, hear, and applause.) They had much money invested; large sums in their gasworks, their sewers, their cemetery, and their markets. Probably they had done rather too much for posterity. They might procure relief ia various ways, but it must not be at the expense of their gas consumers, nor by neglecting to widen our streets as opportunities al- low, nor by delaying to rouse up those lethargic sewers which had b2come practically ceeepools, nay, even sloughe of despond. Above all, they must labour to secure that in- exhaustible well of almost living water with which War- rington was now blessed—thanks to the Waterworks Com- pany. There was still an unconsnmed supply of the best and purest water at their doors equal to the wants of 80,000 inhabitants, which the inhabitants would do well to secure. He did hope they should see their 'way to come to terms with the Waterworks Company. (Hear, hear) In conclusion the Mayor referred to the coming jubilee of the Queen's reign. He need not say that Warrington boas- ted of being not only old Warrington, but loyal Warrington, an it would be both base and degenerate if it took not a place equal te its antecedents at the coming jubilee. (Hear, hear.) He intended asking the Council at a very early day what they legally could do in connection with the jubilee, and then he would convene all their leading townsmen, aye, and townswomen too, their Sunday and day school teachers—in fact all who were willing to aid in the jubilee work. Meantime might he ask the Council, if in the name of the :inhabitants of Warrington' they would accept at his hands, on the 20th of June next, a hereic size statue of her Majesty, in marble or bronze, according as they might decide, and find for it a suitable site and pedes- tal? (Cheers.) Their gifted townsman, Mr. Warrington Wood—(applause)—had been engaged upon the model for many months, and would submit it for their inspection in the Mayor's Parlour at the conclusion of that day's pro- oeedings, if they would allow him. He offered it most heartily, not only as a token of his loyalty to the Queen, but of his profound recognition of the thou- sands of kindnesses received at the hands of his fellow townsmen during a period of almost four-and-thirty years. (Cheers.)

NEW BOOKS, &e. " Grace Montrose" (Messrs. Simpkin, Marshall, and Co.) is the title of what the author himself styles "an unfashionable novel." It is written by Mr. Thomas Greenwood, author of "Free Public

Libraries," " Eminent Naturalists, &c.," and it is cer- tainly altogether different in treatment from the or- dinary run of love tales. Yet it is a love tale, and one which is very pleasantly told. Mr. Greenwood shows deep sympathy with the trials and difficulties of the working classes, and has a wholesome hatred of the cant which is talked about them. His hero
and heroine, though bred in different spheres, have the touch of nature which makes the whole world
kin, a-ilifit is therefore a matter of course to follow
their fortunes with genuine interest. Ale.n born in the purple who desire to be of service to their fel- low-men would do well to read and study" Grace
Montrose."

"The Lady's World, a Magazine of Fashion and Society " is a new venture by Messrs. Cassell, which is likely to be successful. Issued at one shilling, it embraces everything that the fashionable fair can desire. "An Autumn Idyll" makes a charming coloured frontispiece ' • and "Notes of the Month" form a record of all that everybody is doing in the world of ladies; there are the "Fashions for No- vember," with illustrations from London, Paris, Vienna, and Berlin; besides dramatic and musical notes, "Artistic Occupations for Ladies," "Fashion- able Hairdressing," and "The Art of Giving Din- ners." The fashion plates are much superior to the ordinary run of such things, and as there is so much in the new magazine besides mere fashion, it is sure to prove a great attraction to the fair sex. Cassell's " Magazine of Art "for November is the first part of a new volume, and well, indeed, it opens with a highly-finished etching of the painting by C. C. Van Haanen—" Venetian Bead-stringers." Following on, there is a portrait of Van Haanen,with a sketch of his career, and engravings of his works. "Old Blue and White Nankeen China" is capitally treated by Mr. Joseph Grego, and it is suitably illus- trated. Turner's celebrated picture, " The Fighting Temeraire," has justice done to it in a full-page en- graving by 0. L. Lacour, and there is a finely illus- trated article on Hoghton Tower, an extract from which, as especially interesting to Lancashire people, we give in another column. There are be- sides illustrated papers on "Historic Gloves," "Art in New Zealand," &c. An etching, photogravure, or steel plate will in future be issued, as a frontis- piece, with every monthly part of the magazine. Part 10 of Cassell's Shakespere includes an extra sheet, and is distinguished by more than usually powerful engravings. "Love's Labour Lost" is , concluded in this number, and we have the first portion of "A Midsummer Night's Dream." "Gleanings from Popular Authors" has reached part 15, but there is not the slightest sign of any falling off in quality either of text or illustration. "Familiar Wild Flowers" (part 9) deals with goldi- locks, water ranunclus, and the periwinkle, the coloured plates being, as usual, beautifully finished pieces of work. "The Life and Times of Queen Victoria," which is also published by Messrs. Cassell, reaches part 6 for the current month, and, like its predecessors. it is characterised by a well-written text, good paper, and abundant illustrations. There is not a little about Ireland in the number which is worth _

studying at the present moment. "The Book of Health" (part 31) treats of climate and health re- sorts, with especial regard to temperature, winds. and drainage. The November number of Cassell's Magazine con- cludes a volume, and there is a full index given. There is also a promise, which we may be quite sure will be kept, of good things for the new volume. The Family Doctor gossips pleasantly and wisely on rheumatism and how to grapple with it; Dr. R. Garnett tells something of "The Library of the British Museum;" Professor W. G. Blackie recounts some stirring scenes in the life of David Living- stone; there is a second paper on cooking at sea; chit-chat on dress; besides other papers, and " several stories.—" The Quiver" for November pro- vides abundance of material for its readers. r Amongst the more noteworthy papers may be men- tioned "Some great Biblical scholars," by Professor " Roberts; "Lesson preparation in Sunday school," ! by a superintendent; "With the London 'busmen ;" "Notable church porches ;" "The Lord is our Shep- herd:" "The sunshine of tho Christians heart." &c. —" Little Folks" has a pretty frontispiece in "The new baby," and there are numerous other illustra- tions grave and gay. it would be an eclipse to the gaiety of childhood in many a home if this delight- ful serial were to cease to appear. But there is no fear of such a thing; it is in every way doing too well.

Cassell's National Library (3d. per volume) goes on its way rejoicing. The latest issues to hand are the second part of the "Diary of Samuel Pepys," and Plutarch's Lives of Demetrius, Mark Antony, and Themistocles.

The latest addition to the "Camelot Classics," published by Mr. Walter Scott, London, is that highly interesting book, "My Study Windows," by Mr. J. Russell Lowell. There is an excellent intro- duction to the work by Dr. R. Garnett. The essays are all charming, furnishing abundant evidence of Mr. Lowelrs close observation, ready wit, and bril- liance of style. They are readable from beginning to end—which is a great deal more than can be said of a great many essays. "My Garden Acquaint- ance" makes one feel that he is in a paradise .of birds, and hope that, since the American essayist can write in this happy strain, he will, like Tennyson's brook, go on for ever. The "Camelot Classics" are handsomely bound in cloth, and are issued at one shilling each. Any one of Mr. Lowell's essays is well worth the money. • The Canterbury Poets is another cheap series of books (Is. each) issued by the same firm. The volume to hand comprises the dramatic works and lyrics of Ben Johnson with an introductory essay, biographical and critical, by Mr. John Addington Symonds. Amongst the better known plays we have "The Silent Woman," " Catiline," and "Bar- tholomew Fair ; " and the poems include, of course, the celebrated one on Shakespere, with the not less celebrated song—" Drink to me only with thine eyes." The volumes are tastefully bound and are printed on good toned paper, the effect of which is heightened by a red line round the margin of every page. Another shilling volume which is likely to have a large sale is" Money-making-men; or how to grow rich," by Mr. J. Ewing Richie. It is published by Messrs. Charles and Co., Salisbury Court, London, and the frontispiece i appropriately adorned with I a portrait of Mr. George Peabody. There is a sketch of the career of Mr. Peabody and of scores of , other rich and celebrated men. "The table of con- tents" includes among others, chapters on rich men "In the city," "Across the Atlantic," "Money making publishers," "Money-making men in the provinces," "Eccentric money makers," "Money- making M.Ps.," and "Reflections on money-mak- ing.' In the sketch of Barnum, the Prince of Show- men, the following are given as amongst his busi- ness rules :—" Select the kind of business suited to your temperament and inclination ; let your pledged word ever be sacred; whatever you do, do with all your might ; use no description of intox- icating drinks; let hope predominate, but do not be visionary ; pursue one thing at a time ; do not scatter your powers; engage proper assistance ; live within your income, if you almost starve; depend upon yourself and not upon others." Mr. Ritchie has shewn special aptitude for the task he has had in hand; the book is exceedingly interesting, and it is as fall of 'information as an egg is full of meat, Messrs. Griffiths and Farran, 'London, have met a want of the day in the publication of "A Pocket Encyclopcedia of Useful Knowledge." It is from the pen of Mr. henry Grey, who has shown himself well qualified for a work of this kind as the author of those other useful shilling volumes—" Classics for the Million," "Bird's Eye View of English Liter- ateur," &c. The object of the present handbook is stated to be "to meet the demand for general in- formation in a concise form. created by the educa- tional tests to which candidates for almost every kind of intelligent employment are now subjected; and at the same time to assist those who attained to manhood rind womanhood prior to the present facilities for acquiring knowledge in placing them on an intellectual level with the rising generation." It must be said of this Pocket Encyclopcedia that it is admirably compiled, and it is all the better for being illustrated with diagrams which contain " much in little." "The Season" (is.), is brilliant with colotfred plates of the winter fashions ; there is a review of novelties, fiat paper patterns, embroidery designs, illustrations of dress and needlework, &c. Pretty much the same may he said of "Le Moniteur de la Mode" (Is.), with its innumerable illustrations. The contents embrace cut-out pattern for Norfolk Jac- ket, Children's Dress in London and Paris, Fine Art Needlework, Artistic Decoration. &c. We have also to hand " Myra's Journal of Dress and Fashion" (6d.), " Myra's Threepenny Journal," and " Mrs. Leach's Practical Fancy Work Bas- ket" (2d.)
ROBBERY WITH VIOLENCE AT WARRINGTON. FLOGGING AND IMPRISONMENT.

In the Crown Court, at Liverpool Assizes, on Wednesday, before Mr. Justice Day, Peter Fleming, aged 24 years, labourer, and Mary Baldwin, aged 19, hawker, both of Warrington, were found guilty of having, at Warrington, on the 10th of September, 1886, feloniously robbed with -violence Patrick Roach, a farm labourer, of the sum of £4 3s. Mr. Collingwood Hope prosecuted. Prosecutor, who had been working in the neighbourhood of Bold as a farm labourer, came to Warrington on the day ,in question, and in the evening the prisoners WE 7e drinking together in a public-house where the prosecutor was. Some time afterwards the female prisoner offered to.show the prosecutor the way to St. Helens, but instead of doing so, she took him in an opposite direction. On the way Fleming met them, and he knocked the prosecutor down and rifled his pockets, the female prisoner assisting in the robbery. Both prisoners had been previously convicted for a similar offence. His lordship sen- tenced Fleming to twelve months' hard labour, and to receive two whippings of 20 strokes each; and Baldwin was sentenced to 20 months' hard labour.

ELECTION OF MAYOR. The Melon having mentioned that the next business was the electien of his successor, Alderman Daynes said it was now twelve o'clock on the ninth of November, 1886—(hear, hear, and laughter)—and after the two well-earned reprieves that his warship had had Father Time would stand it no longer, and .be (Alder- man Davies) was now in the position of the French herald who had to annousce "The King is dead: Long live the King." Well, it happened that that morning, civically speaking, "The Mayor is dead: Lang live the Mayor." And if the Council would allow him to suggest the necessity of not always continuing the Mayor in office, for however good he might belt was essential for the maintenance of the Council that he should from time to time be deposed and some one else follow him. The Mayor would be in rather a remarkable condition. Monarchs, as a rule, had not the op- portunity of bearing their funeral obsequies, and they had not often the opportunity of seeing the coronation of their successor; but on Alderman Harrison's retirement as the Mayor of Warrington they were happy to receive him in the company of those who had passed the chair before him. (Hear. hear.) He thought the Council would quite Agree with him, and everyone who heard him, that the Mayors who had gone before had been a credit to the chair. (Hear, hear.) He was pleased to think that it had been brought about by the excellent example of Mr. Beamont, who was a living evidence to-day of a Mayor of mayors. It was ex- traordinary that although it was 40 years since Mr. Bea- mont was in the chair, he was still a living example which all other mayors had been pleased to follow. (Applause.) They were entering upon an auepicious year—the year of the Jubilee of Her Majesty the Queen, whom God preserve. (Hear, hear.) He was quite inclined to think that War- rington would not be behind any town in England in show- ing its loyalty to the Sovereign, and likewise in showing by the Mayer they should elect that they were not behind any other Corporation in the kingdem. (Hear, hear.) He was pleased to think that Dr. Mackie, the man whom they would propose RS Mayor, was not the creature of any political party. (Hear, hear.) Dr. Mackie that day stood before them as the creation of that Council—(hear, hear,)—and he (Alderman 'Davie') was satisfied to expect and believe that that day in making him they Mayor they should do so unenimously, and that it would be the voice of Warrington. (Hear. hear.) Let him tell Dr. Mackie that he coneidered that, elected by the unanimous vote of the Council, who were the representatives of the people, the honoar of Mayor was greater than that of member of Parliament—(hear, hear)—for a Mayor was elected by the unanimous voice of the people, while a member of Par- liamedt could only have a majority. (Hear, hear.) As regards the part which he would have to fulfil towards the Jubilee he knew that he was quite prepared, but they must give him the strength of mind and the strength of energy to enable him to fulfil the whole of the duties de- volving upon him. He would have a heavy responsibilitY resting upon him in the approaching winter in regard to the working population of the town. It had been the happy lot of the late. Mayor and Mayoress to be connected with muchlhat was done for the relief of the poor last winter, and he knew that Dr. Mackie and his good wife would not leave that part of their labour unfulfilled. • (Hear, hear.) There was another matter which they should not lose sight of, and he hoped they would pardon him for mentioning it, because it was not connected with the election of Mayor. But he thought it was very necessary that that Council should exercise a very strict economy in the spending of the moneys at their disposal. (Hear, hear.) It happened at the present time that through want of trade there ass a a large amount of idle capital which people were seeking to invest. This had opened a field for the borrowing of money by corporations. Corporations had borrowed very largely at a low rate of interest, and it might be that to some ex- tent it was an advantage; but it had its disadvantages. Towns were encouraged to borrow very largely, and it might be a serious inconvenience for towns to have heavy debts hanging over them even at low rates of interest. (Hear, hear.) He might, then, suggest to Dr. Mackie, that he may not lose sight of what they were dieing in the ap- proaching year. He congratulated the Council that they were electing a Mayor unanimously, and that they repre- sented the voice of the people of Warrington. (Hear, hear.) He had great pleasure in proposing that Dr. Mackie be Mayor of Warrington. He felt satisfied they would have a , unanimous vote, and he congratulated the Corporation upon I its being so. (Applause.) Mr. Alderman CROffIRLD, in seconding the motion, said he rose with great pleasure to second the nomination of Councillor Dr. Mackie for the office of Mayor. In Dr. Mackie he believed they should have a gentleman who had the weight and the power to conduct the business of that Corporation in a satisfactoey manner. (Hear, hear.) Out- side that council Chamber, at Parliamentary elections, there were few people, he supposed, who had hit Dr. Mackie harder than he had, and probably should do again. (Laughter, and hear, hear.) That did not affect him inside that chamber. (Hear. hear.) He was delighted that that day they entered upon a new era. They were going to abandon that miserable political spirit which had kept some of the best of their citizens out of that chamber. (Hear, hear.) They intended in future that they would have in that chamber, as far as possible, large works and big ratepayers represented. (Hear, hear.) Look round the town: there is Dallem Forge, Armitage and Rigby'e Monks Hall, and Co., Roberts, Dale, and Co., and others, and not one of these firms was represented in that Conncil. He said it was a shame. The large ratepayers ought to come there and help them to govern the town. He was delighted that Alderman, in his excellent speech had referred to the question of expenditure. He hoped that Dr. Mackie would no his utmost to make every Committee of that Council be as economical as it was possible in the coming year. (Hear, hear.) He thought now they had got through the large expenditure that was necessary for the bernuab, their rates might be brought down to ss. in the R. (Hear, hear.) As he said before he was delighted to have the opportunity of secoading Dr. Mackie to the Mayoralty, because outside the Council Chamber he had so strongly eppoeed him politi- cally, and therefore he was giving good evidence that he at all events had banished from his mind for ever in that Council Chamber all political feeling whatever. (Ap- plause.) He congratulated Dr. Mackie that he was going to be Mayor during the Jubilee year of her Majesty; and he was sure as Alderman Davies had said, that they, the inhabitants of Warrington, would show that they were as loyal as any town in England. Dr. Mackie WAS the very man to help them to do that, and he rejoiced that it had been his privilege to aeecond such nomination. (Applause.) Mr. Alderman Wives-ma also supported the nomination, and said he had every hope that the coming year, the Jubilee year of her gracious Majesty, ruled over, as they would be, by Dr. Mackie, would be an ever memorable one, and to be looked back upon with plea- sure, not only by Dr. Mackie, but by all of them. (Ap- plause.) The MAYOR said he had known Dr. Mackie intimately from the very first day he came to Warrington, and had had from that time to that hour preserved the most friendly relationship, and bad been associated with him in various matters cennected with their local institu- tions, and had consequently seen a good deal of his inner life As it were, and he was justified in seyingior rather reminding them—for they knew it es well, perhaps, as he did—thet in electing Councillor Dr. Mackie as their Mayor, they were electing a warm-hearted man, full of gene- rous impulses, a gentleman of acknowledged ability and force of character, of great administrative capacity. business tact, earnest thought, and clear perception, and one who while endowed with the suaviter m mod°, was by no means deficient in the foraer in re; for he knew no man within the scope of his acquaintance who could more reso- lutely pat down his foot upon anything savouring of injus- tice, oppression, or wrong doing. The possession of qualities such as these would well qualify a man to become Mayor of any city or borough in Eealand, and he was persuaded that the Mayoralty of Warrington in the hands of Dr. Mackie, to use an ornithological figure of speech. would not " moult a feather." But to give immediate and practical effect to that well-known line from the " Odyssey," "Wel- come the coming, speed the parting guest," he would at once proceed to put the resolution to the vote by asking gentlemen who were in favour of the resolution before them to signify the same by holding up one hand. The resolution was then carried unanimously. The newly-elected M eyor then left the room, accompanied by Alderman Harrison, Alderman Davies, and Alderman Crosfield, and when he returned in a few minutes, invested with the robe and chain of office, he was warmly ap- plauded. Having made the usual declaration and taken the oaths,

WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held on Wednesday morning at the Workhouse. There were present the Rev. G. F. Roberts (chairman), Messrs. Blackhurst, Gibson, Jolley, Heaton, Isherwood, W. Houghton, J. Houghton. Balharry, Strange, Clarke, Pennington, Wright, Eckersley, Hibbert, Woods, Greening, Swinton, Humphries, and Brown; J. C. Sutton (clerk), and S. Sutton (assistant clerk).

HOUSE COMMITTER. This committee reported that its attention had been called to the non-payment of a sum of 8s ad, the payment of which was directed by a minute of the committee under date of 21et May last, and which had not been paid. It was recommended that the sum he immediately paid by the or- dinary cheque of the Board. The minutes contained some other items which were important.—Mr. WOODS moved, and Mr. HEATON seconded, the adoption of the minutes.— Mr. BLACKHIIRST took exception to the minute given above, and said that a member who signed the cheque would be surcharged. He could not see why the 8s 2d could not be paid out of the petty cash of the Workhouse Master,a course ' which he believed the Clerk would tell them bad always been followed.—The CLTRK : It is an invariable rule.—Mr. BLACKHURST, continuing, said he could not see why the re- sponsibility of paying the account should be shifted on to a member of the Board when they bad nothing to do with it, and he therefore moved an amendment that the minutes pass with the exception of tke one he referred to.—Mr. Jowir said he seconded Mr. Blackhurst's amendment for the reason that the Master of the Workheuse had been or- dered by the Board to pay the sum out of his petty cash long ago. He (Mr. Jolley) was surprised that the order should be disobeyed by any officer. They, as a Beard of Guardians, must have their orders carried out to the very letter, and he felt very strongly that it was a slight upon them to let a thing come before them again which a long time ago they spoke so strongly about, and insisted that it should be paid out of the petty cash. It was a piece of Impertinence for any officer to disobey orders.—The CLERK then read a statement explaining the proper procedure in the payment of such accounts as that referred to.—Mr. JOLLY said that that mattet should again come before them was not at all creditable to the Board, and was a waste of time.—After a few remarks by Mr. ISHERWOOD and Mr HEATON, in defence or the action of the House Committee, Mr. Etlackhurst'a amendment was carried by a large ma- jority.

SCHOOLS COMMITTPIE.—A CONTRACT CANCELLED. At a meeting isf the Schools Committee the following minute, in answer to question 14, "Are the provisions and other supplies of the qualities contracted for ?" was passed : —" The groceries are most unsatisfactory, and in some res- pects unusable. The Superintendent is instructed to re- quest the meeical officer's examination of the articles, and to return such things as he may advise. The Clerk is also directed to write to the contractors."—The CHAIRMAN moved and Mr. BLACEHURST seconded the confirmation of the minutes.—Mr. Buows said the groceries they bad had recently at the workhouse were not up to what they expected, so much so indeed that they had decided on returning the cheese they had received. They were very sorry to do so, but it was really of such a charaater, that they could not place it before the poor people, many of whom were old and sick, and had to be protected.—The CHAIRMAN was sorry to say that the same remarks applied to the groceries supplied to the schools.—Mr. JOLLEY said the cheese that was brought before them was simply disgusting and rotten—a most abominable thing to be sent out. He asked the clerk in what position the Board was in regard to the matter. Should they cancel the contract, and enter into another with somebody who would give them decent goods for their money.—The Ca/maw% : Certainly we shall do so.--Nir. JOLLEY said he should have pleasure in moving that the contract be cancelled.—The CHAIRMAN said the proper course would be for the doctor to certify with reference to the quality of the goods. That would put them right tech- nically.—Mr. Hisnenr having also spoken as to the bad quality of the goods, the Crasix said that in the event of a breach of contract the contract was determinable summarily without compeasation to the contractor, and if the health of the people under their charge was at risk it was their boun- den duty, irrespective of consf quencee, to terminate the con- tract and accept the next lowest.—Mr. JOLLEY then moved that the contract for groceries and provisions for both the workhouse and the schools be cancelled, and that the ten- der of Mr. 14. B. Percival, which was the next lowest when the tenders were considered, be accepted.—Mr. WOOD:, in seconding this proposel, said he had never seen such shorn- inable stuff as the Australian meat which was opened before them.—Mr. HIBERRY supported the proposition, which was agreed to unanimously. NEW ASSISTANT OTERSEERS.

Roebuck mentioning he had been ap- pointed to a similar office for Thelwall. The names of two sureties were submitted by Mr. Daintith, and were consi- dered satisfactory by the Board. THB WORKHOUSI MA-STAIR ASKED TO RESIGN. The CLBRK read the following letter which he had re- ceived from the Local Government Beard, viz. :—" Local government Board, Whitehall, S.W., 27th October, 1886. Sir,—Tbe Local Government Board have had under their consideration your letters of the Bth of July and the 23rd of August last, with reference to an erasure and alteration mage in an accsunt for articles supplied and work done by Mr. John Hedgecock. The Board, after a review of all the circumstances of the Case, cannot avoid the conclusion that the conduct of Mr. G. Mackey, the master of the Work- house, in connection with this matter was very reprehen- sible. At the audit in January last he disclaimed any pre- view knowledge of the alteration made in Mr. Hedgcock's account. When called upon by the Guardians for an ex- planation in July last, he admitted that he had made the alteration. So as to save, as he thought, trouble. When, however, the Board wrote to him on the subject, he stated that the date had been altered by a naurier inmate who had acted as his clerk. But, assuming this to be the case, the inmate in question died in December, 1885, and the master must have been aware of the facts at the time of the audit In January last. The Board are of opinion that if the mas- ter did not actually make the alteration himself, he was responsible for it, and that, moreover, he has been guilty of untruthfulness An alteration of this character is so grave an ofleoce that the Board would not feel justified in per- mitting Mr. Mackey to retain the office of master, and they must request that the Guardians will call upon him at their next meeting to place in their hands his resignation of that office.—l am, sir, your obedient servant. S. B. Pnovis, As- sistant Secretary.';—The Clerk added that the surcharge on Mr. Brown in regard to the signing of the cheque , for the above-named account had been remitted by the I Local Government Hoard on the ground that the Guardians were not aware of the illegality.-1 he CHAIRMAN said with regard to the above letter that their course was simple. They could but comply with the reqnest of the Local Go- vernment Board and leave the matter in their hands. It was a matter that rested between the Local Government Board, the auditor, and Mr. Mackey—Mr. BLACKHURST moved that they comply with the request of the Local Government Board, but Mr. BROWN suggested that it would only be courteous to the master to call him in and let him hear the letter read.—This course was adopted. and Mr. Mackey having been called into the roam, the letter was read to him.—The CHAIRMAN then said that the only course open to the Guardians was to comply with the request of the Local Government Board, and call upon Mr. Mackey to send in his resignation.—Mr. MACKEY : Will you allow me a little time to consider the matter 7—The CHAIRMAN : Oh, yes ; this will now remain a matter between you and the Local Government Board.

THE PORTER'S BOOK. The CLERK, explaining the reason why the resolution passed at the previous meeting that a list of the officers' ab- sews from the Workhouse should be transcribed from the porter's biok had not been complied with, said it e had not been able to keep the porter's book at tvs office a sufficient length of time owing to its having been sent for from the Workhouse.—The WORKHOUSE MASTEa alleged that c.qtain alterations bad been made in the books.—The CLERK said that was a most serious allegation, and be urged that it should be very strictly inquired ioto.—lt was then agreed that further consideration of the matter should be postponed till the next meeting, when the master should report in writing as to the alleged alterations. The relief cases were then proceeded with.

Lady Randolph Churchill has promised to sing at a con- cert at Hackney on the 20th inst. Mr. William O'Brien, editor of "United Ireland," is to be
the Nationalist candidate for South Siigo, the representatim
of which Mr. Sexton gives up, having elected to sit for West
Belfast. • The Colonial and Indian Exhibition was closed on Wed-
neEday after being open since the beginning of May. It has been visited .by upwards of five:and:a-half millions of per-
sons, the daily average being 33,846. A supplement to the London " Ci.z4te " contains Royal _ . _
Proclamations further proroguing Parliament to Thursday,

. . December the 9th, and the Convocations of Canterbury an York to Friday, December the 10th. It is expected that the Qneeu will not go to Osborne in December, as usual, hut that she will sperd her Christmas

at Windsor Castle, in consequence of the approaching ac- conchment of Princ.ss Henry of Battenberg. The liquidation of the affairs of the Munster Bank has been brought to a close. Only per share has been called up out of £6 10a callable, and the shareholders at their final meeting on Wednesday expressed their satisfaction at this result.

Early on Monday morning a prize fight took place at Witton, near Birmingham. The combatants were two well- known pugilists, and the fight, which lasted nearly au hour and a half, ended in a draw. Beth men were badly

punished. AN EXTRAORDINARY TOWN COUNCIL. At the Bangor Town Council meeting on TuesdAy, the voting was equal, and after three hears' wrangling, the Council seltc- ted daplicate sets of aldermen. Eventually the ma:l.T was adjourned for a fortnight for a compromise to be ar-
ranged. THREE MINERS BURIED ALIVE.—A shocking accidEnt occurred at Dinaa Colliery, in the Rhondda Valley, on Saturday. While the men were'at work forty tons of debris
accident-.ally fell in, burying two men and a boy. Several hours elapsed before they were all extricated, and the bay, William Williams, was then dead. The two men were bail? . . _

injured. CHARGE AGAINST A CLERGYMAN.—On Slturday, at the Reading County Bench, the Rev. D. S. Shipley was charged, on remand, with obta;ninr; a number of valuable articles, including plate, from Mr. Calla!, ironmonger,

SIR REDVERS BULLER'S IRISH MISSTON.—Sir Redvers

Buller has addressed the following letter to ".The Times ": —"Sir,—As you have referred in a leading article to a report sent to you by your oorrespondent at Cork, imput- ing the exercise of a 'dispensing power' to me, I hope
you will al low me space to ay that I have neither ex- ercised, nor claimed to exercis.e, any such power in _ .
the enforcement of the decrees of the Courts of Law in Ireland.

A LUNATIC ASYLUM CASE. As action brought by Madame Trafani against De. Spurgeon. to recover damages for wrongful detention in a lunatic asylum, was concluded on Tuesday. Justice Denman summed up strongly for the defendant, but the jury, after two hours' consideration, failed to agree, and were discharged; his Lordship, how- ever intimating that he would hear counsel on Saturday, as to whether be should give judgment for the defendant on the evidence before him. _

THE ARREcT OF AN ABSCONDING SOLICITOII.—At South- wark Police Court, London. on Monday, George Bernard Harvey Drew, 42, solicitor, of the firm of Wilkinson. Drew, and Co., Bermondsey-street, was charged with embezzling various sums of money, amounting to over .-C4,000. entrusted to him on behalf of the London Leather Warehouse Com- pany, of which he was the secretary. He disappeared. it was stated, last January, and was arrestsd in t_iydnev, where he lived in the most extravagant manner. He was re- manded. _ _

THE LONDON DOMESTIC TateertnY.—On Monday after- noon an inquest was held relative to the death of Mr. Arthur Egan. who attempted to murder his wife and after- wards committed suicide by shooting himself at Montague- street, Russell-square, London, last week. Evidence was given showing that be had previously threatened to cut his own throat and his wife's, and that for some time he had been very strange in his demeanour. Not long since he attempted to jump out of a train!on a journey to Eastbourne. A verdict that he committed suicide while in a state of un- sound mind was returned. THE ANTI-TIMIS] AGITATION—Lord Wolverton, in a let- ter on the tithe question, says he is not prepared to pro- nounce in favour of abolition. His lordship, however, sym- pathises with those who are compelled to support a Church whose faith they dissent from. At a meeting ,of farmers of the Valley of Llangollen, on Saturday, it was resolved to accept a proffered abatement of 24 per cent. Ths members of the Chester Farmers' Club discussed the subject on Satur- day, and a resolution was proposed to the effect that each farmer s';ould individually ask for a reduction of tithe and rent, but finally a motion for the adjournment of the dis- cussion was carried. LIVERPOOL A SSIZES.—kt Liverpool Assizes on Wednes- day, Thomas Wright, an ironworker, was sentenced to seven years' penal servitude for shooting Frederick Fryer, game- keeper on Lord Sefton's estate. The prisoner was caught by Fryer poac'ing at Tarbock, and to escape arrest he fired deliberately at the keeper, who received a full charge of small shot in his body. In the same court Thomas Isher- wood, convicted of attempting to murder his wife at Black- burn by striking her several times on the head with an are, and also stabbing her, was sentenced to penal servitude for life. A young man named Fleming. for highway robleery with violence, was ordered to undergo 12 months' imprison. went, and to receive 40 lashes with the "cat." SENTENCE OP DEATIL—At Exeter, on Saturday, Thomas Polgraz, a miller, was found guilty of the murder of Chas. Sherman, at Breaze, Cornwall, on July 19 last. At the rear of his house the prisoner had a rick, and Sherman, who had been drinking on the night of the 18th, went and slept under it, partly covering himself with hay. In the morn- ing the prisoner, finding a man under his rick, spoke to bine,. and getting no answer, went indoors, took up a peat hook,. and, it is alleged, smashed the deceased's skull. The pri— soner then gave himself tip to the police. The defence was that the prisoner was not of average intelligence, and acted

as be did through fear. - Sentence of death Was pa,lsed, bat Baron Hnddleston promised to forward the jury's recom- mendation of mercy to the proper quarter. EXTRAORDINARY FORGIOZY AND THEFT OF £5,200.---The Birmingham police are endeavouring to effect the arrest of Arthur Forster, clerk, for obtaining a large sum cf money by forging the name of his employer, Councillor Bradley, of Colemore-row, Birmingham, solicitor. Mr. Bradley had been successful in ob:aining £7.000 Gut of Chancery for some Birmingham clients, and his London agents took- pos- session of the money. Forster was entrusted with most of the cor.espondence, and he conceived a plan for getting hold of the money. He accordingly intercepted his em- plover's letters from the London agents, and forged replies which be forwarded, stating that Mr. Bradley would seed a fully accredited gentleman to receive the money. The

letter of identity was presented by the prisoner at the Lon- don aeents, and £5.200 was drawn out. Aftrwards he failed to appear at Mr. Bradley's office, representing that be was ill, and it was not until the following Saturday the fraud was discovered. It WAS then ascertained that he had absconded. Immediately on the discovery of the crime detectives were despatched to London, Liverpool, and all likely ports, but it is supposed that be has got clear. GREAT GALS AND FLOODS.—Reports from North Wales show that in many places the mountain streams are over bank. Heavy rain fell in Carnarvonshire and Anglesey on Saturday, causing the rivers to rise rapidly. S. Paul's Board schools, with the master's housra at Banger, were wrecked through the flooding of the main drain. Several children hael narrow escapes. A severe gale was experienced in the north of England, on parts of the coast of Wales, and in the Irish Channel on Saturday, and several shipping dis- astere, attended with loss of life, are already reported. In Cheshire and South Lancashire the heavy rain caused fi,,od- ing of the lands and houses. Work was stopped in some factories in consequence of the floods. A telegram from Donaghaclee reports that the schooner Eclipse, of Belfast, bound to Bangor, county Down, from Marypert, foundered at Donag,hadee at 8-30 a.m. on Saturday, aboutthreemitihette east of that port. Captain Oliver and Arexander Paterson, the mate, were drowned. Twenty•seven men, forming entire crew of the Liverpool steamer Juliet, have been landed at Liverpool, their vessel haying ben totally. wrecked on the Bahamas. The Juliet, a splendid iron screw steamer of 2,000 tons register, was going from Cardiff to New (Means, with a cargo of railway iron, and NV"-:4 carried ashore on a coral reef at a place called the Gingerbread. Sho'ale. Heavy gales were reported on Sets-v(I3F, Sunday, awd Monday, from all parts of the United Kingdom. Wreci, age bearing the names of the Swifture, Conquistador, Mar- tin, Kaiesir, and other vessels unidentified, has boen picked up on the Cornieh coast. Farther details received on Mon- day from correspondents in the North show that a consider- able amount of damage has ben done to tlp flooding of rivers and low-lying lands, after Friday'', rainstorms. Two woaden tempo-ary bridges on the Tweed, at Mertorin and. Norham, have been washed away, ad the new bridges dam- aged. There has been a slight fall of snow in portions of the Lake district, and snow made its appearance on Hel- vellyn, on Sunday, for the first time this season. Intelli- gence was received at Dundee, on Tuesday, of tile loss ef the steamer S. Thornak of Arbroath, on a voyage from Dundee to London. She swank; a leak during the gale. and Lank Tne crew were saved, and landed at Cromer, Norfolk. 0 eing to the continuous and heavy rain in North Yor'eshire the rivers have overflowed and great tracts of land are flooded. Five men and four children hive been drowned in the Swale by the capsizing of a ferryboat, and twe farmers lost their lives whilst trying to ford the same river. KAY'S COMPOUND or LINSEED. as someone says, we should be grate- ful to the great that they do us no harm, we ought to be thankful for the speech t,,at Lord SALISBURY made,, on ruesday, at the Lord MAYOR'S banquet. Liberal politicians have usually an anxious time of it when the Tories are in office; they are so r;3ady to.go to war abroad in order to divert attention. from the need of reform at home. But ri change has come over the Tories; they have ceased for a time to worship at the shrine of St. Jingo; and their leaders enunciate tae peaceful doctrine of non-intervention as though they had been familiar with it all their lives. Can it be that this change. for the better is solely due to the.:r burning desire to preserve "the union with the Unionists ?" If this be so, the loss to the Liberal Pany of the Dissentient Liberals will not be all loss. Toryism, tempered by Lord HA.E.T.GTON and Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, 15 more tolerable than Toryism aggravated by Lord RANDOLPH , CHURCHILL and Mr. 43,SHMEAD-BARTLETT. :The Prime Minister's references to foreign affairs, on Tuesday, were wholly reassuring, for he spoke, as well aa he was able, after the manner of Mr.. GLADs-zoNE• Loxl, SALISBURY expressechhe feeling of the cowl- try in its profound sympathy with the people of Bulgaria; but at the same time he made it unmistakeably clear thit England, whatever might happen, would not, single-handed, go to war to support the rights of the Bulgarians under the Treaty of Berlia. "Much spezula- tion," his lordship said, "has been Used as to the attitude which this country would ob- serve with respect to the Berlin Treaty, and to the violence which, in the opinion of some it has received. This country has an interest, but it is not an isolated interest—it is a cor- porate interest. In combination with the Powers of Europe we have signed that treaty, but there rests upon us no isolated duty to vindicate that treaty if it should be broken." And again, "England will perform her duty

in concert with other members of the Euro— pean Confederacy, but she will not accept the duty of maintaining obligations on behaltr of others who do not think it necessary. ,to maintain them for themselves." It is a great relief o know that, with a Ministry composed of men who have for the most part used the most threatening language towards Russia• under circumstances much less provoking. than those of her present tyrannical conduct towards Bulgaria, there is no likelihood °four going to war with the great barbarian of the' north. Mr. GLADSTONE seems to have naged the situation to a nicety, and is naturally con- - tent to let the Tories denounce his foreign policy as much as they like when they are, in opposition, providing they pay him the, un- disguised compliment of carlying out his policy when they come into office. The other day, he was appealed to by a number of leading Bulgarians. to "raise once more his powerful voice in favour of Bulgaria;" andin reply he said there had been no change in his opinions. He believed that liberties obtained for autonomous provinces from the SULTAN were "intended for their own use and benefit; and not as proper to be handed over in whole or in part to anybody else." :lit the most significant point in his letter was• statement that he had not thought it his duty to raise his voice on the present occasion, because, to quote his own words," I have-had, and still have, the. belief that in this country' there is happily no difference of opinion on the subject, and / have no good reason to doubt that the sentiment of the United Kihg- dom is faithfully represented in the Cduncils of Europe by the, Foreign Minister of to-day.?' What could be more valuable than such an, ex- pression of opinion, from such a sc-arce, in strengthening the hands of the present Gov- ernment in the conduct of foreign affairs Yet Lord SALISBURY did not acknowledge it by as much as a word. Perhaps, knc.)vv-ing his audience, he felt that it was quite enough to • adopt Mr. GLADSTONE'S policy without mak, ing a more open confession.

The PRIME. MINISTER'S remarks on Ire- land, at the Mansion House dinner,. were. satisfactory, as pointing to the peace- able condition of the country—thanks to .the- good effect of Enzlish acceptance of the, principle of Irish Home Rule—but with regard , to the prospects. of legislation they were alto- gether unsatisfactory. The CHANcELLOR- ofT the EXCHEQUBR spoke at Bradford in a very, undecided strain as to the course the Govern- ment intended to pursue when Parlian3ent met early next year. He seemed to show him, self interested in dealing with any reform, rather than that of reform in the government of Ireland; and those who read between the, lines could see, as Mr. JOHN MORLEY , last week pointed out, that if the Ministry were left to themselves they would shelve the Irish. question for as long a period as possible. Lord SALISBURY'S speech confirms this im- pression. He says : That being the condition. of aff,,irs in frelstui4.l, will only say that it is not only legislation bit, a, steady course of honest government—if we can. obtain it—that is likely to lead ta the restuotion. of peace in that country. I do not, exclude.legis- lation. It may be necessary; but.l should,sayna: little of it as possible. What we 'lave to do, should. be undertaken with as much caution ajad prudence- as we can command. The solution, of the!ease oE Ireland for the time is to be found ratherin.good, government, than in the, alteration of, the law,; and. the sooner we can dissuade ourselvaa, from. speculating in politics the more .readily shall, wet begin to make more enduring modes of improve- ment prwail there.,

It will be noticed that the PRIME MINISTER merely says legislation " 7,-,gy;be necessary;" it is, therefore, fair to infer that the Govern- ment "may" come to the conclusion,that it is not necessary. Indeed, we cannot think it is doing them any injustice to say that if' they are left to the devices and desires of their own hearts they will endeavour, when Parlia- ment.meets, to scramble along as if there.were no such thing as an Irish question. But shall this, be? This is the question which. Liberals throughout England, Scotland, Ireland, and, Wales have got to ask themselves, and to answer. Shall the. Tories,. who. pro- t-sted against the Liberal Government for taking six weeks to prepare a scheme, be allowed, after ,absorbkig six months in, pre- paring them, to postpone the matter for an indefinite period ? We are sure that the answer of the,lrish Nationalists, an& of the Liberals as a party-4 will bo .that they will stand no such humbug in the government of the country. But what of the Dissentient Liberals ?r Is it possible that they will play into the hands of the Tories in. pursuing a policy of delay ? We would fain.not counte- nance such a sup:z.osition. As Mr. GLADSTONE points out, it wilrl be the duty of the Dissen- tient Liberals, if they desire the union of the Liberal party, to insist on the G:overnment producing their plans, seeing that they them- selves have none. If they. connive at any • attempt to shirk the issue, pledged as, they are to some kind, of ;eform, of the govern- ment of Ireland, it will show that there , Lib(Halism is: not abo-ye suspicion—that they have personal rather than public ends to:, serve in their attitude of hostility to tl-1,: great leader of the Liberal party. But we refuse,. under present circumstances), tp believe thaL they are capable of taking such a questionable: c:ourse. It would be ruinous to their p-fos, pects as politicians,. and would not de!ay,., except for .a very brief period, the settlement of the Irish Question. Four-fifths of,the, Liberal party have decland in favor.; of Home Rule for Ireland); four-fifths of the people of Ireluid demand it; and beforia many years are over Home Rule .will ably be the lava of the land.

Tl,4ere was quite a, happy family at- the Warzington Town. Hall on Tuesilay,, dur- ing the meeting for the election af Mayor and,Aldermen ; and; judging frointall that was said and done, it would seem that the Tlry lion and the Liberal lam' have con- Oicled to lie doNn, together, and ie at peace sor evermore. Aldeman JOHN CROSFIELD said they were entering that da7pupon a new era; they were goinkz to abandon, the miser- able political spirit which had kept some of; the best citizens ort of the Coancili Chamber, We hope this ma be be so, but trust we shalt be forgiven if we express a doubt as to tkit& inauguration of the millennium. Alderman CROSFIEUX is perfectly sincere; of that we. are certain, for he does but preach what he has practised. It is not long since one of the leading Conservatives openly declared that there wasn't a man in the Council that was more straightforward than he in doing what he believed to he best for the ratepayers, irrespective of politics. But the members of the Town Council ale not all CROSNELDS, and we can scarcely believe that we shall hear no more of politics in municipal matters when we recollect that not a month has elapsed since th Tory party Droposed to take to themselves, for purely party purposes, seven vacant seats out of nine. The scheme fell through, as it deserved to do, and it is but fair to the. Toy:Qs to say that the best men

among them were ashamed of it. Further though it seems at the first blush that nothing could be more hopeful than the unanimity which was displayed at the election of Mayor and Aldermen, those who have looked behind thescenes know, as the poethas it, thatthings are not what they seem. Dr. M.AcKrtz. is chosen mayor by the unanimous vote of the Council, and we are not going to withhold our congratulations, seeing that we named him two years ago as a citizen who was fully cap- able of discharging the duties of the high office; but—ah, these " buts "l —it is pretty well known that he owes the unanimity of the appointment to the fortunate conjunction that there were two Liberal aldermen who looked for re-election at the same time. There was a fairly strong section amongst the Conserva- tives who had their eyes on another gentle- man for mayor; but when the Liberals de- cidei to support the nomination of Dr. MACKIE, on the understanding that no oppo- sition should be raised to the re-election of Alderman BURGESS and Alde.rman HOLMES, the opposition recognised at once the help- lessness of their position, made • the best of the situation, and went in for making things pleasant all round. Having said this much by way of fair explanation of the situation, we hasten to say that the longer the new era lasts the better it will be for the ratepayers. The remarks of Aldermen DAVIES, CROSFIELD, SUT 'TON, and the new MAYOR as to the pos- sibility of reducing e:Tenditure, and thus lessening the rates, will find an echo in every street in the town. Warrington possesses the unenviable distinction of being one of the highest rated boroughs in the kingdom, and nobody will lament if it should lose its repu- tation in this respect during the next few years. Corporations, as well as individuals, may practice rigid economy, if they set them- selves resolutely to the task. His Worship the MXYOR has a character for doing thoroughly anything that he sets abceit ; he is right, we believe, in thinking that rather too much has been done for posterity ; and if he will make up his mind to leave the rates less than he finds them, we do not doubt that his efforts will be successful. And how plea- sant it would be to reflect that the year of the QUEEN'S Jubilee had proved to be a year of genuine jubilation to the ratepayers ! We may count, at any rate, on a gain to the town in the shape of a statue to her MAJESTY, by Mr. WARRINGTON WOOD ; Dr. MACKIE, as Mayor, has promised that, and he will keep his word. He lrgins well, and we do not doubt that, continuing as he has begun, he will do credit to himself and the people he represents, as Jubilee Mayor of Warrington.

"TOUCH AND GO." Mr. Justice Day has dealt rightly with a Warrington rough. He had been found guilty of robbery with violence, and his lordship has sentenced him to be flogged. If the lash has its place, it is certainly on the backs of the brutes who are ready to commit murder in order to effect robbery.

"How to commemorate the Queen's Ju• bilee" seems to be the question of questions just now. One happy lather has, we are told, decided to call his little girl Victoria. Another happy man, who has just been pre- sented with two beautiful "pups" has resolved to call one "Vic," and the other "Tory." As may be suppesed, he is a good deal of a Conservative, and a bit of a wag.

Having suppressed the Socialists in con- nection with the Lord Mayor's Show, the next best thing would be to suppress the show itself, which is a barbarous relic of a bar- barous past. It is unworthy of the greatest corpoTation in the world to go "fooling around " after the fashion of the outside (advertising) performances of a travelling circus.

The sad end of Fred Archer, the famous jockey, carries with it the lesson which cannot, it would seem, be too often repeated ; namely, that Nature, one day or other, exacts a ter- rible penalty from those who disobey her laws. Archer had starved himself to reduce his weight, and when fever seized him, body and mind rapidly broke down. Hence delirium, a pistol shot, and an early grave.

There was an extraordinary scene at the closing of the Liverpool Exhibition on Mon- day night. Something like a riot was created by a mob of what are described as well- dressed young men. What with the stir about the awards, and the mobbing of the refreshment-room on Monday, it cannot be said of the Exhibition that it "made a good end on't." it is to be hoped they will order these things better in Manchester.

Things seem to be coming to a pretty pass to the Warrinzton Workhouse; a grocer's contract has• to be cancelled because the goods supplied are unsatisfactory; the Master is asked by the Local Government Board to resign because of 'an erasure and alteration made in an account for articles supplied and work done by Mr. John Hedgcock ;" and now there is to be an inquiry into the statement of the Master as to alleged alterations in other books.

Mr. William Leigh, who is a director of the Ship Canal Company, was on Tuesday elected Mayor of Stockport for the second time. He said, in returning thanks, that he had a little reason for believing that his year of office , would witness what they very much hoped for—the cutting of the first sod of the Man- thester Ship Canal. We wish he could have. said he had a " big" reason ; it would have sounded ever so much better. However, hope sprinzs eternal in the human breast. The Fair Traders are left in the lurch by the Tory Government; they have nothing to say upon the subject; and even Mr. Chaplin is despondent. He r• an only suggest that the public opinion of the country must be educa- ted on the subject. There seemed to be plenty of these educationists about when Mr. Gladstone was in office. Where are they now? Have they been struck dumb? Or is it not the right thing to advocate Fair Traci,: when Lord Salisbury is at the head of affairs?

Alderman Davies, in proposing the new Mayor of Warrington, said he "considered that, elected by the unanimous vote of the Council, who are the representatives of the People, the honour of Mayor is greater than that of member of Parliament, for a Mayor is elected by the unanimous voice of the people, while a member of Parliament can only have a majority." This mode of reason- ing applies equally, of course, to the election of aldermen. There were four aldermen and one Mayor elected unanimously on Tuesday —five persons having honour conferred upon them "greater than that of a member of Par- liament." Sir Gilbert Greenall, M.P., is nowhere: he" can only have a majority." But, perhaps, Alderman Davies was joking; he likes a joke.

About every third week, some speaker or other in 'Warrington refers to our good old town." Dr. Mackie Used the hackneyed phrase in his speech on Tuesday. That it is hackneyed may be inferred from the fact that Dr. 0. W. Holmes has had a hit at it. In his " Autocrat of the Breakfast Table," he refers to his lecturing in various towns, and states the following, amongst other propositions, to hold true :—"(z) The axis of the earth sticks out visibly through the centre of each and every town or city. (2) If more than fifty years have passed since its foundation, it is affectionately styled by the inhabitants the 'good old town of '— (whatever it may hap- pen to be)." Warrington was, of course, founded above fifty years ago; and equally, of course, is the "hub" of the universe. Still "good old town "-is somewhat musty.

VIDNES SAMARITAN LODGE, No. 1,153.—e weekly meeting of this lodge was held in the Lodge-room, Victoria-road, on Manday evening, when an excelle pro- gramme of songs, &c, was gene through. nt CHESHIRE COUNTY FOOTBALL—In the match between Lancashire and Cheshire, at Birkenhead, to.day. the team of the cheese county cont tins no less than six players from the Runcorn club. They are—Woods, back; W. A. Riley, three-quarter back; Hsieh Hughes, half back; and W. id. Broady, W. Wright, and J. Lewis, forwards. WIDNFS BICYCLE AND TRICYCLE CLUB.—The members of this club brought a most successful seaeon to a close on Thursday evening, when they and a number of lady friends, numbering altogether about 60, assembled in linsworth's dining-rcoms, Victoria-road. A capital tea was provided, and subsequently a short musical entertainment was given. The rest of the evcniug was devoted to dancing. WIDNES c.E.T.s. The usual weekly meeting of this society was held on Thursday evening in the National Schools, Waterloo-road. The Rev. A. P. Hamilton ‘Brilson presided, and there was a very good attendance. The fol- lowing took part in an excellent miscellaneous entertain- ment :—Miss Lord, the Rev. J. R. Jones, Messrs. T. Davies, F. Scott, J. Ankers, J. Tomlinson, and Marshall, and Mr. Kenyon and the members of the Widnes C.E.T.S. Band. WESLEYAN FOREIGN MISSION'S.—During the past week services and meetings in ai4 of the Wesleyan Foreign Mis- sions have been held at Widnes. and Halebenk. At the far- mer place two sermons were preached in Albert-road Chapel on Sunday morning and evening, and a public meeting was held in the same place on Monday. At Halebank the Rev. J. Bryant preached on Sunday morning. and Mr. Peter Glover at night. Mr. Robert Booth presided over a meet- ing held on Wednesday. A WIDNES MAN DROWSED AT BOOTLE.—Wm. Frederick Hunt, a flatman, aged about 23, was drowned in the Brocklebank Dock, Bootle, on Saturday night. It appears that the deceased belonged to the flat St. Helens, which is at present lying alongside a ship that is moored to the quay in the above-mentioned dock. On Saturday night he was intoxicated, and, in endeavouring to get on board the ship to cross to his flit, he fell into the water between the quay wall and the ship. An inquest was held on the welts of the deceased on Monday, before Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, and the jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death." THE NEW VICAR OF RUNCORN.—The Dean and Canons of Christ Church, Oxford, have presented the Rev. Alfred Maitland Wood, M.A., vicar of Liscerd. Birkenhead, to the benefice of Runcorn Parish Church, void by the death of Canon John Barclay, M.A., the last vicar thereof. The new vicar of Runcorn proceeded B.A. (31st Wrangler) from Trinity College, Cambridge. in 1863, and M.A. in 1873. He was ordained deacon in 1865 and priest in 1866, by the late Dr. William Jacobson, Bishop of Chester, his first curacy (which he held six years) being tinder the Rev. William Bryans at Tarvin, Chester. In 1871 he became curate to Chancellor Empin at the Parish Church, Wallasey. Here he remained until 1878, when he was preferred by Bishop Jacobson to the benefice of Liscard. RUNCORN Serseeztose ARMY.—The eighth anniversary of the Runcorn Branch of the Salvation Army was celebra- ted last week end, when numerous meetinge were held. Major Rees, of the Manchester and Liverpool Division, con- ducted the gatherings, which excited much interest beyond the ranks of the usual followers of General Booth. The great attraction was the presence of Major ;Jibi and six other officers who have volunteered for service in India; and as they took part in the processions through the streets attired in an Indian cesturne of white robes, considerable sensation was caused. The proceedings were brought to a close on Monday evening, when 400 persons sat down to tea in the barracks; and subsequently listened to accounts of the army's work in England and Canada. The anniver.• sary was considered a great success. HALTON PARISH CHURCH DAY SCHOOL—The annual entertainment given by the children of the Halton Parish Church Day Schools took place on Friday night. Notwith- standing the stormy weather, the!room was well filled, and an enjoyable evening was spent. The Rev. J. Lockwood presided. Lady Brooke delivered an address, and then dis- tributed the prizes for regular attendance. The first four prizes of 5s each were awarded to Lizzie Ray, Edith New- port, Peter Bradburn, and Charles Sanders. The programme opened with the "Harvest Home" chorus by the children, followed by a sketch of "Guy Fawkes," in which eight boys appeared, representing the conspirators Digby, the two Winters, Gaunt, Rokewood, Keyes, Bates, and Johnson' alias Guy Fawkes, afforded a good deal of amusement. Other items of the programme were well received. The accompan- ists were the Misses Brooke and Miss Jeacock. TREAT TO RUNCORN WORKHOUSE CHILDREN.—On behalf of the Guardians, Colonel Ashton on Friday last gave per- mission for 61 children from Dutton Workhouse -to spend a pleasant day at Liverpool Exhibition. The necessary funds for the treat had been subscribed by a number of Runcorn gentlemen, who have previously taken much interest in the homeless waifs. The children, notwithstanding the stormy nature of the weather' thoroughly enjoyed themselves. By the kind influence of Mrs. Heal, formerly of Runcorn, free admission was granted to the Indian Village, and Messrs. Brown and Backhouse deserve thanks for allowing the

Youngsters a free ride down the toboggan slide. The Cocoa House Company supplied the children with food at a re- duced rate. The party leit Liverpool at four o'clock, and arrived home in good time. The schoolmaster and mistress and Mr. Percy Jones had charge of the party. HALTON PAROCHIAL INsTITIITIONs.—On Friday, the 54th anniversary of the Halton Parish Church Clothing Club was held in the school-room adjacent to the church, the Vicar (Rev. J. Lockwood) in the chair. The members of the society during the year have paid weekly sums to the treasurer of the society, to which is added a bounty given by Sir Richard and Lady Brooke and other subscri- bers. The whole of the money was invested in clothing, and on Friday Lady Brooke had the pleasure of distributing upwards of a hundred parcels of clothing. Her Ladyship delivered a short address, in which she adverted to the value of the society in affording its members the means to invest their savings with profit. On the same day the yearly meeting of the Parish Church Sick Club was held, the Vicar being in the chair. He mentioned it as a singular fact that during the eleven years he had officiated as Vicar of Halton not a single member of the society had died. The officers of the society were re-appointed. RUNCORN STARR-BowKETT BUILDING SOciETIES.—The second annual meeting of the Second Runcorn and Dietrict (719) Starr-Bowkett Building Society was held on Thurs- day night, in Bethesda Schoolroom. Mr. S. C. Beckett pre- sided. The report showed that during the year the sum of £615 jee had been received in subscriptions, against £453 93 6d in the previous year. The report was unanimously adopted. The retiring directors—Messrs. S. Pope, W. Arm- strong, G. Moss, and T. Handley—were re-elected. Messrs. W. pewnall and H. Rowe were appointed auditors. At the close of the meeting the ninth appropriation took place. which resulted in Mr. George Marsh. Leinster Gardens. be- ing awarded the sum of £2OO, for 12,1 years, free of interest. Subsequent' the thirty-third appropriation of the first so- ciety was made. The first number drawn was 164; but as the holder had already received an appropriation a fresh ballot was taken, when number 321 was drawn, entitling Mr. Joseph Connah, sen., Frodsbatn, to the use of £lOO, for 12,1 years, free of interest. GRANTS TO RUNCORN SCHOOLS. POPULAR CoNCHRTS AT RuNCORN.—The first of a series of popular concerts to be organised each fortnight during the winter months by the Mill Brow brass band, was held in nethesda schoolroom on Saturday evening. To till what is considered a void in the amusements of the people is the chief object, and the second is to liquidate a debt incurred by the band in providing open-air entertainments during the sum net. An audience of moderate pi oportions aeeem- bled, and bed the pleasure of listening to a vocal and instru- mental programme of much merit. The programme included four pieces by the band, whose performances it would he well to curtail in future, on account of the small size of the room ; and songs by Miss Puckey, of the Liverpool Opera Company, Mr. Richard Morrie, and Mr. Frank Scott. The vocalists acquitted tbernselvee in a manner that elicited the heartiest plaudits of the company, and altogether a pleasant evening was spent. At the close of the concert Mr. R Pierpteint thanked the audience for their presence and net- ronage, and mentioned the arrangements made for foeure concerts. Mr. George Barton's concert company would pro- vide the music on the nest occasion.
