The presents were numerous and costly. The happy couple are spending their honeymoon in London, whence they pro- ceed to Australia. THE STATE OF WESTON POINT ROA.DB.—On Thursday 1 evening, a public meeting of the ratepayers of Weston and: Weston Point were held at the National Schools, Weston, for the purpose of considering what steps should be taken to improve the condition of the roads at Weston Point. M. E. Aaron presided. Mr. R. Clarke said South-road, one of , the main thoroughferes at Weston Point, was quite impasse I able for either vehicular or pedestrian traffic during wet weather. All the owners of property, with one exception, were willing to bear their share towards the repair of the , road, but on account of the person referred to hanging back I it was impossible for them to proceed. The Chairman an Mr. J. W. Kirkham each stated they had brought the matter before the Daresbury Highway Board, but nothing could be done by that body until the road was made. The Rev. J. H. Wilcocksote read a letter that had been written 1 to Mr. S. Yarwood, cab preprietor, Runcorn, with regard to; the dangerou3 character of the roads. After some further', conversation it Was decided, on the motion of Mr. Wilcock- son, seconded by Mr. Clark, "That the Chairman of the meeting be requested to write to the Chairman of the Dares- bury Highway Board respecting the shocking state of the roads at Weston Point, and stating that all the property owners, with one exception, are willing to contribute to the . expense of repairs, and asking him whether the Board can 1 do anything towards putting pressure upon the indivi- I dual in question, or to help the ratepayers in any other I way." A MAGISTERIAL PROSECUTOR. On Tuesday, at the Present Police Court, Henry Scriven and Thomas Singleton, youths, described as butchers from Widnes, were summoned at the instance of Mr. F. W. Earle, J.P., for driving cattle on the highway to the obstruction of the read. Mr. Earle, who sat as chairman, left his. seat, and stated that on Monday, the lot November, about half-past one o'clock in the afternoon, he was driving between Mr. Gladstene's residence at Broadgreen, and his residence at Roby, when he overtook the two defendants driving a qnan- tity of sheep and half a dozen beasts. Scriven, the eldest, was walking on the footpath smoking a pipe and looking on the railway, whilst Singleton was walking in the road. He could not pass the sheep, and he requested Singleton to make a way for him. Singleton refused to do sly, and he then called to Scriven, who took no notice of him. He then asked Scriven for his name, the name of the person to whom the cattle belonged, or where he canoe from, but he refused to give any reply. He had summoned them entirely on public grounds, because such people as the defendants drove sheep and cattle on the road, and were a great nuisance, as they would not get out of the way. He did not press for any fine, but simply wanted to impress on the defendants and others that they must keep the road clear. Had he (Mr. Earle) run over one of the sheep he would have had to pay for it.—The defendants pleaded guilty, and' Mr. Pilleington said that at the request of Mr. Earle he and his brother magistrate (Mr. W. L. Evans) had decided only to call upon them to pay costs on the condition that they promised to be more careful in the future.—The defendants promised this, and paid the costs. A WARNING TO RUNCORN BOATMEN—At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, before Captain Hazlehurst and Mr. A. Thomas, a boatman named George Green was charged with acting in contravention to the bye-laws of the Bridgewater Navigation Company, by obstructing the en- trance to a lock. He pleaded not guilty. He was further charged with wilfully damaging the property of the com- pany by breaking a padlock worth 3s. To this charge the defendant pleaded not guilty.—Mr. F. A. Lake appeared for the company, and stated that the offence took place at four o'clock in the morning of Sunday the 10th October. He remarked that great care and judgment was necessary to regulate the great traffic of the basin and locks at Runcorn; and the defendant's offence was in obstructing the traffic from the tidal basin in to the old basin. Aspey, the lock- tenter, had permitted two boats to proceed from the tidal basin to the old basin, and he therefore decided that a flat , named the " Advance " should come down in turn. The de- fendant, who was in charge of the flat "Clara," persisted in going up the lock in defiance of the lock-tenter's orders, and peshee his boat into the mouth of the entrance. Aspey then placs'd a padlock on the other gate so that the "Clara" could not go any further, when the defendant deliberately walked round the lock and kicked the padlock into the water. He also threatened to treat Awey in a like manner. After blocking the traffic for 15 minutes, the defendant re- trieved his nat. This case was brought to show men in the position of the defendant that the orders of the lock-tenters must be obeyed, and with the object of putting an end to such violent conduct.—William Asney and James Cook- croft proved the case —The defendant contended that when he was shown to be in the wrong he immediately gave way, end offered to apologise and pay for the padlock.—The Bmch imposed a fine of 2s 64 in each case, and ordered the defendant to pay costs amounting to £2 13s,
RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.

An adjourned meeting of this Board was held on Tuesday evening, at the Town Hall, Waterloo-road. Mr. P. Speak- man presided, and there were present Messrs. R. Shaw, Dobson, Grice, Mellor, Fisher, Taylor, Pritcbard, Meadow croft, Lightburn, Lake, Farrell, Hankieson, and White, with Marshall (secretary) and Barker (surveyor).

Board had, however, decided under all the circumstances to assnt to an appointment being made for a period of one year on the terms proposed, but it must be understood that the question of salary would then be open to recomsidera- tion.

The Chairman slid the principal point was whether under the new arrangement the Local Government Board could compel the Board to pay a high salary or whether they could please themselves. The Clerk said he Local Board could please themselves. Dr. Page had said that the new arrangement would not affect the Board in any way in dealing with the officers. Pr. O'Keefle remarked that that letter and Dr. Page's verbal statement did not agrea. _ _
On the snzgestion of the Chairman, the letter was referred to the Health Committee.
THE FLOOD.

Mr. Weght, in moving the adoption of the Gas and Water minutes, referred to the flood of Saturday last, and explained that when the gas holders were completely full, there was as ouch gas stored as would supply tee town for 24 hours. The works were, however, flooded, no gas could be made. and it was thought advisable to give notice to prepare for the worst, as they did not know when the waters would subside. Mr. Carr had handed him a statement showing that the damage done to the gas works amounted to £B3. The Chair.nan said Mr. Carr is issuing that notice took time by the forelock, and be did what was wise and very commendable.—The Clerk read the following letter : .6 Widnes, 6th :November, 1886. G-entlemen,—We beg te give you notice that our works are flooded with water, and we shall bold you responsible for any deinage we may sus- tain in consequence.—Yours obediently, for the Widnes Foundry Co., Bence. Breowx.—The Clerk was instructed to reply repudiating any liability. Mr. R. L. Jones wrote on behalf of the Tharsis Sulphur and Copper Company as follows:—" On Friday night last Bowers Brook commenced to rise very suddenly, and by twelve p.m. the works were flooded two feet deeper than they have ever been, doing an immense amount of damage. Under these ci:-cumstances we uould respectfully ask that the Board would institute an inquiry as to whether there wee any special cause for this occurrence that if such should be found to exiet it may be remedted."—Mr. Carey said not a moment would be lost in ascerteinine; what was the Cause, if any special cause existed, of the flood.—The letter was referred to the Highway Commiitee.

div.head: LIGHTING OF NORMAN•BOAD.
div.p: THE LIGHTING OF NORMAN•BOAD.

The first business was the consideration of the proposal by the General Purposes Committee—" That lamps he pur- chased and fixed at the following places: Eight pillar lamps in Norman-road, three bracket lamps in Okell-street, one bracket lamp in Clarence-street, one bracket lamp in Porter- Street; also that a lamp in Waterloo-road be moved a dis- tance of 12 yards."—Mr. Shaw remarked that several members appeared to take exception to the decision of the chairman and the ruling of the law clerk at the last meet- ing, and there was an idea that the standing orders could be suspended by a vote of the Board. He went on to show that the Board had not that power.—At the call of Mr. Grim the secretary read a letter signed by Messrs. Thomas S. Carr and J. Pevah and the Rev. J. D. lhomae, calling the attention of the Board to the want of gas lamps in Norman-road.—Mr. Grice moved the adoption of the minute. The committee considered that gas lamps in Norman-road which bad been adopted by the Board would be a public convenience.—Mr. Hankinson seconded the motion.—Mr. Shaw, in a long speech, opposed the motion, arid moved an amendment that that portion of the minute referring to Norman-road be struck out. He argued that it bad been adopted in the past as a rule of the Board, in a great mea- sure through the late Mr. Briscoe, who took great interest in these matters, that when property had been erected and tenanted then lamps should be fixed. He contended that this was a safe rule to go upon, and that a case for the lighting of Norman-road had not been made out. During the course of some interruption by Mr. Lightburn Mr. Shaw hinted that perhaps Mr. Lightburn had a hand in this agitation, but Mr. Lightburn denied theallegation.—Mr Meadowcroft seconded the amendment. Mr. Han- kinson pointed out that the road was much used tg vehicles and pedestrian, to Rock Savage and Frodsharn. and said it was positively dangerous in the dark.—Mr. Lake said the rule mentioned by Mr. Shaw was not appliceble to a main thoroughfare such as Norman-road.—Mr. Mellor remarked that 12 months before Mr. Lightburn went to his present residence. Mr. Carr and Mr. Povat mentioned the question of more efficient liehting. —Mr. Shaw said his reference to Mr. Lightburn was in fan. —Mr. Dobson had for years recognised the desirability of lighting this road. At Present it was both dark, unpleasant. and dangerous, and be characterised it as false economy that would prevent the necessary improvement for the sake of a few pounds.—Mr: Lightburn supported the proNsition of the committee, as did also Mr. Fisber.—Mr. Taylor observed that the committee met on the road, and it was so very dark that the members were unanimous in their recommends- tion.—After some observations from the Chairman, the amendment was put and there voted for it Messrs. Shaw, Meadowcroft, and Pritchard. The other members present were against, and the original motiou was then put and carried. THE FREE LIBRARY EXTENSION.

Mr. Fisher moved on behalf of the Finance Committee " that the approval of her Majesty's Tressury be obtained to the appropriation for the purposes of the Library Act of a portion of land and building at the Town Hall." Be ex. plained that this was merely a formal application, and that the nature and extent of the alterations would be dis- cussed subsequently, and they could come to terms with the Library Committee as to an increased rental. The Finance Committee did not want to spend more money than they could possibly help, but at the same time there was no one who wished to prevent the progress of the Library.—Mr Lightburn seconded the motion, which was carried. NVIIO rs THE OFFENDER ?

Mr. Grice asited if be should be in order in now referring to the conduct of a member of the Board.—The Chairman replied in the negative, as that meeting was called for a special purpose. The members then separated.

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting W7a-s- held on Tuesday, undnr the presidency of Mr. F. H. Gossage. Present—Dr. Ols:Peffe, Messrs. S. Sadler. E. Carey, T. Handley, D. Wright, J. Houghton, J. Taylor, W. W. Gossage, J. Midwood, C. Cooke, F. Heyes, J. T. Allen (clerk), W. Higginson (sur- veyor), I. Carr (gas engineer), and J. Dickson (nuisance inspector). THE NIFISANCE INSPECTOR. The Local Government Board, in a letter read by the clerk, signified their willingness to the re-appointment of Mr. Dickson as nuisance inspector for a further period of 12 months. THE MEDICAL OFFICER'S STIpEND. The Local Board having applied to the Local Govern- ment Board to contribute one-half of the salary of the Medi- cal Officer of Health (Dr. Cooper), the London Board 're- plied to the effect that having regard to the population of the district, and to the important duties devolving upon a medical officer of health, the Local Government Board en- tertained doubt as to whether the salary propose,' by the Local Board would afford an adequate remuneration for the efficient discharge of those duties. The Local Government

div.head: DEATH EXTE.-INFANT MORTALITY.
div.p: THE DEATH EXTE.-INFANT MORTALITY.

The Medical Officer of Health reported that during Octo- ber there were 87 births and 47 deaths, being at the respec- tive rates of 37 96 per 1,000 and 20 50 per thousand. Of the deaths 16 were children under one year, and 12 were between one and five years. Zymotic diseases caused 12 deaths.—Dr. O'Keeffe observed that the death rate appeared to be high because it was estimated on a population two or three thousand below what it actually was. The death-rate was estimated on a population of 27,000. The School Board approximated the population at 33,000. and he (Dr. O'Keefe) thought the Boatd ought to base their calcula- tions on a population of at least 30,000. He attributed the large infant mortality to the fact that the children did not receive proper treatment at home, and were generally with- out medical attendarce.

div.head: FLOODED CELLARS.
div.p: FLOODED CELLARS.

Dr. O'Keeffe said the attention of the Highway Commit- tee had been called to the flooded cellars in Victoria-road and Anne-strest. It was almost impossible for the occu- pants of the houses in Anne-street to go into their cellars, because of the horrible stench that arose from them, and this most dangerous nuisance celled for the serious atten- tion of the 'loud.

div.head: WASTE HEAPS -IMPORTANT REPORT.
div.p: THE WASTE HEAPS -IMPORTANT REPORT.

Dr. O'Keeffe said the Health Committee had inspected the waste heaps near the Central Station. Mr. S. Mus- pratt and his manager, Mr. Lewis, were present, but al- though the petitioners as to the nuisance received notice of inquiry through their solicitor, Mr. Peters, not one put in an appearance. The Clerk read the following report on the subject :—On Friday, the 15th Octobtr, three days after the petition was received, tbe committee made a thorough inspection of all the waste being laid at or nea- the Central station. The committee wish to call the attention of the Board to the fact that the railway embankment forming the Central station was made of alkali waste about 10 years ago, and that the property of the petitioners was in e..:istence at that time. The waste now being laid by Messrs. Aiuspratt's close to the property of the petitioners is what is known as "blown" waste, and is said not to yield any yellow or offensive solution It is carefully laid, being thoroughly well "batted" down at the sides and top, and after a short time the sides become like concrete walls. Tl4ere teemed to be very little smell, even when discharging the waste from the wagons. A little further away from the houses the committee noticed a small portion of Cu old emi,nlimsnt to be on fire, and that other potions had been on fire. Instructions were given to write to the railway- compar.y, and Gold, Davis, and Co., on tbe subject. All along the foot of the embankment there were accumulations of stagnant water, and the land north of the railway company boundary was flooded. The committee consider some means of drainage ought to be provided by the railway company and the depositors of waste. The nearest houses are about 300 feet away from where the waste is being deposited, but it is intended to fill up a considerable portion of this space with waste for the purpose of a goods yard. Alto- gether the committee do not consider there is any cause of complaint about the way in which the waste is now beiag laid, and they wish to leave to the Board the question of whether a limit as to proximity to dwelling-houses should be fixed for the deposit of waste. In reply to the Chairman, Mr. Midwood, who is property agent to the Cheshire Lines Committee, said the subject was having every attention.— The report was adopt,d.

div.head: WORE IN COMMITTEE.
div.p: WORE IN COMMITTEE.

Mr. Carr, the gas engineer, reported that at the recent ex- hibition of gas appliances there were 17 cookers hired and 5 sold, 14 heating stoves sold, and 30 houses fitted with gas for lighting. The total number of gas cookers now in use was 84, an 64 beating sores 63. The rainfall for the month hot been 3997 inches. The water in stock on the 27th October was 10,454,634 gallons. Ihe illuminating power of the gas during the month had averaged 16 96 cin- dles. The tender of Messrs. '6ayce and Randle for sewering Bryn-street was accepted. The probable cost is £155. On the recommendation of the Health Committee it was decided to fine the contractor £1 for neglecting to clear away con- tents of ashpits for two days. The surveyor bad been in- structed to prepare plans for a caretaker's cottage at the In- fectious Diseases Hospital, the cost not to exceed £4OO. The receipts of the market for October amounted to £3B 14s 7d, being an increase of £l5 5s Bd, as compared with Octo- ber, 1885. Accounts amounting to £3,639 Os 81 were passed on the proposal of the Finance Committee.

div.head: RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Cemetery Office, on Wednesday. Mr. W. Mellor presided, and there were present Messrs. J. Handley, J.P., G. Moss, W. Littler, E. Imison, W. H. R.)gerson, and W. F. Salkeid (clerk).—The letters from the Rev. W. Preston and Rev. J. Lockwood with regard to banal fees at the cemetery, about which a discussion arose at the last meeting were referred to the General Pur- poses Committee for consideration.—The Chairman reported that daring the seven months ending the 25th October the interments numbered 187 ; corresponding period last year, 192; decrease, 8. The fees received during the same period amounted to £lB5 ss; last year, £202 Sc; decrease, £l7 3s. —The report of the Finance Committee, adopted on the motion of Mr. Moss. showed total receipts of £3B ss. and after paying several small accounts the Mance of £2B 836 d had been paid into bank. The sum of £lOO had been re- ceived from the overseers on account of rate, and had been paid into bank.—Mrs. Margaret E. Gregory, of 4, Shaw- street, had written a letter complaining that on the 7th November, a grave digger named Wright had ruined the plants and shrubs on the grave of her late husband by plac- ing thereon the soil from an adjoining grave which had been opened. When asked to make good the damage by Mrs. Gregory's daughter, he refused, and was discourteous. The members generally expressed the opinion that all such damage should be made geod ; and the secretary was em- poweyed to inquire into the circumstances of this case, and act as be deemed fit. '

RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. The usual fortnightly meeting of this Authority was held at the Board-room at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday after- noon. Lieut.-Colonel J. Ashton occupied the chair, and there were also present the Revs. J. Lockwood and J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. Stoke!, E. Wallington, Aaron, Knowles, W. Whitlow, Speakman, T. Hadfield, T. Lewis, J. Parr, Brandreth, T. Whitlow, J. W. Kirkham, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk). ArponsymExT.—Mr. Farrington, inspector of nuisances, was, on the motion of Mr. Wallington, seconded by Mr. Aaron, appointed inspector under the new Milkshops and , Dairies Acts. TYPHOID FEVER—Mr. Farrington, inspector, read his usual report to the Authority. In it he stated that a case et typhoid fever at Weston Point had terminated fatally. The premises where the case occurred had been disinfected, and some of the a.ticles had been destroyed. The sum of Li was granted to the parties concerned to replace the thins destroyed.—The inspector said that the deceased had caught a cold. and, having taken a patent medicine, went to work during the night. Symptoms of typhoid fever after- wards developed..—.. Mr. Stokes said that it appeared typhoid fever might be brought on through a person taking cold. The case of the celebrated Fred Archer was an instance. Perhaps some cases that had been attributed to insanitary causes had been brought on by cold.—The Deputy-Clerk said that a man in a weak state, who was suffering from cold, might be likely to take disease where a healthy person

r would resist it.—Mr. Aaron referred to a case of typhoid fever in the Authotity's district that bad beer. attributed to I the bad state of a pond near the house. He hid seen the pond, which was a pool of clear water, full of dice and perch. The father of the child told him that the girl went to a school a distance from home, and in wet and cold weather the only place where she could go to eat her din- ner was in the closet. If that was not enough to bring on typhoid fever, or anything else, he was a Dutchman.—The subject then dropped. TBE PUMP AT OVERTON.—The Deputy Clem produced a sample of water taken from Overton public pump, which was very muddy, and had the appearance of being polluted with surface ivater.—Mr. Farrington said he was afraid the pump was a little bit too low. He was going to Over- ton on Wednesday. and would inspect the well and the water.

PUBLIC WELL AT BARTINGTON.—Mr. Farrington stated that he had conferred with the Inspector of the Northwich Rural Authority as to the joint action of the two Authorities respecting the improvement of tnis well, and the conclusion they had arrived at was that the well was not worth im- proving, inasmuch as a much better supply could be obtained at a less cost, if certain arrangements could be made and the quality of the water was found to be satisfac- tory.—lt was o.cided that the Inspector submit a sample of the water for analysis, and if it was found to be good, call the Committee of Inspection together, and lay the particu- lars before them.—Tnis was all the business.
RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. TUE SUPERANNUATION QUESTION.

The fortnig'ntly meeting of this body, held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday afternoon, was presided over by Lieutenant Colonel Ashton. There was an unusually large attendance, the following being present :—Mr. tVeir (vice- chai-man), the Heys. J. Lockwood and J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. E. Aaron, E. Wallington, W. Whittaker, IL Lowe, J Knowlse, E. Jackson. J. Stokes. T. Hewitt, J. Davies, J. Wnitlow, J. Campkin, 'l'. Hadfield, T. Lewis, .1 Parr, J. Brandreth, P.' Hall, T. Forster,J W. Baguley, W. Whitlow, W. Farrell, P. Speakman, S. Tyler, J. Smith, John G. Hamilten, J. W. Kirkham, C Mounfield ; H. Linaker (clerk), W. IL Linaker (deputy clerk).—A lengthy eiscus- eion took place regarding the superannuation granted to Mr. and Mrs. Jones, late master and matron of the Work- house. Notice et' a motion to be proposed by Mr Campkin, to rescind the previous resolution allowing the grant, had been given, but Mr. Hadfield, rising to a point of order, pro- tested against the motion being put to the meeting. He thought Mr. Campkin was wrong in attempting to oppose the unanimous action of a committee, and to upset a resolu- tion passed by the Board. The question was settled, and he maintained that it was not legal to reopen it. Mr. Campkin's motion was out of order, as the sir perannnations had bzen settle'. He then handed to the chairman a memorandum settine fortls his objections as follows : " That Mr. Carnel:in's motion is out of order in consequence of the question of seperannuetion to the late master and matron having been dealt with and settled according to the provisions of the statute, an the orders ire that behalf; that a committee was duly appointed by this Board to consider and deal with the question, and that this Board formally and legally adopted the report of fhat committee; and that the question of Mr. Jones' means (the only reason mentioned in Mr. Campkin'a notice of motion) is quite immaterial, and has no legal bearing whatever on the resolutions adopted by this Board." He wished the chairman to say if the motion could now be put.—Mr. Speakman expressed his astonish- ment thet th 2 question had been raised, as that Board was one that had always been characterised by unanimity and good feeling. The point put by Mr. Hadfield to his mind was a very proper one. The custom of the Board had been that when a motion was pissed at a meeting, the question at a succeeding meeting had simply been one as to the cor- rectness of the reoord of such previous proceedings. He was of opinion that the question could net now be raised.— The Chairman said that he slaould like the Board to work tee:ether amicably; there should be no question as to whether they were actin?: rightly or wrongly. He then recapitulated what had been done in reference to the superannuation of Mr. and Mrs. Jones. Eight or ten weeks ago the resignation of the master, which included that of the matron, was sent in, and a committee was appointed to consider the question of superannuation. It was composed of fifteen mem- bers of the Board. comprisine six from the Budworth ois- trict, five from Runcorn, and four from Frodseam. That committee met on-the following Tuesday, wheel there were present four from Budworth distrie, four from Runcorn. and four from Frodsham. They bee before them the Act of Parliament under which Guardians were empowered to act; the suggestions of the Local Government Board ; and statements made out by the clerk showing what the salaries of Mr. and Mrs. Jones were, and what the emolu- ments were worth when they were commuted. The Local Government Board made their basis at one-sixtieth. if an eflicer had served 20 years they suggested that 20 60ths of his salary should be allowed him as superannuation; if 30 years. 30410ths; and so on up to 40-60ths. the limit. If the officer had done his duty well, the Guardians could add a number of his years to his term of service, not exceeding 10 years. Mr. Jones's salary was £BO a year. his rations I worth £3l year, and apartments £l5, making £126. They also found he had served 29 years, and considering Mr. Jones's state of health, and what he had done for that Board they thought it would be a proper thing to add five years to hie term, making his length of service thirty-four years, and on that they gave a grant of 34-60ths, which made the sum .£7l B.s. They adopted the same course with respect to Mrs Jones's salary, but they did not add any extra number of veers to the term of her service. She had served 29 Years, and they gave her 29-60 the. which amounted to £4B 16s 4d. The Act required that a month's notice of the intention to grant such superannuation pay should be given to each member of the Board. That was done, and he thonght it was well- known to every Guardian what the decision of the com- mittee was. The meeting of the Board took place three weeks after the meeting of the committee, and he thought if there bad been any objection to the grant oeing made it was great pity it was not made on that day. On the morning it was brought forward no one rose to say a word against it. He naturally concluded that it was going to be carried unanimously, but on putting it to the vote 11 voted for the grant and six against it No amendment was proposed, and he thought it was a pity the matter had been brought for- ward again that day. Before he gave his decision as to the , legality of the notice of motion. he should like Mr. Camp- kin, at the eleventh hour, to consider and see if he could not withdraw it. He should like the harmony of the Board to be considered, and hoped Mr. Campkin could see his way to withdraw the notice of motion.— Mr. Campkin said he felt it bis duty to protest against the grants. He considered that it was their duty to look after the interests of the ratepayers, and could not withdraw his motion. He thought Mr. Jones had been well paid.—Mr. Hadfield : You should not make a speech until the chair- man has decided.—The Chairman said it was a do :Will question as to what should be done, and suggested that the opinion of the Local Government Board be asked as to whether the motion should be put or not.—After further discussion the Clerk, replying to a member, said the matter was one in which no clerk in the county had as yet had any I experience. He did not think such a thing had arisen be- fore, either in that or in the adjoining county.—The De- , nutv Clerk expressed the opinion that the Guardians, having exercised their powers by granting the annuities, could not now withdraw the grants they had vested in Mr. and Mrs Jones. Oct the strength of the grants Mr. and Mrs Jones had incurred liabilities they perhaps would not otherwise have done.—A Member : The public is against it —Mr. Hadfield : Why did not von say so at the time.—Mr. Campkin: Unfortunately it was a wet day and a great many members were not here.—Mr. Aaron seconded Mr. Hadfield' s proposition that the motion be not put.—Mr. Campkin :If the members represent the ratepayers they will vote for my motion.—Mr. Hadfield protested against such a remark.— The Clerk said he did not see how any harm could arise by deferring the matter for a fortnight, for the opinion of the Local Government Board.—Mr. Campkin: This question has called together a great number of Guardians. and I wish to take a vote to-day. Why defer it ?—Mr. Hadfield : It will be to the interest of the rate- payers if those Guardians will come again.—Mr. Lowe : Take the result to-day, Mr. Campkin. They know they are beaten, and that is why they don't want it taken to-day.--- The Rey. J. Lockwood then moved that the Board act on the advice of the law clerk, and that the opinion of the Lo- cal Government Board be taken as te whether the notice of motion was legal, and that the matter stand adjntirned for a fortnight.—The proposition was seconded by Mr. Taylor. and on being put to the meeting 18 voted for, and 13 against it.—The motion was therefore carried.

div.head: ALLEGED ROBBERY BY A MOTHER-LN-L&W AT
div.p: ALLEGED ROBBERY BY A MOTHER-LN-L&W AT
WIDNES.

At Widnes Police Court, on Mon:lay, before Mr. F. H. Gossage, Mary Ann Holding, a Tim lie-aged wonaan, for- merly living with her son-in-law, Thomas Fildes, botcher, Widnes-road and Waterloo-road, was charged on remand with having on Saturday. the 30th ult.. stolen £B2, the pro- perty of that person. Mr. Swift, of St Helens, defended. The facts of the case have already been given. P.S. Strickland stated that he had examined the drawers in which the money was placed, but had found no marks of violence upon them. They must, in his opinion, have been opened with a key. Mrs. Fildes said she was in the hones on the Saturday night in question with the prisoner and her (witness's) little sister. She and the little girl wpnt into the shop, leaving prisoner in the kitchen with a child which she was going to take upstairs. Shortly afterwards her (witness's) attention was called to the state of things upstairs, when she found the drawers open, and the mousy gone. The silver placed in the other room was also missing.

Mr. Swift said the prisoner had lived four or five yews at the prosecutor's. She bad had the run of the house during the whole of that time, and money had been repeatedly left about without being locked up, and she had bad numerous opportunities of stealing if she bad been of that disposition Neither Fildes nor his wife had the slightest suspicion n't her, and they asked that she might ba discharged. He might remark that workmen had been employed doing , repairs about the house on the day of the robbery. and the window had been left open. It was quite within the range of possibility, therefore, that they might have been con- cerned in the robbery, or if they tbetwelves were not con- cerned, they might have told some one that the money was lying about, and the person thus informed take advantage of the information given. _

Inspector Wood asked for a remand until Tuesday week, in order that further inquiries might be made with the ob• ject of discovering the rest of the missing money. The remand was granted Mr. Swift applied for baillbot the Bench refused.

div.head: WIDNES WORKS FLooDtp.
div.p: WIDNES WORKS FLooDtp.

The heavy rains of Friday and Friday night last week produced serious results in that part of Widnes known as Lugsdale and Newtown. Through the incessant downpour water accumulated to a depth hitherto unknown in that part of the town; and much discomfort and damage was caused. In many quarters it is supposed that some defect in Bower's Brook, which drains an outlying portion of the town, was the main factor in the flood, but the Highway Committee of the Lecal Board have instituted a strict in- vestigation, and from them some explanation may be ex- pected. Late on Friday night numerous houses became flooded to a depth of from three to six feet, and the unfore tunate inmates bad to take refuge in tee upper rooms, leav- ing what furniture they could not take with them to the mercy of the " waste of waters." At the gas works the water rose to such a height that all operations had to be suspended, and although there was a considerable quantity of gas stored, there was every appearance on Saturday morning that the townspeople would have to return to the primitive method of lighting by means of oil and candles. With commendable forethought Mr. Carr, the managing en- gineer, issued notices to that etfect to the large consumers of gas, so that they could prepare accordingly. Fortunately. however. the rain ceased about ten o'clock, and the workmen by strenuous exertions which were admirably directed by the manager, contrived to again get the processes in working order during the after- noon to the great relief and convenience of manufacturers, statien officials, and tradesmen. The damage is estimated at £B3. The works of the Widnes Foundry Company were also flooded, but not to such an extent that the men had to entirely cease labour. Much inconvenience and loss was, however, eustained. and the firm have notified that they will hill the Local Board responsible. Perhaps the greatest sufferers were the Tharsia Sulphur and Copper Works. Within the boundaries of this rnanufac•ory water accumula- ted to a depth of nearly six feet, Ike furnace fires were quenched, and the flues flooded, and operations had to en- tirely cease at midnight on Friday. Several days elapsed before the works resumed their normal condition, and the damage, it is stated, will total to about £l,OOO. A danger- ous ircident occurred in Lugsdale-road on Saturday morn- ing. A number of men employed by Mr. David Forster, ironfounder, started in a waggonette with tbe intention of going to Warrington. After proceeding a short distance through the water, the wheel of the conveyance became fast against a submerged stump, and all the efforts of the occu- pants to release the vehicle proved futile. The traces were cut as a last resource, and dry land was reached on the horse's back. The waggonette was allowed to remain until the water had subsided.

div.head: WESLEYAN FOREIGN MISSIONS. RUNCORN.
div.p: WESLEYAN FOREIGN MISSIONS. RUNCORN.

The annnal sermons in aid of the Wesleyan Foreign Mis- sions were preached in St. Paul's Church, on Sunday. The preacher was the Rev. Jatez Marrat,, of Bradford. At Camden School Chapel in the morning, Mr. William Shaw preached, and in the evening Ur: Rev. R F. Hornbrook officiated.

On Monday evening the annual meeting was held in S. Paul's Chapel, and there was a good attendance. Mr. J. Simpson occupied the chair, and• he was supported on the platform bY the Revs. Jabez Marra% of Bradford, and Robert Morton, of Liverpool (deputation), E. Wood, A. P. Watson, J. D. Thomas, and E. Williams ; Messrs. R. Shaw, R. Norman, T. Sip:lister, J. R. Frith, B. Kniveton, Lord, F. J. Norman, &c. The Rev. E. Williams having offered up prayer, Mr. T. Simister reed the annual repo' t. He stated that the number of circuits on the mission stations was 209, chapels and other places 1,273, missionaries 304, other paid agents L7lO, unpaid agent', local preachers, and so on 3,519, church members 30,808, on trial for church member- ship 4,274, and scholars in bunday schools 55,608. The gross income of the society for 1883, iecludine a small bal- ance from the previous year, amounted to £138,183 103 6d. The expenditure amounted to £142.866 8s 11d, leaving a deficiency of £4,682 18e sd. The following were the amounts received from Runcorn Branch for this year :—By Mrs Soulby £8 18s, Miss Speakman £5 18s 6d, Miss Nor- man and Miss Peacock £l4 63 6d, Mr. and Mrs Johnson's box 15s. The public collections in St. Paul's on the pre- vious day amounted to £l5 18s 14, ard the collection at Cam- den School Chapel amounted to 13s .1-d. At Camden Sunday' School there was collected in the male classes £5 85101 d, and in the girls' classes £3 14e 7d. The girls collected with books £ll 13e id, and in the infant class £7 7s 98 was raised. On the previous day £1 45 9d was collected in the school. At Camden they had an invaluable secretary, and they had done well indeed to raise the total of £22 9e Id. At Bruns- wick School there was collected in the girls' classes £3 6s 11d, boys' classes £8 14s 101 d. The boys with books collected £22 is 11d, whilst the girls in the same manner gathered £3l 2s 6d. The amount collected at the two missionary meetings held in the school during tbe year was £l5 3s 6d. The total sum raised at Brunswick School one year was £75, and then they went down. Last year, how- ever, they sprung up to £77, and this year the total had risen to £BO 19s 31 for Brunswick School. (Applause.} The total amount raised in the Runcorn branch was £159 Os. (Applause.) They were £2 193 5d behind last year. Mr. Stmister spoke words of commendation and encourage- ment to the young people who had taken so important a part in the mission work. The Chairman, who was cordially received, said he could not but remember that of those who used to meet on that platform he was the only one left. All the rest bad passed away. He was vers thankful that others were present to take their places. Year after year, as one and another dis- appeared from their midst, they found there were others to succeed them, and so the work went on. He had been in- terested in missions all his life. He believed that it was either 61 or 62 years since in the old chapel—not Brunswick Chapel, but the one before that—since he attended the first missionary meeting that he remembered. He could remelts. ber his father sitting on the platform, and he stood between his knees. Then when his father went to live in the coun- try, and he was about nine or ten years of age, he was a col- lector, and he had the honour of being treasurer of the Ju- venile Missionary Association. For a number of years he had worked very hard in that little society which a -few of them established. In the country, riding sometimes two together on a pony—(laughter)—they managed to get £lO or £l2 a year, a great part of it being in weekly subscriptions. Of course for a good many years he had had to satisfy himself with being a subscriber. No longer a collector, be did all he could to encourage the collectors, and especially in con- nection with Brunswick Sunday School. (Applause.) His own experience taught him that to interest the children in missionary work when they were young was one of the best things they could do. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Simpson men. tinned the fact that on the second Tuesday in November 21Y years ago that beautiful chapel of St. Paul was opened. (Applause.) Of course they all remembered their old friend Mr. Thomas Hazlehurst—(applause)—in connection with the chapel. He had passed away, and Dr. Hanna and Mr. Walker, who preached the first two sermons in the chapel, had also gone. Alluding to the growth of their missionary society. Mr. Simpson said the report published this year was the 72n8—(applause)—and the last report printed for Runcorn district was the 69th. (Applause.) He had somewhere the first report for the Warrington circuit, and he did not snppose there was one single person liv- ing now whose name appeared in that report for 1817. Mrs. Biddlebrook was the last whose name appeared in the report and she was now gone. In concluding the Chairman ex- pressed his thankfulness that there was so much missionary spirit in connection with the one with which he himself was associated, and be hoped that as years went on the interest would increase, and that year after year they would not find that Runcorn was falling back. (Applause.) The Rev. Jabez Marratt referred to his residence in Run- corn 18 years ago, and the mission changes that had taken place during that period. He described the labours and difficulties of Missionaries in the West Indies, where be had held a position. The greatest event in the West Indies was the emancipation of the slaves, and this event was largely brought about by missionary labour. (Applause.) From the beginning Methodism had uttered its protest against slavery. John Wesley had more faith—King George then in Parliament; he was opposed to progressive legislation, condemned the rising spirit of American independence, and looked on such men as Edmund Burke and Charles James Fox as dangerous demagogues. But no man bad tenderer pity for those who were suffering cruel wrong in slavery—no man applied a keener caustic than he did to the abominations of slavery. His followers caught his spirit, and they found Adam Clarke denouncing slavery as a system cursed at both ends and blasted in the middle; and 'Richard Watson rising to his loftiest pitch of eloquence in asserting the rights of slave.; and many ministers and lawyers helped forward emancipation by word and action, until in the end, the great boon of freedom was granted. (Applause.)

The Rev. R. Morton then delivered an' eloquent address upon Missionary enterprise in China and Africa, and com- bated the statement sometimes made that Missions were 3 failure, and contended Missions had been a glorious suc- cess beyond reasonable expectations. If the temporal benefits to arts and commerce were the only standard of their success, these were an ample reward; but by means of the Missionaries, those ferocious as lions had been transformed into doves, and had manifested the gentleness and innocence of the lamb. (Applause.) Mr. R. Norman moved and the Rev. A. P. Watson secon- ded a vote of thanks to the deputation, which was carried and replied to. On the proposition of Mr. B. Kniveton, seconded by the Rev. J. D. Thomas, the retiring Committee were thanked for their past services and re-appointed. In terms of eulogy, Mr. Frith moved, and Mr. R Shaw seconded a vote of thanks to the Chairman, which was ac- corded with acclamation. The proceedings closed with the singing of the Dox- ology.

FELONIES AT BL'ETONWOOD.—On Monday, at an Occasional Court at Warrington, Bridget Ann Walsh was charged on remand with receiving stolen goods, the propertv of John Prescott, at Burton- wood, and John I'V'alsh was charged with stealing potatoes from a field belonging to John Prescott. They were remanded to the Petty Sessions to be held at Newton. • WESLEYAN FOREIGN MISSIONS, APPLETON.—On Tuesday evening the annual missionary meeting was held in Appleton Wesleyan Chapel. Mr. J. J. Sanderson presided, and there was a large attend- ance. Addresses were delivered by Mr. James Knowles, of Yew Tree Farm, Appleton; Mr. G. E. Young, and the Rev. J. llowell Jones, of Warring- ton. As a result of the anniversary £lO us has been contributed, being .-Cl. more than last year

div.head: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. Moistm.Y.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), Alder- man Davies, and Councillor Greening. A DISORDERLY YOUNG Wousx.—Mabel Gandy was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Butter- market-street on Satardv night, and with having assaulted Police Constable Johnson. There WAS a further charge against her of having been drunk and disorderly on the 28th ult. She was sent to prison for fourteen days on each

charge. ASSAULT ON A WOMAN.—Martin Fleming, for having been drunk and disorderiy, and for having struck a woman named Hennersey, in Scotland-road, was fined 20s. and costs, the alternative is case of non-payment being 14 days'

imprisonment. MancrxwaNce CASIL—A painter named Barnes was sum- moned for not maintaining his wife, for whom Mr. A. " Browne appeared. The parties. it was stated, bad been mar- ried about four years,but in 1884 defendant left his wife un- provided for, and went to liye with his mother. Defendant, who said he would rather suffer death than live with his wife, was ordered to pay 105. a week towards her mainten- ance. EVADING DISTUAVT.—Patrick Prendergast, charged with removing his goods in order to avoid distraint, was ordered to pay double tbe value of the goods. DRUNEBNNBSS.—Catherine Salmon, Esther Clarke, and Mary Burns were tined for drunkenness. BRBACH OF TUB PBACIL—James Richardson was bound over to be ot good behaviour for six months on a charge of fighting. TRIA2ORLIZY TRANSFERS or LICSINSES.—The following were granted :—Royal Exchange' Golden Square, from Thomas A,-cher to Peter Lawless; Lord Rodney. from Alex- ander Baird to Thomas Massey.; baerhouse in-Queen-street, from Thomas Jackson to Alexander Baird; and an off license from George Beard to Sarah Ann Howard. WIDNIODLY.—Before Alderman Chandley, Councillor I Greening, and Mr. John Fairclosigh. DRUNKISINBSS.—A. man named Griffiths was fined 103 and costs for being drunk and disorderly in Bewssy-street on the previona afternoon.—Mary Nicholson, for being drunk in Arpley Walk and acing indecently, was fined 5s and costs.—William Marsh, charged with drunkenness in Scot- land-road, was dismissed on premising to leave the town. FAILING TO REPOUT.—Mary Ann Taylor, a young woman under police supernsion, was remanded to the Sal- ford police on a charge of failing to report herself at Sal-

lord. Tarnsiosy—Before Major Litton and Alderman W,beter. DRUNKENNESS.—RaIph Taylor, for being drunk and dis- orderly in Buttermarket-street on Ilia previous evening, was fined ss. including costs. ASSAULT ON A STIPMOTHER.—Annie Barrow, a young woman, was sent to prison for fourteen days for assaulting Hannah Barrow, her stepmother, who alleged that she wounded her on the head with a smoothing iron. Prisoner, in defence, pleaded great provocation, and the Bench ad- monished complainant to learn to restrain her temper. FAIDAY.—Bef ore Captain Reynolds, Mr. John White, Mr. R Garnett, and Dr. Gornall. MISCELLANBOUS.—Andrew Duffy, for being drunk in the Market-place, was fined 103 and costs.—Sarah Ward.l for being guilty of indecent behaviour, was sent to prison for seven days. RUNAWAY APPWANTICHS. Tbe following apprentices were summoned, at the instance of Mr. John Platt, for ab- senting themselves from work, and were ordered to resume their employment :—Esily Andrews, Annie Clark, Cather- ine Ellison. Annie Hands, and Maria Read. Ellen Flynn and Sarah Jane Jones did not appear, and warrants were ordered. Elizabeth Ann Wotdsworth, who did not appear, was committed to prison for seven days. Carnm.—John Partington was summoned at the in- stance of R.S.P.C.A. for ill-treating a horse on the 30th nit. The horse was one of a pair drawing a load of furni- ture, and was seen by an inspector to be very lame. He was ordered to pay costs. TEIRELTS —Thomas Birchen was summoned for using threats to Thomas Stirrup, and was bound over in his own recegnisances of LS to keep the peace for six months. Stir- rup was summoned for assaulting Edward Birchen, the son of the previous defendant, hut as the witnesses were too young to give evidence, the case had to be dismissed.

WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. F. H. Gossage. DETINKENNISS.—The following persons were fined 53 and coats for this offence :----John and Ann McCormick. James Keogh, James Fleming, Joseph Patton, Bernard Feeney, Patrick Connor, and John McDonald.—Mary Moran was fined 7s 64 and costs for a similar offence. ALLEGED TUE-FT Ori DIZAER.—Thomas Martin, a tramp, was charged with having on the sth inst. stolen a drake, value 43 8.1. the preperty of Geo. Munslow, labourer, from a field at the back of Fairfield House, Appleton.— About seven o'clock en Friday night prisoner went into the Cuerdley Cross public-house, and cffered the drake for isle for is. He was suspected, and Sergeant Cairns, of the War- rington Division, took him into clastody.—Mrs. Munalow identified the drake as her husband's property, and said she Saw It safe at two o'clock on Friday afternoon, and missed it the same day about five.—Prisoner was remanded for a weal.,

RUNCORN t•EfTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Captain Hazlehurst end Mr. A. Thomas. THIIPORARY AITTHORITY.—ttobert Gorst was granted tem- porary authority to sell beer and wines at the confectioner's shop lately occupied by Miss James. DRI7NYBNNESS.--John Monaghan was fined 58 and 9s 6,1 costs for being drunk in Vicar-streot on the 2nd Novembar. P.C. Millington Droved the Case.—Samuel Whitby, Prod- sham, was fined 10s and 17s costs for being drunk and dis- orderly in Bridge-street on the 14th September. P.C. Smith proved the case.

Cusapirs? House in the city for Glass, China, Oriental Wares, and Fancy Goods.-175. Oxford-street, Manchester.— Advt. ANOTHILIt CABINET MESTING.—A Cabinet Council was held at noon on Thursday at the Foreign Office. The first Minister to arrive was Viscount Cross' who walked over from the India Office shortly before 12and joined Lord Iddesleigh, who had previously arrived from Windsor. Lord Salisbury did not arrive at the Foreign Office until 12-20, the train from Hatfield baying been delayed. TAMPERING WITH THE TELEGRAPH. At Marlborough. street Police Court, Lcndon, on Tuesday, Myer Myers was again charged with attempting to obstruct the sending of certain telegrams by endeavouring to induce the manager of the Exchange Telegraph Company to send private sig- nals over the company's instruments, to denote the winners of races, and enable the prisoner to back them. Mr. Gregory, manager of the company, recalled, said It would be im- possible to carry out the prisoner's suggestions with- out detection. He was committed for trial, bail being

allowed: Tms CLINICAL IMPOSTII2.--" The Rev. Dr. Keating was again brought before the Dublin magistrates on Mon- day, charged with fraud and also with failing to report him- self to the police, he being a convict under supervision. Evidence was given as to the assistanoe granted to the pri- soner by the Priests' Protection Society on his representa- tion that he had been a priest of the Romish Church, and in asking fora committal counsel forlthe prosecution pointed out that daring part of the time that the prisoner srid he was in Rome he was actually in prison in,this country. The prisoner was committed for trial. THI NATIONAL LNA.GITH MIITINGS IN TRILAND.—A largely-attended meeting under the auspices of the Yeughal branch of the National League, was held on Sunday, and was addressed by Messrs. Lane and Flynn, The Ponsonby tenants who were present. were advised to carry out the plan laid down by "United Ireland," and to boy- cott those who opposed this measure. Several thousand persons attended the National League meeting at Skib- bereen. Dr. Kenny, Mr. O'Shea, and Dr. Tanner, M.P.'s, spoke, and advised farmers to adopt the programme pub- lished by United Ireland," and to pursue a firm and un- yielding attitude towards rack-renting landlords. A National League demonstration was also held at Castlebar. SERIOUS ENCOUNTBR BITSVIURN FISIIING CRINTS.—A Lowe9toft correspondent telegraphs that great excitement VMS caused there on Tuesday by the report that a Lowestoft trawler had been fired at on the fishing grounds by a Belgian fishing vessel. It appears that on Monday night the lugger Clyde shot her nets, 25 miles from Lowestoft, and that at seven o'clock a Belgian trawler, No. 137, sailed into the nets and came into collision with the Lowestoft boat, her bow- sprit striking the capstan of the Clyde. The Belgian men then, it is alleged, commenced to stone the Lowestoft men with pieces of granite. after which she sailed away, Shortly afterwards, however, she returned, but the Clyde made off so fast to windward that the Belgiin boat could not over- take them. A gun was then fired three times from the Belgian vessel, the shot striking the rigging of the Clyde. The same night, the Evening Star, another Lowestoft lug- ger. was trawled by a foreign vessel, which afterwards
escaped. KAy'S COMPOUND, a demulcent anodyne expectorant for Coughs and Colds. Bold by all Chemists, *L., Is. lid., 25.9 d. —Advt.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

' Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to thehead office. Berney-street. Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.

RUGBY RULES. COCICEEDGE RIOTERS T. WARRINGTON EXCELSIORS Played on the ground of the latter, and after a noisy game ended in a dispute and draw. SANKEY RANGERS V. HOWLEY ROVERS.—Played on the ground of the former on Saturday, and after a roußh game ended in a win for the Rangers by 2 tries and 12 minors to
1 miner. STAMFORD RANOTiRS V. BLUE COAT RANORRS.—This match was played on the ground of the latter on Saturday. and resulted in an easy victory .for the former by 2 goals, 3

tries, 6 minors, to nil. COCKHEDGE MISSION STAR OE HOPE (2ND TEAM) Y. S. JAMES,' LATCHFORD.—PIayed on the ground of the former on Saturday, and after a one-sided game victory rested with the" Stars" by seven points to nil. WARRINGTON TRUE BLUES T. TYLDHSLEIT FREI WAN- DIRERS.—PIared at Tyldesley on Saturday, on the ground of the latter. The game resulted in a win for the Warring- ton True Blues by 1 try and 6 minors to 1 minor. WIDNES RECREATION (2ND TEAM) T. WIDNES TREE Bmas. On Saturday these two teams had a trial of strength on the " Rees' " ground, which, after a rather rough game, resulted in a draw ; the "Blues" scoring five minors, and the "Rees" two. WIDNES RECREATION E. SWINTON "A " TEAM. Played at Swinton on Saturday, in wretched weather, rain falling all the time. After an hour's good play the result was a draw—Swinton scoring six minors, " Rees" one. The score, however, hardly indicates the state of the game, as Swinton scored most of their minors by long kicking. RUNCORN RECREkTION v. SUTTON (2ND TIAMS).—& match was played between the above teams on Saturday, on the Sutton ground, resulting in a victory for the visitors. The tries were obtained by T. Cotteralt and P. Brookes. Result : Runcorn, 2 tries, 3 minors; Sutton, 1 minor. Runcorn Recreation had only 14 players to their oppo- nents' 15. RUNCORN FREE WANDERERS V'. WEST BANE WATER. LILLIES.—This match was played on the ground of the former on Saturday, and after a pleasant but hard- fought game victory rested with the home team by 1 goal, 1 try, and 2 minor.; to 1 minor. Garrett and Hughes scored the tries for the winners„Robinson obtaining the major point. RUNCORN RECREATION v. SUTTON.—This match was played on the Rinreation ground before a fair number of spectators on Saturday last. The visitors arrived rather late and with a short team, but they obtained the services of T. Davies, W. Stubbs, and J. Ford, of the Runcorn Foot- ball Club. Sutton, winning the toss, decided to play down. hill, Acton kicking off with the wind. The game was con- fined to the visitors' quarter most of the first half, during which Davies was forced to touchdown, and Booth gained a try which was not improved upon. The second half was played in semi-darkness, Berlinson scoring a try for Sutton, but failed at the place, the game ending slightly in favour of the Recreation by one try, one touchdown, to one try. Teams: Sutton : J. McCulley, back ; three-quarter backs, T. Davies, Wilson, and Bickerstaff ; half backs, W. Harrison and W. Green ; forwards, Unsworth, H. Harri- son. P. Critchley, T. Fowles, R. Fowles, J. Ford,W. Stubbs, Berlinson, and W. Travis. Recreation: D. Barton, back; three-quarter backs, James Clare. S. Abrame, H.Pendlebnry, and E. Howard; half backs, W. Woodward and J. Pendle- bury ; forwards, Acton. Pennington, Worrell, Massey, S. Booth, John Green, A. Peacock, T. Carr. SANEST T. ST. PAUL'S. A match between the above clubs was played on Saturday on the ground of the latter, ' which, owing to the recent rain, was in very bad condition. A short and rough game ended in a draw slightly ia favour of the visitors. The ball was started by the home team and Jefferson put in a long kick which was not returned Some smart scrimmaging near the line ensued, and Sankey obtained a couple of minors in quiet succession. From the drop oat the St. Paul's forwards rushed the ball up the field ' and Harding's kick being charged down, Evres obtained a try which, although the place was an easy one, was not im- I • proved open. Harding dropped out, and no return being made, Sankey were again in their opponents territory, and Fair had hard lines in not scoring. In the second half Sankey had much the best of the game. Their forwards. worked well together. Ashton was conspicuous with a good run, being only brought down on the line. Barton at last, however, made the score equal by obtain;ng a splendid try, rounding his opponents in good style. The place, which was a very difficult one, was entrusted to Ashton, who made a good attempt, and the match remained drawn. The St. Paul's players when pressed had a trick of constantly dropping on the ball, thereby stopping the play and causing unpleasantness. RUNCORN v. NEW BRIGTITON.—OnIy a moderate com- pany assembled at Liscard on Saturday, many being no doubt deterred by the unfavourable condition of the ele- ments. The ground was very heavy, and it was with diffi- culty that the players kept a foothold. Combination, aided by quick action on the part of the Runcorn men, asserted its superiority, early en in the game no less than nine minors being conceded. In the second half the Runcornites again held the upper han-1, and though towards the close of the game New Brighton played up splendidly, they even- tually suffered defeat by a goal, two tries, and ten minors to a goal (dropped) and one minor. Rome kicked off, and after a moderate return by Broady play settled down in Runcorn's 25. The green jerseys eventually broke through and Leitch soon had to save. From this point Runcorn completely mastered their opponents by their qeicknees'and passing tactics, minor aster minor being conceded, and by the time the interval was reached Runcorn had nine minors to their credit. After facing about Lewis's kick was charged down. Speakman then got away, and a series of passes brought the Brideeites near the home lines. where Rip; kicked out. After the line out Townsend tackled Hughes, and though Rome relieved the pressure with a flying kick, it was only temporary, as Riley came hack rapidly, and the visiting backs showed some excellent passing in front of goal, bat ulti- mately the ball was loose, and being dribbled over, Broady fell on it, and the same player placed a neat goal. Runcorn again besieged the home quarters after the kick off, and soon compelled a touchdown. Leose play again gave Runcorn much advantage, and Riley and Andrews between them took the ball from mid-field to within five yards of the line, where, after a fierce struggle, Hughes succeeded in getting over, but the place being a difficult one. it failed. New Brighton now pulled them- selves together, Rome, Leitch, mid Rigg doing a power of work. Following the kick out the ball was scrimmaged at Runcorn's 25 mark, and after some hot work Leitch snapped up and, whilst running sideways, dropped a grand goal amid great cheering. This splendid bit of play seemed to place Runcorn on their metal, and, quickening the pace, they, despite grand checks on the part of Rome, Rigg, and Dutton. broke through, and carried everything before them. Rome then attempted to kick the ball dead, but Broady was quickly on to it, and gained a try. The place was taken very close in, the result being that it was charged down. When the whistle blew the result was as above stated. Teams: Runcorn—T Weed, back; W Riley, H Cawley. and H C Speakman, three-quarter backs: H Hughes and H G Andrews. half backs W Wright, J Lewis. J Barnes, W Broady, J Clarke, J Gatlev, W Faulkner, F Joule. and G Wainwright. forwards. New Brighton—Edwards, back; W J Rigg, W Rome, and H R Townsend, three-quarter backs; W Leitch and H Slater, half backs; J G Gif- ford, S R Williams, H Dodd, B J Browne, W Dut- ton, J Cowper, C Manifold, H P Blunt, and A Williams, forwards.

WARRINGTON V. WIDNES. Matches between Warrington and Widnes teams are al- ways looked forward to with a great deal of interest by the numberless admirers of football in the two localities, and consequently, although Saturday was anything but a pleasant day to tarn out, there was a great gathering of spectators—estimated to number 4 000—on the ground off Wilderspool-causaway, when the two teams aeein met. Neither side played their full strength, but the game, never- theless, was keenly contested, with the result that in the end Warrington won by one goal and two minors to nothing. , Mr. Cronshaw, president of the Wizen Clue, was the referee, 1 and it was chiefly through his fair and unbiassed decision that the game was so pleasantly contested, not a sign of a squabble at any period of the game being discernible. H. Ashton won the toss, and elected to play with the wind in his favour. Morris, therefore, kicked off ea behalf of the Chemicals, and Massey, being on the alert, returned finely. Feerell, the famous Widnes half back, was the first to lead off with a smart run, but his career was checked about the half way flag. This was closely followed by a nice kick by Barnes, and Massey following up prevented a return, the ball going into touch. Dillon, Ashton, Povey, and Fair Turner now broke away, and with the aid of "Tommy " the ball was taken to the line, and for some time the visiters' goal line was in danger. Farrell, however, proved himself equal to the occasion, and removed danger to tei 25. A good kick by Welsh was the next feature, and then Barnes took a drop at goal, after a pass by Speakman, a minor be- ing the result of a good attempt. Morris took the drop, the ball landing into touch in neutral quarters. The Warrington forwards still assumed the aggressive, until S. Bingham, by a nice dribble, took the meal to the half way deg. Here • Barnes took a pass intended for Harding, and when checked passed to Jolley, whose career was only stopped on the has. Here the home team made strenuous efforts to score, but the Whinesians made equal efforts to prevent it, with the result that ia a short time the Chemical forwards relieved the pressure, and came through with a rush to halt way. Barnes picked the bell smartly up from under , their feet and punted to touch. Speakman now came to the fore by a free kick, from whice advantage the sphere was quickly propelled to the visitors' territory. Barnes next received a pass from Gilbert, and had a second try at goal, the attempt, although a rod one, only' result- ing in another minor, being a few inches wide. From the kick out excellent play was exhibited by Parkinson, Gil- bert, Farrell, and Jolley, the Warrington pair taking the ball to the Widnes quarters, where Gilbert gave terms ' another chance of displaying his goal-kicking abilities, and this time, as the little centre said, " The third time pays for all," for be landed a grand goal, which proved to be the winning point of the match. This put the Chemicals on 1 their mettle, and for some time play raged in neutral quar- ters, until W. Dillon managed to break away, but was ! checked by Farrell. The Widnes half beck shortly after- wards obtained a free kick, to which Fair Turner replied by 1 a tremendous rush. Farrell again got in a nice run, and ' then the Chemical forwards, beaded by Smith and Wilkin- son, broke away with a beautiful dribble to the home line ; 1 but Gilbert relieved and passed to Barnes. who removed still , farther to touch. A good rush by J Smith brought about half time, with the score Warringtor, one goal two minors to nil. The second half was splendidly contested, neither side being able to notch a siugle point, the Warringtoniaes striving hard to increase the score, and the Widnesiane striving hard to equalise matters. With regard to the play, Warrington certainly bad the best of it nearly all through. The only time when they were really put upon their defence was towards the close of the first half, and it mat be eonfessed that it was some- what of a relief to their admirers when the whistle blew. More than once, too, the Widnes players broke away with with the ball, and things began to look critical, but Walsh was always equal to the occanion. Farrel, it need hardly be said, worked hard all through, and was a host in him. eel( for his aide. On behalf of the home players Barnes, Jolley, and Gilbert were particularly conspicuous; the last- named indeed seems to improve at every match. Jolley was more than usually quick in getting hold and made some strong runs, whilst his opponents found it almost impos- sible to lay hold of Barnes, who, in fact, kicked his goal and minors when surrounded by their forwards. Massey was a little off form, probably owing to the slippery Feet(' of the ground, bat, as usual, he always turned up when his ser- vices were needed. The Warrington forwards one and all played so well that it is almost an injustice to the rest to specify individuals, and it is scarcely needful to say that Ashton, the two Turners, Poesy, Dillon, and Hough were to the fore. Teams :—Warringtou : Back, Walsh ; three-quarter backs, Jolley, Barnes, and Massey; half backs, Gilbert and Speak- man; fcrwards, Fairfield 'Turner, Frank Turner, Haves, Dillon. Povey. Littlewood, Davies, Hough, and Ashton (captain). Widnes : Back, J Wilkinson ; three-quarter backs, Harding, Parkinson, and Morris ; half backs, Farrell and Howard ; forwards, Kiddie (captain), Wilkinson, Hughes, Corns, Smith, Bingham, Brannon, Fogg, and Meagher. Referee, Mr. Cronshaw, president of the Wigan Football Club.

div.head: WARRINGTON V. WIDNES "A" TEAMS.
div.p: WARRINGTON V. WIDNES "A" TEAMS.

• • --- These teams met at Widnes on Saturday last in boisterous weather. The visiting captain having won the toss, elected to play with the wind. Sampson kicked off, and the home forwards following well up prevented a return, a scrimmage being formed in the visitors' quarters. After a series of scrimmages, Molyneux and Jones broke away in a splendid dribble, Johnsen stopping their progress near half flag. Wilson now passed to Johnson, lint Ashurst:taking the pass caused play to be located in the Widnes 25. The home for- wards, beaded by Goulden, Locke, and Woods, dribbled to half flag, but Unsworth saved nicely. F Wright, receiv- ing the ball from Johnson, put in a grand run, Unswortb, however, stopped his career. The Warrington forwards re- lieved, and Antrobus kicked across the field. where Randalls got hold, making a capital run, and finished up by punting the ball to the Widnes full back, whom he brought down before he could return. Sampson, Locke, and Goulden cleared their lines, and play continued for some time in the Warrington quarters. Dillon, Nevins. and Telford now broke away and dribbled the ball down the field. Appleton kick, tand Nevins n h viins foils esslopweisnsgwioen.ll wavascnolelxatreadllothweedfna re full bfacek with be ball The Warrington front rank now rushed the ball over the line, but Widnes saved by kicking the ball dead. From the drop out Randalls received the ball and kicked to Wright, who mulled, and Randalls coming up took the ball, but lost it before he reached the line. This Naas a piece of bad luck . for Warrington, who ought certainly to have scored. From the scrimmage the ball became loose, and Whittle passing i to Appleton, this player put n a good punt, and Unsworth, who had followed well up, almost scored, Widnes saving by kicking dead. Nothing further of importance occurred up to half time, although Warrington had the best of the game. On resnming Whittle kicked off against a strong wind, and Anhurst catching the ball ran to Widnes 25. The home forwards, however, ran the ball down the field and Jolley kicked dead. Ashunt dropped out, and no return being made, play raged in the centre for some time. until Wright put in a beautiful run, Unsworth bringing him down, a touch in goal resulting. Widnes now obtained four dead balls in succession, owing to the strong wind, but could not obtain a major point, the tackling of the visitors being so safe. Antrobul and Randalls saved splendidly during this half. Nothing further was scared,. and the game ended in a draw, the score being —Widnes six minors to Warrington two minors. Widnes were best represented by F Wright and Wilson, backs, and Sampson, Goulden, and Locke, forwards ; whilst on behalf of Warrington the whole team played a safe and combined game. Teams :—Warrington : T Jolley, full back ; Unmoral. Appleton, and Randalls, three-quarter backs; Antrobns and Whittle (captain), half backs ; Molyneus, Jones, Dillon, Ashursr, Eyes, Adamson, Nevins, Telford and Boyle, for- wards. Widnes : J Wright, full back; BarLor, Johnson, and F Wright, thres-quarter backs ; G Wright and Wilson, half backs; Locke, Wepds,'Hoole, Goulden, Barber. Samp- son, Gregory, Williams, and Bingham, forwards. Referee, Mr. Burrill, St. Helens.

NOTES BY THE WAY. The game between Warrington and Widnes or. Saturday should confirm the opinion of those superior persons who have just discovered that the Warrinaton team is one of the first rank. It was one of the most tenacious- ly fought and was creditable to both clubs, neither of whom played their full strength, but Warrington showed a marked superiority. A Mossley correspondent states that the Warrington spec- tators are a bullying lot, but Warrington players say that their spectatprs are not to be compared with Mossleyites in that respect. IS is quite certain that there are rougher spectators than those of Warrington. On scanning over the county team against Cheshire, we fail to notice Fair. Turner's name. Warrington people are ' beginning to wonder when the merits of this player will be recognised. Why not let Liverpool and Manchester play the county matches themselves is the cry of a good many in South-West Lancashire. We may remind oar readers that Castleford team visits ; Warrington to-day, and as they laa—e beaten Wakefield Trinity, and played a good game with Batley. Ashton's followers will have to strain every nerve to beat them. The game is sure to be an exciting one, but it is to be hoped that the spectators will not give any ill-natured critic even the shadow of an excuse for complaint. It is said that a more unbiassed class of spectators was never seen than those on the Castleford ground when the Warringtonians visited the glass-blowing town. Mr. A. N. Hornby's name as referee at this match should be an attraction to spectators. Among the leading matches played on Saturday wore the following :—Corinthians 3, Derby County 2; Oxford Uni- versity 1, Old Carthusians 2 ; Crusaders 9, Old Weetmin- titers 4 ; Cambridge University U. Notta Forest 3 ; Derby- shire 2, Litscalnshire 2; Mitchell St. George's 4, Port Vale 3; Crewe Alexander 3j Walsall Swifts 3; Queen's Park 0, Renton 4; Glasgow Rangers 5, Danharton 5. Cambridge University are much weaker so far this season than they were last. They had to put up with defeat far fourth time this season on Saturday, when Notts Forest vanquished them to the tune of three goals to nil. The I play is just about represented by the score. The two new footballing shires, Lincoln and Derby, tried conclusions on Saturday, with the result that they were found to be of about equal strength, the game ending two ; all.

div.head: FORGERY AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: FORGERY AT WARRINGTON.

At the Liverpool Assizes, on Wednesday, Charles Flannagan, aged 18 years, a soldier, belonging to the King's Liverpool Regiment, stationed at War- rington, pleaded guilty to having, on the 12th Oc- tober, forged and uttered a cheque belonging to Major Browne, for the sum of £7; and also to hay- ing, on the 10th October, stolen an envelope con- taining the cheque. Mr. Coßingwood Hope and Mr. Cooper were for the prosecution. Prisoner was employed as a mess waiter in the officers quarters at Orford Barracks. Re got possession of Major Browne's cheque book, forged a cheque for £7, which he cashed at Parr's Bank. Re also stole an envelope containing a cheque, which was found in his possession. The prisoner was sentenced to six months' hard labour.

The Royal Commissioners applinted to inquire into the working of the Lend Act in Ireland commenced their inquiry at Limerick, on Monday. At Ballylummin, near Lough Neagh, on Thursday morn- ing, a farmhouse was burned down, and a Mrs. Blair and her two grandchildren perished. Mr. Herbert Gladstone left Llndon on Thurpday morning to embark in the Peninsular and Oriental steamer Malwa en route for Calcutta, on a visit to his brother Henry. Mrs Egan, who was shot by her husband at their house at Montagu-street, Bloomsbury, died on Wednesday evening about the time that the bode of her husband was being interred.

A TRAIN AMONG SKEET. On Wednesday the mail train for the North which left Preston station about 2-30 rent into a flock of 40 sheep that had strayed on the line from a field near the cattle market, just outside the borough. Twelve of the sheep were killed on the spot, and many others were so much maimed that it was tounl nec-,ssary to slaughter them. The passengers in the train escaped with- out injury. TRH MIIRDIIIII OF A POLICIDIA.W.—At the Leicestershire Assizes en Thursday, James Banton and Josoph Gadmby were indicted for murdering Police-constable Barratt, whose body was found in a brook at Breedon, with terrible wounds on the head. Banton and the officer had been heard quar- relling, and the former admitted next day that he had "killed the bo)by." Gadsby was acquitted; but the jury returned a verdict of guilty against Banton, who was sen- tenced to death.

TUB WINDFALL TO A COLLIER IN WALES addition to the fortume of £30,000 left to a coal miner in the Rhond- da Valley, named Albert Henry Saint Leicester, by his grandfather, a Manchester merchant, Leicester has received an intimation that an uncle who died recently in America has left an estate to him and 20.000 dollars in cash. It ap- pears Leicester, who is in his 20cla year, was born ire Man- chester, and, after the death of his parents, lived with his grandfather. Two years ago he visited Wales, aud would not return, and, being reduced to penury, worked in a coal mine.
