THE EXAMINER. SATURD Mf, NOVEMBER 139 1886. ATTEMPTED SUICIDE ON THE lOUR LONDON LETTER RAILWAY. . EXCITING SCENE. Mrs. Elisabeth Broxton. Wife of a labourer living at Simms Cross, Widnes, was brought before the ' Mayor (Colonel Gamble) at the St. Helens Town ' Hall, on Wednesday, charged with attempting to commit suicide on the railvray.—Janes Henry Perkins, a detective in the employ of the London- and North-Wes:ern Railway Company, stated about ' 10 minutes to nine on the previous night he was on . duty at the St. Helens Railway Station, and saw the prisoner come on the premises. She seemed very excited, and was crying and mumbling to herself. She hurried up the platform, and when opposite the parcel office she threw down her hat and shawl and basket, and rushed along to the end of the platform. ; Thinking something was wrong, he followed, and 1 though Nil- a few minutes he lost sight of her, he eventually found her on the , main line under the Raven - street Bridge, lon the Liverpool line. He took hold of her to pull her off, knowing an express goods train from Liverpool to Carlisle was coming down the bank, but she resisted, and told him to go away, as she would be sooner dead than alive. Witness called Ticket-collector Wilding to his assistance, and by their united efforts they pulled her to the side just as the express dashed along. Had prisoner re- mained there a few moments longer she must have been cut to pieces. On the way to the Town Hall witness asked her why she had attempted such a rash act, to which she replied that she had. a boy fifteen years of age by a first husband, and that her second husband was unkind to him. It nearly broke her heart, and had made her feel that she would sooner be dead than alive. Witness added that prisoner must have been lying down on the line at the time he could not see her.— Prisoner, in reply to the Mayor, said she was very sorry. She meant to make her way to Widnes, and thought, as there was no train, that if she could follow on the rails she would get there.— Detective Perkins said prisoner threw down her hat, shawl, and basket 200 yards away from the place where he found hen—Prisoner said she had 'no intention of taking her life away. She wanted to get to Widnes, and didn:t know the road.—Pri- soner's husband, a labouring man, who said he had worked for ten years at the Tharsis Copper Works, Widnes, said there were two children, one of his own, and one of his wife's by a former husband.— The Mayor: Do you think if she is let out you can manage to make her comfortable, so that she won't do this kind of thing again ?—The Husband: Yes, sir, I shall be only too glad to got her home.— The Mayor: Then you had better take care of her; Mind you do take care of her; I shall ask Mr. Pritchard how you are getting on with her.—Pri- soner was then discharged.

LONDON'. THURSDAY. Lord Randolph Churchill is, it is said. about to enter upon a new field of conquest. He is going on the turf, and has already a few modest horses in training. This is a characteristically bold expedi- tion, seeing Lord Randolph can boast that he has not been assisted in his career by possession of money. He acquired at the outset a younger son's fortune which, in a family as heavily handicapped as the Marlboroughs, was not a rich sum.. It is true that he married the daughter of a millionaire. But the shrewd proprietor of Jerome Park arranged that his beneficence should be prospective. When he dies Lady Randolph will be wealthy. In the meantime it is understood that she has but a mo- dest allowance of pin money. The late Duke of Marlborough left everything he could to his favour- ite son. But the estate being closely entailed, and ready money not being abundant, that did not amount to much. It must be his salary as Chan- cellor of the Exchequer that has emboldened Lord Randolph to enter upon this thorny path. But £5,000 a year will not go far against a day's run of ill luck on the turf. Still the engagement if only temporary will suit Lord Randolph's purpose as rounding off his character as a popular minister. He based the earlier stages of his career upon imitation of Mr. Disraeli. But ,Lord Palmerston is. I believe. his beau ideal of a prime minister. A close connection with the turf by our leading statesmen is much less a matter of course than it used to be. It would be interesting to know when, if ever, Mr. Gladstone saw the Derby run. Sir Francis Doyle's reference to Mr. Gladstone on horse- back is a revelation to many people. Yet we read in the memoirs how Mr. Gladstone had a long fight with a mare that would not stand still while he
PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Preseot Board of Guar- dians was held at tits Union Workhouse, Whistoa. on Thursday, when there were present Mr. John Lowe (chair. man), Rev. C. W. Wool!, Rev. Father Finegan, and Messrs. James Fisher, William Gerrard, Joseph Jackson, W. Br- (shall, John W. Wareing, William Middlehurst, James Bur- shall. John Whal4y, T. Ratock, C. B. Johnson. Thomas HosIC W. Swift, R. A. Graves, Peter Longton, John Ken- weight, E. Syder, and S. H. Hartley 'clerk). Ramis; Riarrnem—The Workhouse Master reported there were 488 inmates of the house this week, 450 last week, and 449 in the corresponding week last year. The vagrants relieved were 48, against 37 in the corresponding week last year. Trim Sorrow MHDICAL OFVICHR.—A letter was read from the Local ri4ivernment Board, approving of the payment of a salary of £7O per annum to Dr. Casey, as the medical officer for the Sutton district.

PABISCCYr WATCTIMAYBBS. LIVBLY DiSCIISSIOIL—Th e Clerk stated that the Central Poor Law Conference would ' be held on December Bth, at Exeter Hall, London. If the Guardians wished to send a deputation notice of motion would have to be given, and it would be brought on at the next Board meeting. At the Conference Mr. C. B. Loch would read a paper on " Exceptional distress, " and he thought it important a deputation should attend, as the Guardians would know there had been a great deal of exceptional distress in Prescot amongst the watchmakers. Tney were a class of people 'umbering about 500. whose trade had been very bad for borne time in consequence of unfelt competition by foreign made watch movements being put into English Hall-marked cases.—Mr. Johnson (Preecot) said he had had interviews with Mr. A. B. Forwood, M.P., and 11%scount Cross, who he thought were disposed to favour same steps being teller) to put a stop to this state of things, but at the same time they wished to make it understood that it was not a *ideal move. There were in Prescot ardent free traders who supported this move- ment.—Mr. Jackson said he thought the people of Prescot might throw more energy into their manufactures. They had no energy in them. (Laughter, and cries of "Chair.") Mr. Jackson (continuing) said there was scarcely a watch- maker in Prescot who would not take every month an ex- cursion or outing. They had made wealth in times past, but now they would not spend it in creating in- dustries among their own townsmen.—The Chair- man: Mr. Jackson, that is not the question before the board.—Mr. Jackson : It is the question, Mr. Chairman.—The Chairman : No, no.—Mr. Jackson : They should instil more energy among the people, such as Mr. Johnson and others. (Cries of "Order.")—Mr. Johnson: I must protest against Mr. Jackson making use of such ex- pressions in an extremely offensive manner. They are en- tirety outeide the question. For some months past the Board has conducteel itself as a body of gentlemen, and I hope we are not going back to the personalities which for- merly exis,ed. (Hear, hear.)—Rev. Father Finegan sugges- ted that instead of sending a deputation they should send a letter to the conference strongly representing the grie- ancee referred to.—The Clerk said rather than miss this favourable opportunity he would pay his expenses out of his own pocket.—Mr. Johnson said he would do likewise.— Ultimately Mr. Wareing gave notice of his intention to move at the next meeting that a deputation, comprising the clerk and Mr. Johnson, be appoiated to attend the con- ferenee.

Thtil MILK SUPPLY.—Mr. Wm. Lowcock, of Bold, the contractor for the supply of milk to the workhouse, wrote that in consequence of the Guardians requiring such a high standard as seven degrees of cream on the milk, and it being almost impossible to attain the standard regularlv, the contract was not worth having, and he asked the Board to cancel it.—The Rev. T. Finegan moved that the con- tract be not cancelled, and Mr. P. Longton moved an amendment that the contract be terminated.—Five members voted for the amendment, and nine for the motion, the latter being carried. This was the principal business.

The position, even amongst judges, very dignified and very secluded. It is customary to speak of promotion to the bench as the shelving of a lawyer, but in the case of common law judges this is scarcely so. Sir Alexander Cockburn cer- tainly was not shelved in the Queen's Bench, and Mr. Justice Manisty was pretty well to the fore. But Downing-street differs from Carey-street. A Privy Council Judge drops out of public life with a good salary. Even Lord Monkswell would scarcely be remembered but for the " colliery explosion of some dozen years ago. In one respect a change has come over the spirit of our appointments. The older of the puisne judges used to be pushed up, so that the Appellate Court looked very venerable, though it was rather deaf. Latterly the youngest there have been put over the heads of their seniors. Thus , their judicial life on that bench was longer, they I 1 had more time to learn their business, and their judgments were more respected. I believe the new i appointment will be from amongst the junior of the !puisne judges. Theatrical events are forecast for months in ad- vance. No one can well understand why Mary Anderson has recently hung back so much. She is neither going to be married nor engaged to be mar- ried. One hears of her indisposition and her need for rest, but then she went to Dublin and played for a week, for a charity, her old round of characters. She is not on the list of theatrical ladies who never ' would be missed, and lam very glad to hear that next London season will find her fulfilling a lengthened engagement—they say at the Gaiety. In the following July she was tried again, when the mother of the murdered child cathfessed all. Charlotte Winsor was found guilty and sentenced to death. Lord Wensleydale took up her case, protesting against anyone being tried twice for a capital offence. The case was long argued before the judges at Westminster, the wretched woman being frequently reprieved pend- ing the decision. It confirmed conviction, but after the long torture, the public would not see the wretched woman hung, and accordingly she was sentenced to penal servitude for life. The Eighty Club which received a severe blow at the birth of Dissentient Liberalism is beginning to hold up its head. The members will presently dine together. entertaining Sir Charles Russell as the principal guest of the evening. The odd thing about the Eighty Club is that though it has a name it has no local habitation. It dines once or twice a year at various places. The last time was at the Grosvenor hotel. It is called the Eighty Club, not because it is comprised of eighty members as is generally supposed, but because it had it had its birth in the year 1880, and was established with the object of propagating Liberal principles, as then triumphantly established under the direction of Mr. Gladstone. It was composed chiefly of able young men, enthusiastic Liberals, ready to make any per- sonal sacrifice to spread the truth. A typicalmember was Mr. Albert Grey, a stout Gladstonian six years , ago, but now, alas! a castaway, unseated for his sins by an uncompromising Liberal constituency. All the Dissentient Liberals have withdrawn from active participation in the procedure of the Eighty Club, if not from actual membership. It is the faithful few who are beginning again to bestir themselves, and announce their willingness to send out lecturers upon invitation. We shall soon bear of a change:on tbe:bench. Legal promotions have been latterly very slow. At the commencement of a new term, and especially of a new legal year, there are always plenty of rumours about. For the last five or six Novembers it has, year after year, been confidently asserted that Vice- Chancellor Bacon would accept a pension and mike way for some promising senior counsel who might be forty years his junior. But the Vice-Chancellor shows all the virtues except resignation. The pro- phets have ceased to prophesy, and perhaps the V.C. might yield. In the meantime Lord Monk- well's death has caused a vacancy, and the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council cannot be left with a gap in its ranks. The salary is £5,000 a year.

GREAT STRIKE Or CITAINICALERS IN STAFFORDSHIRE.— On Monday, th3chainmakers in the South Staffordshire dis- trict came out on strike, in consequence of the employers *.ot unanimously consenting to concede an advance in wages. About 2,800 have thereby thrown themselves out of work. The rivetmakers in the saute district also struck for an advance in wages. SHILLING WINES.—When under the French Treaty of 1860 claret was introduced into this country at one shilling a bottle it was a matter of surprise how a good sound wine could be retailed to the public at such an exceptional price. The introduction no doubt met a want long felt by a large class of consumers for a light beverage wine. The Treaty recently concluded with Spain has advanced matters one step further, for A. Gilbey now quote sherry Messrs. NV. Sz and port at one shilling a bottle. and in doing so guarantee that the wines in question are the pure juice of the grape shipped direct from Swim It will be interesting to know if the introduction by this firm of port and sherry at a price confined hitherto to French wines meets with success, as if Spanish Treaty will have con- ferred a great boon on the consuming public in bringing within their reach sound wholesome wines at prices which will allow of their entering into the daily consumption of every household.—" Morning Post," November 9th, 1886. _

NEAR THE VILLAGE OF ZILLINGDORF, Lower Austria, lives Maria Haas, an intelligent and Industrious woman whose story of physical suffering and final relief, as related by herself, is of interest to English women. "I was employed" she says," in the work of a large farmhouse. Overwork brought on sick headache, followed by & deathly fainting and sicknesS of the stomach, until I was unable to retain either food or drink. I was compelled to take to my bed for several weeks. Getting a little better from rest and quiet,.l sought be do some work, but was soon taken with a pain in my side, which in a little while seemed to spread over my whole body, and throbbed in my every limb. This was followed by a cough and shortness of breath, until finally I could not sew,land I took to my bed for the second, and, as I thought, for the last time. 149 friends told rae that my time had nearly come, and that I could not live longer than when the trees put on their green once more. Then I happened to get one of the Seigel pamphlets. I read it and my dear mother bought me a bottle of Seigel's Syrup, which I took ex— actly according to directions, and I had not taken the whole of it before I felt a change for the better. MY last illnees began June the 3rd, 1382, and continued to August Sth, when I began to take the Syrup. Very soon I could do a little light work. The cough left me, and I was no more troubled in breathing. Now I am perfectly cured. And oh, how happy I am! I can rot express enough gratitude for Seigel's Syrup. NoW I must tell you tbat the doctors in our district distribee ted handbills cautioning people against the medicineo telling thorn it would do them no good, and many were thereby influenced to destroy the Seigel pamphlees ; but now wherever one 15 to be found it is kept like a relic. The fee; preeeryed are borrowed to ,read, and I have lent mine for six miles around our district. People have come eighteen miles to get me to bay the needle's.° for them, knowing that it cured me, and to be sure to get the right kind. I know a woman who was looking like death, and who told them there was no help tor her, that she had consultei with several doctors, but none could help her. told her of Seigel's Syrup, and wrote the name down for her that she might make no mistake. She took my advice and the Syrup, and now she is is perfect heelth, and the people around us are amazed- The medicine has made such progress in our neighhourhoed that people say tney don't want the doctor any more, but they take the Syrup. Safe ferers from gout who were confined to their bed and could hardly Imes a finger, have been cured by it. There is a girl in our district who caught a, cold by going through some water, and was in bed five years with costiveness and rheumatic pain'', and had to have an attendant to watch by her. There was not a doctor in the surrounding districli to whom her mother had not applied to relieve her child, but everyone crossed themselves ani said they weld not help her. Whenever the little bql rang which is rung in our place when somebody is dead, we thought surely it was for her, but Siegel' Syrup and Pills saved her life, and now she is ae healthy as auybody, goes to church, and can work even in the fields. Everybody was astonished when they saw her out, knowing how many years she had been in bed. To-day she adds her gratitude to mine for God's mercies and Seigel's Syrup." MARIA HAAS.

- - - - - "BUST UP." Sir,—Warrington and its vicinity is on the tip-toe of ex- citement about a bust for your retiring Mayor. With all due respect I should like to know what sort of a bust it has to be. ill a knife and fork "bust" I'm out of the running; if a carved bust I'm your man. For your information I may tell von that lam a barn artist. At the age of tan I carved a full moon out of a turnip; and when shown to enr worthy old rector be declared that, with a little more expression, it would have been perfection. Encouraged by his kind words I have worked and " sculpt " ever since 31y works of art out of wagon soles and Billing° Hill gran- ite have electrified the civilised world. I should like the Council to get a bast worthy of the town. If desir- able I will wait upon the Doctor or Joseph with speci- mens of my handicraft. I may inform you that my fertile brain teems with ideas of beauty, and my 30s life size oils are unapproachable by any living artist, and give universal satisfaction (nett cash.) Since my juvenile attempts, practice has made me perfect is expression, and if the commiLtee select me I will guarantee to Warrington a thing of Nauty and a joy for ever.—Yours truly, Thorawalden Villa, Earleetown. BILSTIO, R.A.S.S.

KNIGr' HTS OF LABOUR. Sir,—ln your issue of Saturday last I read a letter on the Knights of Labour, an I was pleased to find that you had one reader, at least, who does not allow the governmental farces of the Continent to occupy his mind to the exclusion of all internal topics. If we may judge from the reports that are printed from time to time, we have quite plenty of statesmen and departmental officials, who, while they are surveying the foreign aspect of affairs, are neglecting to take care that our soldiers are properly armed and fed, &c., after the country has found the money for that worthy pur- pose. Now it was something of the same condition of affairs that the Knights of Labour of America found them. selves in at the commencement of their organisation. And the first reform they went in for was a department from which, without fear or favour, they can draw sound arms, viz. facts and figures, to prove Chair condition and to de- marLl a faker share of the just fruits of their labour. We thank Mr. Bradlaugh for establishing the above department In England, for should the working-men of this country be backward at joining our noble order they will at least re- ceive the benefits of one of its foremost principles. When will the working-men of England throw if that apathy which exists amongst them towards one another and stand firm as they do in America in one great army, pledged to follow their leaders of various branches, and not be led by the nose at election times by politicians who pretend to know all about the wants of working-men, but when any legislation is brought before the House of Commons they either know nothing about it, or shrink from it as if It were a law that was framed to bring about the disruption of the Empire. The Knights of Labour admit into its fold employers as well as employed ; any trade or calling except beersellers, lawyers, or professional gamblers. There has been nearly 8,000 assemblies chartered by the Order. And I say, for the information of " Jaques," that it is the most powerful, as well as just, organisation on earth. I must conclude this long letter by urging every working-man to use the educa- tion and benefits which he has already obtained for the ad- vancement, both moral and physical, of the well-being of his fellow-man.—Yours, rkc., A KNIGHT OF LABOUR. 'Bt. Helene, N'ov. 0,188 d.

SPIRITU ALISNI V. VONJURING. Sir —A letter was Inserted in the " Examiner " with the above heading. I believe it was written with a goad inten- tion, but "Bb" should have taken into consideration the trick that the Professor was performing at the time he Mai, the answer humbug to the question—What is Spiritualism ? Now as I believe it is humbug so far as spirit writing is concerned, and I also believe the Professor wa9 mining this trick at the time, I for one will take this question up, and if "Beta" wishes for light on this subject. I propose that he tries to persuade some of his friends (perhaps the tradesman in this town could do it for him) to get a good medium to come to Warrington and give a seance or two, and perform that favourite manifestation, spirit writing. If this can he arranged, I will allow the medium three satinet; to accomplish it in. He shall se- bet his own room and Committee, with myself included and the admission of a press representative to report on the proceedings ; the press representative to select the question that is to be answered ; the answer to be received on a blackboard, slate or paper, or on anything that the medium may select, and if he can obtain an answer in three sittings I undertake to prove that it has been obtained by a trick. Hoping that some arrangement will be made so that we may have light on the subject, I am, sir. yours &c., THOMAS ACTON. 90, Priestley•street, Warrington.

Sir,—lt is rather disappointing that no one should have 1 taken up the above question. "Beta" could not once upon 1 a time have thrown out a more interesting subject for dis- cussion. Possibly the doings of the Davenport Brothers, or the Messrs. Maskelyne and Cook, have caused the people to hesitate a little before, with meekly folded arms, they" shut their eyes and open their mouths, to see what " scientific, literary, and other distinguished personages; also ministers and will send them. All the same, I should like to have seen same doughty champion of the spiritual istic " hum- bug " step forth and bravely give us the benefit of his or her experience. " Beta " states that he has heard much of this subject lately; from this I should gather he knows much of the subject, more especially as he happens to be in possession of " " Beta " wishes to know what some of your subscribers think of it, and what has been their "personal experience." Well I must confess that outside of a pot house I never had any experience with "spirits." To me the whole sub- ject has always appeared uncanny, and I could never see the good of it. It is possible " Beta " may have heard of a gentleman, or I may say two, who have figured largely in American history. I refer to Andrew Jackson Davies and Robert Dale Owen, who with the occasional help of Judge Edmonde, have fairly succeeded in making spiritualism at clear as mud. Take the following The use of a physical bone is to make a spiritual bons; even se the physical muscle makes a spiritual muscle; not the essence, but the form thereof. Inside the visible spine is the spiritual spine invisible." Perhaps if I was to leave "Beta" alone with this interesting information I should receive few thanks, and should likely enough be told that something more substantial was wanted. Well, I suppose, although I never saw it, that tables turn, and tilt, and old ladies of both sexes float through the air; that musical instruments are played upon, and that various other, shall I say unseemly acts are performed. If this be so we must acknowledge that the substantial portion of the business is also very material. Now I ask " Beta "to quietly turn the matter over in his mind and resolve, if be can, how it is possible for the immaterial, unsubstantial shadow of a spirit to guide and control these antics without the general public becoming thoroughly cognisant of the fact that the spirits were not at all unsubstantial, but were very substantial, or shall I say material. I hope, Mr. Editor, you will dot insist upon any explan- tion to the above. I couldn't give such if required, so kindly allow "Beta " and myself to lose ourselves in a spiritual maze. I read in the Penetralia, p 19I—" That within the physical man there is a spiritual man, corres- ponding in form and size with its fleshy exterior." Now what interests me in this statement, is the fact given that we all possess this deut,le nature alike, therefore I and Bcta " are not one whit behind the humbugging, conjur- ing spiritualist. We have been taught that matter is known

only through its phenomena or properties ; spiritualism is known through its phenomena alone. " Beta" will be kind Enough to return thanks for this information at once if con- vtnient, and to further understand—" That spirit possesses the properties of matter." I know that it (spirit) often has the power of knocking down nutter, which is perhaps what is meant. I have sometimes thought that the spiritualists use the two terms spirit and soul as interchangeable ; but I pre- fer to keep to the one term "spirit," because I know so much about it, as your readers will before new have

guessed. I must suggest o " Beta " the desirability of limiting our researches to the material substance with which the spirit clothes itself ; to go ferther would be presumption or waste of time, because we might find that " spirit," like ether, required careful watch and ward or all might ey.ipo-

rate. Mr. Davies says—" After the event called physical death, his (man's) spirit, preserving its individuality, and all its endowments, goes forward and gains a higher and better state of existence." This seems to me tantalising, as it states in Billy's ROSA :- ** You must die before yo ere able all these blessings to enjoy." lam of opinion, presumption on my part perhaps, that we should be no worse if we had a higher and batter state of existence this side the physical death spoken of; but this we must not expect, inasmuch as the "substantial and im- material spirits" float and dive about the earth's physical atmosphere, dispensing not only social harmony, but " join- ing in occasional moral and intilectral feasts at spiritual tables." This, " a " will join wit'l me in saying, is something coin ,r og to look :orward to; but, as usual, even this has its drawbacks, because spirits ere they depart must be made pure, or in that silent spirit land they will "linger around men and women both day and night in order to gratify their unsatisfied passions and prevailing propensities." This, sir, is awful, and perhaps accounts for the large amount of sin we see around us but, if true, the police courts should be shut up, and the 'bobble. " dis- charged, as it would be manifestly wrong to punish a man for simply obeying a controlling spiritual force. "Insanity, murder, suicide, licentiousness, arson, theft, and various evil impulses, are causal by the direct action of the will of false and malignant spirits." Bless as, and save us! Mr. or Mrs. "Beta," what infernal spirits you have caused us to raise, and all because you "want t 3 know, you know," something about the work entrusted into the hands of the " medium " who, I must state, has no "private rights or powers of will which the spirits are bound to respect," and who asserts that "whatever is is right." The subject is, "Beta" will allow, a knotty one, but if your correspondent will say in your next issue that he would like a little more, we may see whet tile doctors say about it.
CLIFFORD DIX.
THREE LETTERS.

Sir,—Allow me, a; one of your readers, to thank your- self, and three of your coi:espondents, foreletters on Edu- cate," and" Home Rule." and the" Knights of Labour." "Progress "does well to urge the Liberals on to educate the people; it is the only method whereby we may hope for success to the people's cause, but it is a costly and a slow way of convincing a nation what is right and just. We are hearing a deal just now about education, and I often wonder hew it will all end. In the religious world we have a party contending for religious and sectarian education, contending that the voluntary system is all that is required, forgetful that it did not educate the people previous to 1870, alsk , that if there is anything good in it, those who are most vehement against Disestablishmeut might have a little more faith in voluntaryism. Now, lam disposed to think we are altogether wrong in laying so much stress on the power of education, that is to say, on its Dower far good. I aek a few plain questions, not forgetting my second para- graph. Shall we not set the Irish people against their law- ful guardians and rulers if we educate them ? Was it not better to make them feel the iron hand, to keep political education as far away from them as possible, so that , " poor Pat's" only comfort lay in feeding pigs and ducks, and during the wee small hours snoring cheek by jewl with the porker that was soon to piy his rent? " Where Ignorance is bliss, &c, &c." The happiest days of Ireland are past. Who that has dipped deep into the long list of Irish novels can fail to be convinced of this, when remem- bering how the landlords used to, night after night, roll under the tibia gloriously drunk. Alt! they were grand old days, alas, I fear never to return. Why, sir, when George the third was king the people took no thought of to-morrow, neither what they should eat nor what they should drink, content that their " pastors and masters " had enough both to eat and to drink, and sufficient also to enable them to spend a rollicking life in London and Dublin. Now von are edu- cating them. and what is the result? Why, they have the impudence to assert that they are men. In Ireland they want Home Rule ; throuettout Great Britain they are pro- testing against paying tithe, are talking about "free educa- tion" and " free libraries." I can tell you Mr. Editor, this education question will be an eve-opener in a thousand different ways. Men who are working in mills and factories are beginning to ask why clerks, who are engaged in corporation work, like the gas works, should receive £3 103 and £4 per week, and should be allowed to manage their snug business between the hours of 9 a.m. and 5 p.m.. while fustian hai to work from six to six. Of course it is wrong of the Horny-band; be ought to be pleased to see the bright shining face of the clerk as he bustles along with his kid gloves and his walking stick. What a lot of human nature there is in this world! By the way, Mr. Editor, I think I shall give ever going to chapel and take to church going: its more respectable. You see everybody that goes to church either gets rich, or, what would do far me, marries into a rich family.

I wonder who "Jaques" is. I like his last letter; he seems to be coming to hie senses. Hitherto I bave thought with "Rosalind '' that he was "a melancholy fellow." I think they have "Free Education "in America; it grows, like " Topsy " did, and the result is " Mr. Henry George,the nominee of the great labour organisation. the Knights of Labour, has been supported by nearly seventy thousand votes." Will it bring about a similar state of things in "dear" old England I wonder? If so, we had better keep it out. Just fancy, Mr. Hyndman, Prime Minister • Mr. Champion, Secretary of State ; W. Morris, Chancellor of the Exchequer, and Poet Laureate of the British Empire? Why at one stroke educatioa would put Horny-hand on a level with the clerk; "Eight hours work and eight hours play, eight hours sleep and eight bob a day." Thank goodness, Warrington can boast of a LL.D., who for at least twelve months well save es from the horrors of a socialist mayor. It the worst comes to the worst, and education brings us down to the level of a Socialist Mayor. I have my eye on a world-renowned Warringtonian vegetarian anti-everythingist who will just be the man. I keep rambling. 11 Z.igues wants iö poke a bit of fun at "Tory i herring." Take my advice, don't do it; red her- rings are toothsome when there's nothing else. It's all very well to wish that the Knights of Labour "may grew in this country ;" but does "Jaques" understand the question? If working-men begin to unite in England something „awful will happen; the monopolies to which he refers would be- come the property of the people, and then we should see the supplies cut off from a lot of very ancient and useless Institutions. Whatever would the church, the army, and the navy do, if they hadn't the people to drain? Why, "chaos would come again.' If we could only fancy work- ing-men owning that splendid intellectual concern that has just been floated for brewing Dublin stout, what fine times we should have : brown stout and beef steaks. Just fancy Wilderspool brewery belonging to us Warrington chaps, and Sir Gilbert and Sir Arthur promoted to be head brewers, and all this through socialism and education—what "pro- gress "we should have, surely. Just allow me. Mr. Editor, in conclusion, to ask" Pro- gress " and" Jaques" a last question. I've no doubt they will see that I am rather chaotic in some of my views; they will understand this when I tell them I am just emerging from a Board School, and this will account for my question. I understand that at all the large ironworks throughout the kingdom they are training lads to take the best paid posts where a little scholarship is required, and the uneducated, of course, are doing the donkey work. Is it true? lam anxious about this, because it will enable me to take my father's post, and of course he will go to the workhout Educated lads and ignorant men are going to do the work of the future, When the lads become men, anti-Socialists will kindly open the workhouse door for them. now the milk of human kindness will flow in the future! JIM TODD.

div.p: FRODSHOL

THE LIGHTING DISTRICT.—At a recent meeting of the inspectors for the lighting district of Frodsham, the Secre- tary, Mr. Joseph Cunnah, tendered his resignation in conse- quence of leaving the neighbourhood, when it was unani- mously resolved that Mr. Samuel Davies be appointed his

successor. MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS.—kt the weekly meeting of this class, held on Friday, the Chairman. the Rev. E Messcrop. gave a paper on "Christianity: Evidence from Miracles." The attention of the members was directed to passages of Scripture, by which it was contended that Christ's miracles were disinterested, acknowledged, and con- vincing, and which also bore infallable marks of the reality of miracles. INQUEST AT PRODSHAM BRIDGE.--011 Monday an inquest was held at the Bridge Inn Frodsham, by Mr. Henry chur,. ton, coroner, on the body of Thomas Houghton, of Seven Houses, Frodsham Bridge, aged 30 years. which was found in the river Weaver Canal. near to the Rock Savage Turn Bridge, on Sunday last. Thesdeceased was returning from Runcorn late on Saturday, the 3eth ultimo, and the night being very dark it is supposed that he lost his way and fell into the canal. The jury brought in a verdict of "Found drowned." PAROCHIAL COMMITTHES.—A meeting of the Frodsham and Frods'Aam Lordship Parochial Committees was held in the Town Hall on Friday, Mr. A. Thomas in the chair. A plan and specifications for covering the trial wells at New- ton Were produced, and it was decided to obtain tenders for carrying out the work from Mr. J. Littler, and Messrs. Kirkham and Co. The Inspector of Nuisances reported that he estimated that the probable cost of the sanitary work in hand, aLI which would be required to be carried out during the ensuing half year ending Lady Day, 1837, would be as follows :—Township of Frodsham, £ds; town- ship of Frodsham Lordship, £25. Plans of two new houses proposed to be erected in Frodsbam, for Mr. H. Tiley, were submitted by Messrs. C. E. Linaker and S. Davies, archi- tects, Frodsham, and the same were recommended to the Authority for approval.

SENTENCES ON ELECTION RIOTERS.—At Cambridge As- sizes, on Friday, a number of men were found guilty of rioting at Ford ham during last West Cambridgeshire Par- liamentary election, upon which occasion the police were savagely attacked and a school-room wrecked, necessitating postponement of the election for a day. Mr. Justice Field sentenced Charles Baird, George Cadmaia,and John Cadmium each to eighteen months' imprisonment, and fourteen others to terms varying from six to fifteen months. ARCHER'S Fusee/era—The remains of the late Fred. Archer were interred on Friday by the side of his wife ia Newmarket Cemetery. Business was suspended throughout that town. Despite the incessant rain, very large numbers assembled at the cemetery, among whom were Lords Grosvenor, Alingtnn, Cerdross, the Hon. E. Boxiwn, General Renny, Colonel Chains, Messrs. Tattersall, the leading trainers, jockeys, and others well known in sporting circles. The coffin was of polished oak, with brass fittings, and bore simply deceased's name, with date of birth and death. THE BARNSLEY MURDER: VERDICT AND SENTENCE.— The Crown Conn at York Assizes, presided over by Mr. Justice Hawkins, was crowded in every part ou Friday morning', on the occasion of the trial of James Murphy, 45. collier, for the wilful murder of Police-constable Austwick, at Dod worth, near Barnsley, on the 15th of August. After hearing the evidence, the jury, without retiring, returned a verdict of guilty. His Lordship, in passing sentence of death, said the prisoner bad been found guilty of doing a wicked brutal act, when Austwick was only in the discharge of his duty, and without the least provocation. He had no doubt that for many a long day the prisoner had entertained against him feelings of wicked cruel malice and had deter- mined to take his revenge. His Lordship concluded with ' the words, "May the Lord have mercy on your soul." As Murphy was leaving the dock he saia, " Well, the Lord have mercy on us all."
MICHAEL DAVITT ON IRELAND.
NEW YORE, FRlDAY.—Michael Davitt, addresaing an im- mense audience at Columbus, last night, said the next elec- tion in the United Kingdom would met Ireland free.
THE LATE M. PAUL BERT.

PARIS, FRIDAY —lt is stated that the Government,will propose that the day of the funeral of M. Paul Bert shall be ibserved as a day of national mourning. M. Lan( on, the well-known R Zeal Deputy, is mentioned as his prob- able successor.

div.head: LIBERkLISAI IN NORTIIWICH DIVISION.
div.p: LIBERkLISAI IN NORTIIWICH DIVISION.

A meeting of the Executive Committee of the Northwich Division Liberal Council has been held this week. As this was the first gathering of the members since the death of Mr. G. W. Latham, it was unanimously resolved,:—" That the Executive of the Northwich Division Liberal Association, at this, its first meeting since the decease of G. W. Latham, Esq., places on record its deep sense of the loss sustained by Liberalism in Cheshire in his re- ' moval by death, recognises his unwearied and life- long devotion to the cause of advanced political progress, and attributes in a great degree to his influence and fidelity the growth of a sturdy Liberalism through the whole county."— Mr. W. Handley, the secretary, was instructed to forward the resolution to the relatives of the de- ceased gentleman.—Mr. T. E. Ellis, attended the meeting, and stated that the Marquis of Ripon would address a public meeting in the Division in the early part of December if arrangements were made therefor. The committee requested Mr. Ellis to obtain the Marquis's consent to visit the con- stituency on the 7th prox., and it was further unanimously resolved that as Runcorn afforded the greatest accommodation for a large attendance the public meeting be held in that town. This gather- ing will be preceded in the afternoon of the day named by a conference in which the Liberal Asso- ciations in the surrounding district will be invited to take part. The members of the Executive in the Runcorn district have control of the arrangements. The Executive decided to recommend the Council to affiliate themselves to the National Liberal Federa- tion.

True Peenet WOUNDING OASE.—A.4; the Town Hall, on Monday. before Mr. W. Blinkhorn and Mr. B. Biram, James Seddon, of Parr, a young man, was again charged, on re- mand, with unlawfully wounding Joseph Pennington, under circumstances previously reported.—Mr. R. W. H. Thomas, who appeared to prosecute, stated that the injured man was still unable to appear, and asked for the prisoner to be retnanded for a week.—Mr. T. Garner, who defended, had no objection to the remand, and the prisoner was re- manded accordingly. EARLESTOWN BUILDING SOCITIM—The twenty-third annual meeting of the Earlestown Building Society was held on Thursday week, when there was a large attendance of shareholders. Mr. J. W. Emmett presided, supported by Messrs. R. Davies and Kirkcoanel (Messrs. Davies, Sharp. and Kirkeonnel, soliciters), Mr. T. Wood (Messrs. Appleby and Wood, chartered accountants), and the secretary, Mr. P. Chandlev. On the motion of Mr. J. Prescott, seconded by Mr. Dobson, the report was ta- ken as read. The Chairman remarked that the directors in their report expressed them- selves gra' Med in being able to meet the shareholders with satisfactory results. and he thought the directors were .en- titled to he gratified, and the menebers might fairly congra• tulate them on the work they had done during the past year. He thought the state of affairs in connection with the Earlestown society reflected great credit upon the managers. (Applause.)—Mr. T. Wood said the accounts were kept in a very satisfactory manner, and the secretary deserved congratulating upon the way in which he had done his duties. If the society was liquidated to-day it would be able to pay the members more than 20s in the pound. They possessed a good reserve fund equal to 63 per cent of the original advances on these properties, and they might satis- fy themselves that it was impossible to sustain any loss on account of these properties.—Mr. R. Davies spoke at length on the prospects of the society.—Mr. Birks proposed, and Mr. J. Dobson seconded the adoptioa of the balance sheet, which was passed.—The trustees, directors, surveyor, audi- tors, arbitrators, stewards, and secretary, were re-elected.— Votee of tlvinks to the auditors and to the chairman termi- nated the proceedings.

DELIBERATE MIIRDEII.—A deliberate murder was com- mitted in Norwich Market Place on Monday night. A fish hawker from &cotes, in Suffolk, met his wife, and, patting his arm round her neck, cut her throat with a razor, inflict- ing such a wound that she died in a few minutes. RESULT OF A CAROUS&L.—EarIy on Monday morning, a man, named Thomas Currie, was ascending the stairs at his house Hall-street, Barrow, after a drinkicg carousal with his wife and two men, when he missed his footing, and fell backwards from the top to the bottom of the stairs, fractur- ing his skull, and dying almost immediately.

LY"11. ENTeRTAINUENT.—An en: 14 men tin connection with Lymm Congregational Band 01 .lope was held on Monday evening, the Rev. J. H. Oneton in the chair. Mr. G. L. We(ford, of Lymm, gav, an address on the temperance ques- tion, and this was followed by songs, recitatiocs, &c., given by members of the Band of dope. POLICE COURT.—At the police court, Pet•ir Winstanley, fustian cutter, Lymm, was sent to prison for one month, with hard labour, for drunkenness.—Martin McLouglin, for being drunk and disorderly at Lymm, was fined 2s 6d and costs.—Patrick Cunningham, labourer, Lymm, was charged with committing a breach of the peace by fighting at Lymm, on toe 7th inst. He was remanded until the next Petty Sessions, bail being allowed. MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT ASSOCIATION. On Monday evening a lecture was delivered is connection with this as- sociation in the We4eyan echool-room, Lymm, on " CoaL and coal mining," by Mr. J. Tonga (lecturer on mining to the Church Institution.) The chair was taken by Mr. R Dutton, and there was a large attendance. In the course of his lecture Mr. Tonge mention< 1 that the present British supply of coal was something like 163 or 164 million tons per year, but the quantity of unworked coal was so great that none need fear its being exhausted for a great many years to come. A rote of thanks was accorded Mr. Tongs for his excellent lecture.

LIBERAL CLUB DEBATING SOCIETY. Last evening the first meeting of the newly- formed debating society in connection with the Warrington Liberal Club took place at the club in Bewsey-street. There was a very good attendance, The President of the S3ciety, the Rev. R. Picher, delivered the opening address, taking for his sub- ject " Party politics.' Prefaratory to dealing with the subject, the Chairman thanked the members of the society for the honour they had conferred upon hint by electing him president. One great reason why he had not hung back was that he had felt strongly for a long time that they had not done enough to promote their principles, especially as re- garded their younger members. Mr. Pilcher then dealt with his subject in a very able manner, his remarks frequently being applauded. His first pro- position was, he said, that politics were to a nation what politics were to an individual. poli- tics were both a science and an art. When he had been twitted that Liberal rr9asures had not pro- duced the great results that had been prophesied, he had always replied that their measures had never had a fair trial, and that they had always been hin- d3red by the restrictions laid upon them by their opponents. The two main classes in this country were the aristocracy and the democracy. Bott, so far as the essenn of politics went, were agreed on the principle of government for the people. But when they came to tip art of politics they fol—ici that the aristocracy held that government she 'O. - be by the best, by the pick of the nation, and that they themselves were really the best. Bat this they might safely say, was the government of the worst. The government of the democracy was prac- tically the government of the people by the people, and by that government they had a far greater chance of fairness all round. (Applause.) After the address the President, several short speeches were made. Mr. S. Kenyon said that he was-glad to see so many people present, and spoke in terms of eulogy of the address that had been given by Mr. Pilcher. Mr. W.' Diggle and Mr. R. Roberts also spoke, and Mr. H. Whitham said that all present would be in accord with what the chairman had brought forward. Mr. 0-. Wallington and Mr. Sut- cliffe also made a few remarks on the subject dealt with by Mr. Pilcher, who was accorded a hearty vote of thanks, on the motion of Mr. Dun- bobbin, seconded by Mr. S. Barlow. After the tran- saction of a little routine business, including, as will be seen by OUr advertising columns, fixing on a subject for next week, the meeting was brought to a termination.

div.head: AN:" OBSERVER" CALUMNY REFUTED.
div.p: AN:" OBSERVER" CALUMNY REFUTED.

The following is'a copy of a letter which was sent last week for insertion in the "Warrington Ob- server" as a refutation of a gross calumny that had appeared in that journal. The Editor declined its insertion; he is evidently "a coward in his own esteem," and the truth is too much for him : To the Editor of the " Warrington Observer." AN "EXAMINER •' MIRACLE.

Sir,—Under the above heading, you last week printed a leading article which appeared in the "Warrington Examiner" on October 23, side by side with a leader taken from the "Eastern Morn- ing News" for October 20th. With the exception of one sentence, the leaders, as you pointed out, were identical; and, under the circumstances, I cannot profess to be surprised that you should, in the absence of any explanation, conclude that "the article from the Hull journal is copied word for word," particularly as that, is a sort of offence of which, it is well-known, you yourself have been pre- viously found guilty. Two blacks may not make one white, but, on the other hand, company in distress makes the trouble less. This being the case,l am almost sorry to have to disabuse your mind, and the minds of your readers, of the delusion you and they are, unner as to the article in the " Examiner" being "a miracle of paste and scissors," and copied word for word from the " Eastern Morning News." As a matter of fact, I have not at any time seen a copy of the "Eastern Morning News ;" and the simple explanation of the coincidence is that the leader in the "Examiner" was supplied, during an illness which incapacitated me from work, .by the same London Agency which furnishes leaders to the "Eastern Morning News." Through some misunder- standing, leader matter was sent to the" Examiner" which was written for daily papers, like the Hull , journal, whereas the articles which we desired to ' to have supplied to us were such as would be fur- nished to the weekly papers doing business with the Agency in question. You will perhaps see that there is a wide difference between stealing an article and paying for it as I have done. With regard to your " serious doubts as to• the authorship of the leading articles appear- ing in the Warrington Examiner," I may tell you that, previous to my recent breakdown in health, every line which has appeared in the edi- torial columns of the "Examiner," for the past two years and a half has been written by me. More than tiat, prior to this illness, I had for ten years, without the break of a single week, written on an average three leaders, or leaderettes each week. When you have reached such a record, and crept out of the glass house in which you reside, you will perhaps be less disposed to throw stones. Meantime I trust you will have the grace to apolo- gise for having stated that the article from the "Examiner," which you reprinted last week was copied from the "Eastern Morning News." Yours truly, THE EDITOR OF THE "WARRINGTON EXAMINER." Warrington, November 4th, 1886.

"HAPPY NED" IN COURTS At Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday morning, a woman named Margaret Kiliala, who lives at 3, Wainwright's Yard, Warrington, was charged on remand with stealing a purse contain- ing £4. The money was the property of a woman who also lives in Wainwright's Yard, who was de- ' scribed as Harriet Taylor, or Harmiston. She is, however, known by several names' the most com- mon of them being "Happy Ned." It is said that under this cognomen she, dressed in male attire, worked for several years in the dockyards at Liver- pool, and afterwards laboured in the same dress as a field hand in the neighbourhood of Warrington. She contrived to save money, and is now said to be in receipt of about a pound a week. The appear- ance of the prosecutrix, who is an elderly woman, caused some amusement in court, her style of dress being rather eccentric, as well as her mode of con- ducting herself. It was alleged against the prisoner that on the morning of Saturday, the 30th ultimo, at about eight o'clock, she went into the house of "Happy Ned," saying that she had nothing to eat. Prosecutrix gave her 2s. Gd., and told her to fetch a half-pint of beer. Prisoner did so, and handed over the change to the prosecutrix, who went to pur- chase some mutton chops. The meat was cooked and eaten, and later on prosecutrix accompanied prisoner to her house, where a pint of beer was sent for. The parties sat down by the fireside, and pri- soner, it was alleged, placed her arms round the prosecutrix, and said "I wish I had your purse. Our Johnnie has only made three days last week." Shortly afterwards prosecutrix went home, and then missed her purse, which contained two sovereigns and four half sovereigns. Constable Turner after- wards apprehended prisoner, who, when charged, replied "I have not done so," and later on she re- marked to the officer "You will find it (the purse) on me; it's all right." Prisoner was taken to the police station, and on being searched the money was not . found on her. In answer to the charge, she replied "I never got it. It will be found in her (prosecutrix's) own house."— No trace of the money could afterwards be found. On being called upon to give evidence prosecutrix said that she was a "poor afflicted person," but added "I am not poor exactly, I have a woman who lives with me as a companion."—Alderman Davies: What is your name? Prosecutrix : I never used my name. I never was christened. (Laughter.) They call me anything. My name is Elizabeth Har- i riett.—Alderman Davies: Elizabeth Harriett what? Prosecutrix: It is Urmston now, but it formerly was, in my younger days, Taylor. Well, this woman came into my house and turned me over in bed. She said she had nothing to eat, and I said "Oh, bless me, why didn't you tell me that before; go for a pint of bitter beer," and I fetched a pound of mut- ton chop. .We fried it and shared it, and she put 1 her arm round my neck and said "I will go for some more beer; I wish I had your purse." She went dut, and I have not seen the purse since.—The Mayor: -You say you didn't see her take it. Pro- , secutrix : Well, it couldn't have flown, and the cat wouldn't take it. honourable gentlemen. (Laugh- ter.)—Prisoner put several questions to the prose- cutrix, who, raising a stick, said she knew prisoner was a confounded thief.—Prisoner said she had not taken the money.—Prosecutrix : You are a thief, and if I had a revolver I would shoot you. I could find it in my heart to strike you. (Laughter.)— , The Mayor said there was no direct evidence on

which to convict the prisoner on the charge, al- though the magistrates believed she had stolen the money. She would be bound over in her own re- cognizance to appear when called upon.—Prosecu- trix thanked the Mayor for his expressions.—The Mayor: I am sorry that you have lost your money. —Prosecutrix : It is not the loss of the money, it is the dirty action. Such People ought to be Put out of the land. (Laughter.)—She then left the cou7t.

WARRINGTON. SUDDEN DEATH. -Sarah Lees Ashton (75), who resided with a married daughter in Folly-lane, died suddenly early on Monday morning. The cause of death is supposed to have been heart disease. TKE BRIDGE-STREET EXCAVATlONS.—Exeavations are still being made irf Bridge-street, and during the week some further portions of the outer wall of the ancient church have been uncovered, this latest discovery tending to give a more exact knowledge of the Size and shape of the edifice. GRAPPENHALL DRAMATIC SOCIETY.-011 Thurs- day evening the large room at Grappenhall was crowded on the occasion of the third performance given by the above society. Two farces were placed on the boards, Mr. 1.1( oods officiating as stage manager. The performance was very successful, :Le merits of the members of the company being hown to advantage. lIOLY TRINITY LITERARY AND DEBATING SOCIETY.. . —At the meeting of this Society on Monday even- ing, Mr. Felix Summers read a paper on "The good and the evil of vaccination," in which he spoke ad- versely of vaccination. In the debate which fol- lowed, however, there was a preponderance .of opinion expressed in favour of vaccination. A cor- dial vote of thanks was accorded Mr. Summers at the close.

THE WARRINGTON lIARRIERS.—Owing to the unfavourable weather on Saturday for cross-country running there was a poor muster, only six men putting in an appearance. The following members donned their jerseys, and had a very enjoyable run of about six miles :—G. Stokes, R. Sherlock, J. Bowen, H. Maddock, and A. and G. Ratcliffe. The above harriers will shortly have an inter-club run with the Wigan Harriers. LEGH-STREET PRIMITIVE METHODIST MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS.—On Monday evening the , third weekly meeting of the above class was held in the schoolroom, the Rev. J. Calvert, president, in the chair. An interesting and instructive paper was read by Mr. E. Williams on " Coal," tracing its origin and formation down to the present time, with a description of its different kinds and its uses. Nearly all the members took part in the dis- cussion, which was ably answered by Mr. Williams. There were upwards of 32 members present. A GOOD IDEA.—Mr. Thomas Greenwood, author of "Free Public Libraries," writes to the London papers stating that there could scarcely be a better way of celebrating her Majesty's Jubilee than by every parish in London adopting the Public Libra- ries. Act, and establishing for the use of its inhabi- tants a Free Library and Art Museum. The editor of our neutral contemporary has expressed similar views, and now that he is Mayor it is to be hoped he will do what he can towards making our library absolutely free to the inhabitants, FOOTBALL: WARRINGTON GRIMMAR SCHOOL V. MANCHESTER GRAMMAR SCHOOL.—This match was played on the Salford Football Club ground on Wednesday. The Warringtonians played their usual team, and Manchester Grammar School were strongly represented, Warrington started the scor- ing by a goal from a try by Scotson, and finally won by three goals (nine points) to a try (one point). In the latter part of the game Brundfett, having made a fair catch close to the half way line, Fisher took the place, and, to the surprise of all, kicked a magnificent goal. HAYNES'S Great Sale for only 21 Days is now on. Come early to secure targains.—.Advt. WYCLIFFE MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS.—On Tuesday evening a paper on "American Humour- ists " was read before the members of the above named class by Mr. J. Jones, 8.A., of Chorley. The Rev. J. Yonge presided, and there was a fair atten- dance. Mr. Jones gave sketches of the leading American homourists, such as Lowell, Bret Harte, Artemus Ward, Max Adler, and Mark Twain, anti gave selections from the writings of most of them, the readings from Max Adler and Mark Twain be- mg particularly successful. The paper was an ad- mirable one, Mr. Jones giving considerable promise as a lecturer and literary critic. WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.— The usual weekly meeting of this society was held on Wednesday evening. the Rev. J. Howell Jones occupying the chair. Mr. J. E. Richardson intro- duced the subject for discussion, "The civil list," in a carefully compiled paper, showing the vast ex- penditure of public money, some of which went in salaries to the aristocracy, for which there was no real services rendered. The essayist, whilst not in favour of a Republic, thought the time had come when Parliament should take the matter in hand, and greatly reduce some, and altogether abolish other payments, which come under the civil list. An interesting debate followed, in which Messrs. C. Plinston, W. 11. Butler, 11. Whatmough, J. Hor- ton, J. Toft, J, S. Green, W. Furness, and the Chair- man took part. THE PUBLIC lIALL.7-During the present week Mr. R. Mansell's London Company have been suc- cessful in their performances of the drama, "The Crimes of Paris,"• at the Public Hall. The drama is a sensational one, and has achieved an unusual popularity. All the parts are well filled by members of the company, some of /whom have fre- quently been called before the curtain by the plaudits of the audience. New and special scenery is introduced, and tends considerably to heighten the effect. The principal characters are represented as follows :—Mr. C. Melville, as Pepin Cardell, a detective; Mr. John Webb, as Devisnes, a demon; Mr. Norman Watts, as Jules Martel, an artisan; Mr. Edward Russell, as "The Dandy;" Mr. E. Sennett, as M. Pierre Pelport, a money lender; and Mr. W. E. Richardson, as Joshua John- son, a cockney. The piece will be again produced to-night (Saturday). COMPLIMENTING THE Ex - MAYO. —At the Borough Court, on Monday, Mr. A. Browne, solici- tor, addressing Alderman Harrison, said that he could not allow the opportunity to pass without congratulating him upon the satisfactory termina- tion of his three years' term of office as Chief Magistrate of the Borough. The assiduity and carefulness Alderman Harrison had given to the general cases that had been brought before him had been noticed by all, but more especially by ad- vocates practising in that Court. In reply, Alder- man Harrison thanked Mr. Browne for his ex- pressions of confidence, and approval of the course he had pursued as Chief Magistrate. If he had failed it was certainly not from inattention, and it had always been his desire to do what he con- ceivPd to be right and impartial. How far he had succeeded he could not tell, but it was gratifYing to receive such an expression of opinion on behalf of Mr. Browne and his brother solicitors practising in that Court. INDEPENDENT ORDER OF GOOD TEMPLARS. —The weekly entertainment of the Wesley Lodge was held on Saturday at the Sankey-street coffee- house. There was a very good attendance, and an excellent programme was given by the following members and friends :—Song Sister Grove, reading Brother Grove, song Sister Sheath, song Mr. P. Green, recitation Master Frain, song Brother Grif- fiths, reading Brother Frain, song Mr. Cottrell, song Brother Jackson, song Sister Gleaves, reading Bro. Grove, song Mr. P. Green. A very pleasant evening was brought to a close with a vote of thanks to the chairman, Brother William Grove, p.w.C.T., and Brother Stacy for his address on temperance.—The monthly penny entertainment of the above lodge was held in the Mission-room, Academy-street, an Monday, Mr. John Kneen in the chair. There was an excellent attendance, the following Programme being given in good style by members of the juven- ile temple and friends :—Glee "Look not upon the wine," juvenile choir; recitation Brother C. Sheath, song "The Christian martyr," Brother Grove; duet "The echo," Misses . WYCLIFFE CHLTECIL—In Wycliffe Congregational Church, on Sunday evening, the Rev. J. Yonge preached a special sermon on "The Real Presence at, not in, the Lord's Supper." There was a large congregation.

"-ANTS AND THEIR WAYS." —On Wednesday evening Mr. H. Burns, of Liverpool, gave an in- teresting lecture on " Ants and their Ways," in the Wesleyan School-room, at Penketh, in connection with the Mutual Improvement Association. There was a very good attendance. The chair was taken by Mr. R. Garnett, J.P., who, prior to introducing the lecturer, remarked that Solomon said, "Go to the ant, thou sluggard." He had, he remarked, known persons in Warrington who went to their "uncle," but he did not think that their "uncle" was very friendly to them. (Laughter.) He then called upon Mr. Burns to give his lecture. The lec- turer, who was received with applause, prefaced his paper with a few interesting remarks on ants and their habits. He showed how the ants had great intelligence, and conducted their communities in a most orderly manner, and, by magic lantern illus- trations, gave additional force to his remarks. The

lecture was an exceedingly interesting one, and, being also instructive, gained general approbation. The illustrations, in which the movements of live ants were very clearly depictetl on the screen, met w!th great favour, and were much appreciated by the audience. Mr. Comersall proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Burns. lie felt, he said, a little diffi- culty in doing so, as be was not connected with that useful society, but if he could make any return for the kindness that the society had done him in inviting him to the lecture that evening he should be glad to do so. The lecture had been a great pleasure to him. Ile thought that if anybody wanted to make a name in natural history, or any- thing else, they would have to be a specialist. The time for generalities had passed. Mr. Burns had taken up a subject and mastered it, and he hoped they would all take up some particular subject and study it, so that they might come before the world in a way like the lecturer had done. Mr. Watson seconded the proposition, which was supported by Mr. C. E. Parker, and carried with enthusiasm. Afterwards, those present had the pleasure of view- ing a number of live ants, which had been brought to the meeting by the lecturer.
Whilst some men were enKaged on a new sewer near the Midland railway station, Hereford, on Saturday, a quantity of earth fell, crushing a young man named Thos. Johnson to death.
The Queen, accompanied by Princesq Beatrice, Prince Henry of B atenberg, and suite, arrived at Windsor, on Saturday, from Edinburgh, at a quarter-past nine, being ten minutes late.

Sir Edward Guinness has presented three months' salary tk) each member of his commercial staff and one month's wages to each dravman and tankman. The amount of the gift is £50,000. A mass meeting of the unemployed of Glasgow was held on Monday, on the Green, at Nelson's column. ft was agreed to wait upon the Lord Provost to ascertain what measures the city authorilies purpose taking to relieve the starving unemployed during the winter.
